title: Does a Language Server Save Tokens for Coding Agents? A Measurement Methodology and Preliminary Study
summary: Coding agents spend most of their context budget on retrieval. Lexical retrieval (grep) is universal, instant, and zero-setup, but noisy: it cannot tell a definition from a call from a comment. Semantic retrieval via the Language Server Protocol (LSP) is precise and typed, but needs a running, indexed server and pays a per-symbol round-trip. The claim that semantic retrieval is more token-efficient is, we find, asserted almost everywhere and measured almost nowhere: no public source isolates the LSP-vs-lexical token delta for an agent at equal task-success. This paper formalizes the question with one metric (tokens-to-success), specifies a five-arm ablation isolating semantic retrieval from confounds, maps three pre-stated failure modes onto measurable variables, and reports a preliminary study (Python and TypeScript repos; Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5). The answer is conditional and usually negative. On symbol-named localization the LSP costs tokens (+6% to +118%) and the agent ignores it when free. On reference-completeness it buys precision but not token savings and cannot raise the recall ceiling set by agent thoroughness; it saves tokens only for the weakest model. Tool choice is task-dependent: models default to grep on localization (0-6% semantic use) but reach for the LSP about half the time on reference tasks, unprompted. On edits scored by real test execution the gap is starkest: grep solves multi-file renames perfectly, a location-only LSP fails three-quarters of them by missing a call site, and even a complete, index-warmed, text-enriched LSP (each reference's line inline, as production LSP-MCP servers do) recovers most of the gap but cannot close it, since a rename must touch comments and strings that semantic references exclude. The implication is not LSP-always but an adaptive router keyed on task class, model capability, and lexical noise.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether semantic code retrieval via LSP is actually more token-efficient than simple lexical grep for coding agents, and finds that this common assumption is usually false or at least strongly task- and model-dependent.
AI.motivation: Most coding agents heavily rely on retrieval and there is a widespread but weakly evidenced belief that semantic retrieval (via LSP) is more token-efficient and thus preferable to lexical grep. However, no public work isolates and measures the token difference between LSP and lexical retrieval at equal task success, leaving tool choices largely based on intuition rather than data.
AI.method: The authors formalize a metric called tokens-to-success and design a five-arm ablation that isolates the effect of semantic (LSP) retrieval from other confounding factors. They predefine several hypothesized failure modes and map them to measurable variables. Using multiple real-world Python and TypeScript repositories, they run coding agents (Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5) under different retrieval setups (pure grep, various LSP configurations, and hybrids) and compare token usage and success across localization, reference-completeness, and editing tasks.
AI.result: For symbol localization tasks, LSP-based retrieval consistently consumes more tokens (from +6% up to +118%) and is often ignored by agents when they are free to choose tools. For reference-completeness tasks, LSP improves precision but does not reduce tokens overall and cannot surpass the recall limit imposed by the model’s own thoroughness; token savings only appear for the weakest model. Tool usage behavior is task-dependent: models overwhelmingly choose grep for localization (0–6% LSP usage) but call LSP around half the time on reference tasks without explicit prompting. On realistic multi-file edit tasks evaluated via actual test execution, grep alone solves multi-file renames reliably, while a location-only LSP misses about three-quarters of cases due to overlooked call sites. Even an enhanced, warmed, text-enriched LSP configuration recovers much of this deficit but still fails to match grep, because semantic references exclude comments and strings that must also be renamed.
AI.conclusion: The common wisdom that semantic LSP retrieval is categorically more token-efficient than lexical grep is not supported by these experiments. Instead, the optimal retrieval strategy is conditional on task type, model capability, and lexical noise. LSP is not a universal upgrade; a more effective design is an adaptive routing policy that dynamically chooses between lexical and semantic retrieval (or combinations thereof) based on the problem being solved, the model’s strengths, and the characteristics of the codebase.

title: Think in Latent, Explain in Language: Self-Explainable Latent Reasoning
summary: Latent reasoning has emerged as a powerful alternative to text-based Chain-of-Thought (CoT), offering significant gains in computational efficiency by compressing verbose reasoning into compact embeddings. However, compressing reasoning into the latent space renders the thinking opaque, hindering its interpretability. Current methods present a stark trade-off: they either function as unexplainable ''black boxes'' (e.g., Coconut), where the latent reasoning is not human-readable, or rely on separate post-hoc decoders for explainability (e.g., Heima), introducing architectural overhead and decoupling the explanation from the actual reasoning process. In this work, we present a unified framework for Self-Explainable Latent Reasoning (SELR) that trains a single model to perform efficient and inherently explainable latent reasoning. Our core contribution is a novel multi-task training objective that optimizes for two goals simultaneously: (1) an Answer Loss that optimizes the latent reasoning trajectory to produce accurate final answers, and (2) a CoT Loss that explicitly trains the same model to decode its own latent representations back into human-understandable reasoning steps. This design ensures that generated latent representations are both task-effective and semantically interpretable, eliminating the need for external decoders. We validate the effectiveness of SELR on both Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), demonstrating that SELR achieves superior token efficiency and accuracy compared to baselines, while uniquely providing self-contained explainability without auxiliary models. Project page is available at https://jasondayuan.github.io/SELR/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SELR, a self-explainable latent reasoning framework that keeps the efficiency of latent reasoning while making the internal reasoning process human-interpretable, without separate decoders.
AI.motivation: Latent reasoning compresses reasoning into embeddings and is more token-efficient than text-based Chain-of-Thought, but it becomes opaque and non-interpretable. Existing approaches are either black-box or require additional post-hoc decoders, leading to architectural complexity and a disconnect between reasoning and explanation. The authors aim to remove this trade-off by designing a method that is both efficient and inherently interpretable.
AI.method: They introduce Self-Explainable Latent Reasoning (SELR), a unified framework trained with a multi-task objective using a single model. The model is optimized with: (1) an Answer Loss that shapes the latent reasoning trajectory to yield correct answers, and (2) a CoT Loss that trains the same model to decode its own latent representations into natural language reasoning steps. This joint training encourages latent states to be simultaneously task-effective and semantically meaningful, avoiding any need for external decoders. The framework is instantiated and evaluated on both LLMs and VLMs.
AI.result: Across language-only and vision-language tasks, SELR outperforms baseline methods (such as Coconut and Heima variants) in both token efficiency and answer accuracy. It uniquely maintains or improves performance while also providing human-readable explanations directly from the model, without auxiliary decoding models.
AI.conclusion: SELR demonstrates that latent reasoning can be both efficient and self-explainable when a single model is trained under a joint answer-and-explanation objective. By aligning latent representations with Chain-of-Thought-style decodings, the method removes the black-box nature of previous latent reasoning approaches and eliminates the need for separate explanation modules, making it a practical and interpretable alternative for both LLMs and VLMs.

title: Not All Tokens Are Equal: Inflation-Aware Routing for Agentic LLM Systems
summary: When a language model fails to answer a query on the first attempt, an agentic system retries, consuming additional tokens each time. This retry overhead creates a gap between what a model's per-token price implies and what a full workflow actually costs. We call this gap \emph{token inflation} and define it as the ratio of true workflow cost to single-call cost. Systems like FrugalGPT route based on the latter, which can underestimate real cost by more than $2\times$ on difficult tasks. We address this with InflationAgent, a four-stage router that (1) measures token inflation systematically across model tiers and task types, finding inflation as high as $4.25\times$ for a 7B model on multi-hop question answering; (2) introduces CoT Branching Entropy (CBE), a pre-execution difficulty signal computed entirely from local inference, which predicts high inflation with AUROC 0.887; and (3) selects models by maximizing a Semantic Exchange Rate (SER) that divides expected accuracy by predicted true cost, with a fresh-escalation policy that discards failed chains before routing to a stronger model. On GSM8K under a fixed budget, InflationAgent achieves 94.7\% accuracy versus 91.0\% for FrugalGPT while using 31\% fewer tokens, and we show that forwarding a failed reasoning chain to GPT-4o reduces its accuracy by up to 34.8 percentage points, validating the fresh-escalation design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and studies “token inflation” – the extra token cost incurred by multi-step/agentic LLM workflows compared to a single model call – and proposes InflationAgent, a routing framework that selects models using an inflation-aware cost–accuracy trade-off signal.
AI.motivation: Existing cost-aware routing systems (e.g., FrugalGPT) assume the cost of serving a query is close to the per-token price of a single LLM call. In multi-step or agentic setups, queries often require retries, escalating to stronger models, or long chains-of-thought, which significantly increase the total tokens used. This unaccounted “retry overhead” means that current routing policies underestimate real costs, misallocate queries across model tiers, and can be suboptimal in both spending and accuracy on harder tasks. There is a need to formally characterize this overhead, predict when it will be large, and design routing strategies that explicitly optimize for true, inflation-adjusted cost rather than nominal per-token prices.
AI.method: 1) Define token inflation as the ratio between the actual token cost of a full workflow (including retries/escalations) and the cost of a single call to the chosen model. Empirically measure token inflation across different model sizes (tiers) and task types (e.g., multi-hop QA, math word problems) using agentic workflows. 2) Propose CoT Branching Entropy (CBE), a pre-execution difficulty signal derived only from local inference: it measures the entropy/branching in chain-of-thought reasoning to estimate whether a query is likely to induce high inflation (many retries/steps). Train or calibrate a predictor that maps CBE to expected inflation, reporting AUROC as a detection metric. 3) Design InflationAgent, a four-stage routing framework that uses predicted inflation and model accuracies to compute a Semantic Exchange Rate (SER) for each candidate model, defined as expected accuracy divided by predicted true cost. Incorporate a fresh-escalation policy: when escalating to a stronger model after a failure, discard the previous reasoning chain instead of reusing or forwarding it. Route each query to the model tier that maximizes SER under a given budget constraint.
AI.result: Empirical studies show token inflation can be substantial: up to 4.25× for a 7B model on multi-hop question answering, and more than 2× underestimation of real costs for difficult tasks when using naive per-token routing. The proposed CBE metric is an effective predictor of high-inflation queries, with an AUROC of 0.887. On GSM8K under a fixed token budget, the InflationAgent routing policy attains 94.7% accuracy while using 31% fewer tokens than FrugalGPT, which achieves 91.0% accuracy under the same conditions. Experiments also demonstrate that forwarding a failed reasoning chain to a stronger model (GPT-4o) can reduce its accuracy by up to 34.8 percentage points, empirically supporting the fresh-escalation strategy of discarding prior chains before escalation.
AI.conclusion: Token inflation is a significant and previously under-accounted factor in the real cost of agentic LLM workflows, especially on hard reasoning tasks. By explicitly modeling and predicting inflation, systems can make better budget-aware routing decisions that improve both accuracy and cost-efficiency relative to prior methods that consider only nominal per-token prices. CoT Branching Entropy provides a practical, locally-computable signal for identifying high-inflation queries, and the Semantic Exchange Rate–based routing with fresh escalation leads to substantial gains on benchmarks like GSM8K. The work suggests that future cost-optimized LLM systems should reason about the full workflow’s expected cost, not just single-call model pricing, and avoid naively reusing failed reasoning chains when escalating to stronger models.

title: BCMT: Blockwise Causal Memory Transformer
summary: Transformer architectures rely on dense self-attention to model long-range dependencies, but this mechanism exhibits quadratic complexity with respect to sequence length. We introduce BCMT (Blockwise Causal Memory Transformer), an architecture for long-context language modeling that decouples local token interactions from global context propagation. Dense causal self-attention is applied independently within local blocks, while each block produces an adaptive summary aggregated through an exponential causal memory. This memory is subsequently injected back into the token representations, enabling efficient propagation of long-range contextual information without relying on explicit global attention. Unlike standard Transformers and recurrent memory architectures, BCMT maintains neither dense interactions between distant tokens nor learned memory states. Its memory mechanism is fully parallelizable and remains compatible with standard implementations of dense self-attention. Experiments on language modeling with context lengths of up to 1024 tokens show that BCMT achieves validation performance comparable to that of Dense Transformers while significantly improving training throughput and reducing memory consumption. An ablation study further confirms that these improvements arise from the proposed memory mechanism. These results demonstrate that an exponential causal memory constructed from block summaries provides an effective alternative to dense global attention mechanisms for long-context language modeling.

AI.tldr: BCMT (Blockwise Causal Memory Transformer) replaces global dense self-attention with local blockwise attention plus an exponential causal memory over block summaries, matching dense Transformers’ performance on 1K-token language modeling while being more efficient in training speed and memory use.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers use dense self-attention, whose quadratic complexity in sequence length makes long-context language modeling computationally expensive and memory intensive. Existing recurrent memory variants often require maintaining learned memory states or dense cross-token interactions, limiting scalability and parallelism. The paper aims to design an architecture that preserves strong long-range modeling ability while reducing computational and memory costs and remaining compatible with standard Transformer implementations.
AI.method: The authors propose BCMT, which partitions sequences into local blocks and applies standard dense causal self-attention only within each block. Each block then computes an adaptive summary representation. These summaries are aggregated along the sequence using an exponential causal memory mechanism that propagates information forward in time in a parallelizable way. The resulting memory is then injected back into token-level representations, allowing tokens to benefit from long-range context without explicit global self-attention. The design avoids maintaining explicit recurrent states and preserves compatibility with existing dense-attention infrastructure.
AI.result: On language modeling tasks with context lengths up to 1024 tokens, BCMT achieves validation perplexity comparable to or matching standard dense Transformers. At the same time, it offers significantly higher training throughput and reduced GPU memory consumption. An ablation study shows that removing or changing the proposed exponential causal memory degrades performance or efficiency, demonstrating that the memory mechanism is central to the gains observed.
AI.conclusion: An exponential causal memory built over blockwise token summaries can substitute for dense global self-attention in long-context language modeling, maintaining model quality while improving computational and memory efficiency. BCMT thus provides a practical, parallelizable alternative to dense Transformers and recurrent memory architectures for scaling to longer contexts, without requiring learned persistent memory states or complex new attention kernels.

title: Inducing Reward-Free Judging Rubrics that Reduce Over-Crediting in Agent Evaluation
summary: Evaluating language-model agents at scale increasingly relies on a second language model as an automatic judge, because the gold signal, an executable environment reward, is expensive, slow, or unavailable at deployment time. Such a judge is a reward-free proxy whose value depends on whether it can be trusted, yet existing judges either hand-write the scoring rubric, as in G-Eval, or fine-tune the judge's weights, and both tend to credit fluent but unsuccessful trajectories as successes. We instead induce the text of an agent-judging rubric from a small set of ground-truth-labeled trajectories, grounding it in true outcomes. We present RubricForge, which evolves a judge rubric by reflective evolution against labeled trajectories to maximize agreement with the environment reward, freezes it, and applies it to held-out trajectories in one model call with no environment access. The optimized artifact is human-readable text, so every verdict is attributable to named criteria. Using one frozen 7B model as both agent and judge, on tau-bench (173 labeled trajectories drawn from 220 rollouts) and WebShop (160), the principal gain is faithfulness rather than raw agreement. The edge over a generic G-Eval judge is not statistically significant (McNemar p = 0.248), and absolute-score calibration marginally favors the generic judge (|err| difference -0.048, p = 2x10^-4). Yet RubricForge over-credits failed trajectories roughly half as often (0.115 vs. 0.173 false-pass rate on tau-bench, with three over-credit catches and zero reversals) and ranks graded WebShop outcomes more faithfully (Spearman 0.410 vs. 0.370). For a reward-free evaluator the false-pass rate, not aggregate agreement, is the deployment-relevant quantity, since a false pass ships a broken agent whereas a false fail merely costs a retry.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RubricForge, a method for automatically inducing human-readable rubrics that let a language model reliably judge other language-model agents without direct access to environment rewards.
AI.motivation: Current large-scale evaluation of language-model agents often uses another language model as an automatic judge because running full environment-based evaluations is costly or impossible at deployment. However, existing judges either rely on hand-crafted rubrics or fine-tuned models, both of which tend to be misled by fluent but actually unsuccessful trajectories, leading to untrustworthy evaluations. There is a need for a reward-free evaluation method that is more faithful to true task success, especially minimizing the risk of incorrectly approving failed agents.
AI.method: RubricForge starts from a small set of trajectories labeled with ground-truth environment rewards. It then uses a process of reflective evolution to induce and iteratively refine a textual scoring rubric that best agrees with those true outcomes. Once optimized, the rubric is frozen and used by a language model judge to score unseen trajectories in a single model call, without any further environment interaction. The rubric is fully human-readable and decomposes judgments into explicit, named criteria, making decisions interpretable and attributable.
AI.result: Using a single frozen 7B model as both the agent and the judge, RubricForge is evaluated on tau-bench (173 labeled trajectories from 220 rollouts) and WebShop (160 trajectories). Compared to a generic G-Eval judge, RubricForge does not show a statistically significant improvement in overall agreement with environment rewards (McNemar p = 0.248) and is slightly worse in absolute score calibration (|error| difference -0.048, p = 2×10^-4). However, RubricForge substantially reduces the false-pass rate—over-crediting failed trajectories—on tau-bench (0.115 vs. 0.173), with three instances where it correctly denies credit that G-Eval misassigns and no opposite reversals. It also produces more faithful rankings of WebShop outcomes (Spearman 0.410 vs. 0.370).
AI.conclusion: RubricForge demonstrates that inducing a human-readable rubric from a small set of ground-truth-labeled trajectories can make reward-free language-model judges more faithful to actual task success, especially by reducing false passes of failed agents. While aggregate agreement and calibration are similar or slightly favor generic judges, the deployment-critical metric is the false-pass rate: a false pass can deploy a broken agent, whereas a false fail only incurs additional evaluation or retries. Thus, rubric induction grounded in outcomes offers a more trustworthy evaluation strategy for language-model agents in practice.

title: Jais 2: A Family of Arabic-Centric Open Large Language Models
summary: Jais 2 is a family of Arabic-centric large language models developed jointly by MBZUAI, Cerebras, and Inception, designed to advance Arabic-centric language modeling, with strong performance across the Arabic and culturally grounded benchmarks evaluated in this report. The family includes, to our knowledge, the largest open Arabic-centric LLM trained from scratch at 70B parameters, and a competitive 8B-parameter variant among the evaluated open models. A custom Arabic-centric vocabulary enables efficient training and inference. In addition, an optimized architecture and training recipe yield highly compute-efficient training. With a substantially smaller token budget than comparable models, Jais 2 achieves strong Arabic performance on the benchmarks considered in this report and competitive English results. The models obtain leading results among the evaluated open models on OALL2 and AraGen. They also perform strongly on several culturally grounded Arabic benchmarks, including poetry, religion, cuisine, and dream interpretation, as well as in general tasks such as translation and summarization. We release the models in HuggingFace under a commercially permissive license. Jais 2 70B is also released as a chat app on the Web, iOS, and Android; it runs on Cerebras hardware, delivering up to 2,000 tokens per second, and enabling high-throughput Arabic-centric chat serving in our deployment setting. By uniting scale, linguistic diversity, cultural fidelity, openness, and speed, Jais 2 provides an open-weight foundation intended to support further research and development in Arabic-centric LLMs.

AI.tldr: Jais 2 introduces a family of large, Arabic‑centric language models (up to 70B parameters) that achieve state-of-the-art performance on several Arabic and culturally grounded benchmarks while remaining competitive in English, and are released openly with a commercially permissive license.
AI.motivation: Most existing large language models are optimized for English and only secondarily support Arabic, leading to weaker performance, limited cultural grounding, and fewer open, production-ready models for Arabic speakers and applications. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating powerful, open-weight LLMs that prioritize Arabic language and culture while still performing well in English.
AI.method: The authors train a family of LLMs from scratch with parameter sizes up to 70B, using a custom Arabic-centric tokenizer/vocabulary to better capture Arabic morphology and usage. They adopt an optimized architecture and training recipe focused on compute efficiency, allowing strong performance with a smaller token budget than comparable models. They systematically evaluate the models on a mix of general-purpose (e.g., translation, summarization) and culturally grounded Arabic benchmarks (e.g., poetry, religion, cuisine, dream interpretation) as well as Arabic/English benchmarks like OALL2 and AraGen. They also deploy the 70B model as a high-throughput chat system on Cerebras hardware to validate serving performance (up to 2,000 tokens/s).
AI.result: The Jais 2 models achieve leading results among evaluated open models on OALL2 and AraGen and strong performance on multiple culturally grounded Arabic benchmarks, while maintaining competitive English performance. The compute-efficient training setup attains these results with fewer training tokens than other models of similar scale. In deployment, the 70B chat model runs on Cerebras hardware with high generation speed (up to 2,000 tokens per second), enabling large-scale Arabic-centric chat services.
AI.conclusion: Jais 2 demonstrates that an Arabic-centric, open-weight LLM family—equipped with a tailored vocabulary, efficient training recipe, and large-scale deployment—can deliver state-of-the-art results on Arabic and culturally grounded tasks while remaining competitive in English. By releasing the models, weights, and a fast chat deployment, the work establishes a strong, open foundation intended to spur further research and practical applications in Arabic-centric language modeling.

title: Depth-Aware Sensitivity Analysis of Mixture-of-Experts Models via Magnitude-Based Expert Masking
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale large language models (LLMs) while preserving computational efficiency through sparse activation. Despite their widespread adoption, the relative importance of individual MoE layers remains insufficiently characterized, particularly for model compression. This paper presents a systematic layer-wise sensitivity analysis of the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model (40 MoE layers, 256 experts per layer, top-8 routing) using magnitude-based expert masking on the XLCoST cross-lingual code translation benchmark. We conduct a multi-phase study spanning 100, 300, and 500 prompt evaluation scales across three H100 GPU servers. Our central finding is that layer sensitivity is strongly depth-dependent: early layers (0-9) and middle layers (10-29) are highly fragile to expert masking, while late layers (30-39), and especially very-late layers (35-39), tolerate aggressive masking of low-magnitude experts. Flat all-layer masking at 30% retains only 150/300 Good+Similar outputs at 300-prompt scale, whereas late-focused policies retain 249-255/300 while masking 640-1,145 experts. On a later 500-prompt held-out validation slice, the narrow very-late policy (layers 35-39 @ 50%) achieves the strongest quality/masked-expert tradeoff among tested candidates, retaining 419/500 Good+Similar outputs while masking only 640 of 10,240 total experts. We additionally characterize top-k routing width reduction from 8 to 6 active experts per token, which shows a large observed wall-clock reduction on a 100-prompt probe with no Good+Similar loss, though it does not yet compose cleanly with aggressive expert masking. These findings provide an empirical foundation for depth-aware MoE expert masking and establish a practical path toward physical weight surgery, activation-based expert scoring, and training-based recovery.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes which layers in a large Mixture-of-Experts language model are more or less sensitive to pruning experts, finding that late MoE layers can be heavily masked with minimal quality loss, enabling depth-aware compression strategies.
AI.motivation: Mixture-of-Experts LLMs use many experts but activate only a few per token, providing computational efficiency but leaving models with very large parameter counts. For deployment, it is important to compress these models without hurting quality. However, it is unclear which MoE layers are safe to prune and how layer depth affects sensitivity to expert masking, especially in a realistic cross-lingual code translation setting. The paper aims to systematically quantify layer-wise sensitivity to guide practical compression policies.
AI.method: The authors study the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE model (40 MoE layers, 256 experts each, top-8 routing) on the XLCoST cross-lingual code translation benchmark. They apply magnitude-based expert masking (disabling low-magnitude experts) according to different policies: flat masking across all layers and depth-aware policies that concentrate masking on late or very late layers. They run a multi-phase evaluation at scales of 100, 300, and 500 prompts on H100 GPUs, measuring the number of outputs classified as Good+Similar under each masking configuration. They also experiment with reducing the routing width from 8 to 6 experts per token and measure wall-clock speed and quality changes.
AI.result: They find a strong depth dependence of sensitivity to masking: early (layers 0-9) and middle layers (10-29) are fragile and lose quality when experts are masked, while late (30-39), especially very late (35-39), layers can be aggressively masked with little performance loss. A flat 30% all-layer masking retains only 150/300 Good+Similar outputs, whereas late-focused policies retain 249-255/300 while masking 640–1,145 experts. On a 500-prompt held-out set, masking 50% of experts in only layers 35-39 preserves 419/500 Good+Similar outputs while removing 640 of 10,240 experts. Reducing top-k routing from 8 to 6 experts per token yields significant wall-clock speedups on a 100-prompt probe with no observed Good+Similar degradation, but this change interacts poorly with aggressive masking.
AI.conclusion: Layer sensitivity in MoE LLMs is highly depth-dependent, and late MoE layers, particularly the very last ones, are promising targets for substantial expert masking with limited quality loss. Depth-aware masking strategies dramatically outperform flat masking in quality/parameter tradeoffs. These insights can guide practical model compression techniques such as permanent parameter pruning (weight surgery), more informed activation-based expert scoring, and potential fine-tuning strategies to recover from pruning. Routing width reduction also shows promise as an orthogonal efficiency lever but requires further study to combine effectively with heavy masking.

title: IterCOMP: Reasoning-aware Adaptive Prompt Compression for Multi-hop Question Answering
summary: Multi-hop question answering requires complex reasoning across multiple evidence segments, which often overwhelms retrieval-augmented generation systems with lengthy and noisy contexts, thereby undermining both efficiency and accuracy. While existing prompt compression methods attempt to address this issue, they are typically designed for single-turn queries and fail to capture interdependent reasoning steps. We propose IterCOMP, a unified, training-free prompt compression framework that incorporates multi-hop reasoning within an iterative compression loop. IterCOMP decomposes documents into evidence segments, evaluates question answerability, and generates targeted follow-up questions to iteratively integrate essential evidence, producing a compact, reasoning-oriented prompt. Experiments on MusiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA demonstrate that IterCOMP achieves substantial improvements in Exact Match and F1 scores while reducing the token budget, outperforming existing baselines and exhibiting robustness as reasoning complexity increases.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IterCOMP, a training-free, iterative prompt compression framework for multi-hop question answering that improves accuracy and efficiency by constructing compact, reasoning-focused prompts.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation systems for multi-hop QA struggle with long, noisy contexts that hurt both performance and efficiency. Existing prompt compression methods are single-turn and do not model interdependent reasoning steps, making them ill-suited for multi-hop reasoning scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose IterCOMP, an iterative prompt compression loop. It first decomposes documents into smaller evidence segments, then repeatedly: (1) checks whether the current context is sufficient to answer the question, and (2) if not, generates focused follow-up questions to retrieve and integrate only essential additional evidence. This process yields a compact prompt explicitly oriented around multi-step reasoning without requiring model fine-tuning.
AI.result: On three multi-hop QA benchmarks—MusiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA—IterCOMP substantially improves Exact Match and F1 scores compared to prior methods, while also reducing the token budget. It remains robust or even improves as the reasoning depth and complexity of questions increase, outperforming existing prompt compression baselines.
AI.conclusion: IterCOMP effectively addresses the challenge of noisy, overlong contexts in multi-hop QA by embedding multi-hop reasoning into an iterative compression framework. It delivers better accuracy and efficiency than existing approaches, and scales well as reasoning complexity grows, suggesting it is a practical, training-free solution for advanced retrieval-augmented QA systems.

title: Modular Cognitive Architecture Emerges in Large Language Models
summary: The human brain exhibits a striking degree of functional specialization, with distinct networks supporting language, formal reasoning, reasoning about other minds, and reasoning about the physical world. Is this modular organization a fundamental principle of how intelligent systems must be built, or an evolutionary accident specific to biological brains? Here, we test whether a similar organization emerges in Large Language Models--another class of intelligent systems created through a very different optimization process. Using circuit analyses across N=46 tasks spanning four cognitive domains (language, formal reasoning, social reasoning, physical reasoning), we find that LLMs develop a modular architecture that mirrors the human brain: tasks drawing on the same network in humans recruit overlapping neurons in LLMs, whereas tasks drawing on different networks recruit distinct neurons. The convergent emergence of modularity in brains and neural networks suggests that it may be a fundamental property of intelligent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether modular functional organization, like that seen in the human brain, also emerges in large language models (LLMs), and finds strong parallels across four cognitive domains.
AI.motivation: Human brains show clear modularity, with different neural networks specialized for language, formal reasoning, social reasoning, and physical reasoning. It is unknown whether this modularity is a general principle of intelligence or just a biological quirk. Large Language Models are intelligent systems trained via very different processes, so they provide a testbed for whether similar modular organization emerges independently.
AI.method: The authors perform circuit-level analyses of LLMs across 46 tasks that span four cognitive domains: language, formal reasoning, social reasoning, and physical reasoning. They identify which neurons are recruited by each task and compare overlap patterns: tasks that rely on the same network in the human brain versus tasks that rely on different brain networks.
AI.result: They find that LLMs exhibit modular organization analogous to that in the human brain. Tasks that in humans draw on the same functional network tend to activate overlapping sets of neurons in the LLM, while tasks associated with different brain networks engage largely distinct neuron subsets.
AI.conclusion: The similar modular structure found in both human brains and LLMs, despite their very different origins and training processes, suggests that modularity is not merely an evolutionary accident but may be a fundamental property of intelligent systems.

title: Measuring Fairness in Large Audio Language Models via Semantic-Aware Bias Estimation
summary: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) have seen increasing use for audio understanding tasks such as speech recognition and audio question answering, raising concerns about fairness across demographic subgroups. Fairness evaluation in spoken-input settings is challenging due to confounding factors, including semantic variation in spoken content and speaker-specific characteristics. Ignoring these factors can result in misleading conclusions about model bias. We propose a semantic-aware mixed-effects regression framework for fairness evaluation in LALMs that explicitly accounts for these confounders. Our approach incorporates sentence-level semantic embeddings of reference text as covariates and models speaker identity as a random effect. Notably, semantic representations are extracted from the same LALM under evaluation, enabling semantic control over variation as perceived by the model itself. Experiments on simulated data and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach substantially reduces spurious fairness findings and yields more robust and interpretable estimates of subgroup performance differences.

AI.tldr: They introduce a new, statistically principled way to measure fairness of Large Audio Language Models by controlling for semantic content and speaker identity, making subgroup performance comparisons more reliable.
AI.motivation: Current fairness evaluations for LALMs can be misleading because performance differences between demographic groups may be driven by confounding factors like differences in what is being said (semantics) or who is speaking (speaker characteristics), not actual bias of the model. There is a need for an evaluation framework that can disentangle true subgroup bias from these confounders.
AI.method: They propose a semantic-aware mixed-effects regression framework. Sentence-level semantic embeddings of the reference text are included as covariates, and speaker identity is modeled as a random effect. Crucially, the semantic embeddings are extracted from the same LALM being evaluated, so the control is aligned with the model’s own representation space. The framework is applied to both simulated and real-world datasets for tasks such as speech recognition and audio question answering.
AI.result: On both synthetic and real benchmarks, the method significantly reduces apparent but spurious fairness disparities that arise when confounders are ignored. It provides more stable and interpretable estimates of performance gaps across demographic subgroups.
AI.conclusion: Accounting explicitly for semantic variation and speaker identity via mixed-effects regression yields a more accurate and interpretable assessment of fairness in LALMs. Using embeddings from the evaluated model itself enables semantic control that reflects the model’s own perception, leading to more trustworthy subgroup comparisons and reducing false alarms about bias.

title: A Year in LLM Serving: Workload Evolution, Caching and Load-Balancing
summary:
Large Language Model (LLM) serving has become a critical cloud workload, and realistic traces are essential for motivating and benchmarking serving systems. However, existing LLM serving workload studies remain limited in scale and scope. They often observe short time periods and provide limited visibility into how users interact with models in production. As a result, they do not fully capture how LLM serving workloads evolve over time or how user-model interactions shape production traffic.
  In this work, we further the understanding of real-world LLM serving workloads through both a global characterization and a longitudinal study of a one-year production trace from Chutes. Unlike prior studies, our trace captures full production behavior across many models and users, including both popular and long-tail models. We analyze the workload from aggregate, temporal, model-level, and user-level perspectives, revealing workload evolution and user-model structure that are typically hidden behind aggregate views. To support future research, we will release the full one-year trace with the paper, enabling downstream studies of production behavior without relying on sampled or synthetically generated workloads.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a one-year, large-scale production trace of LLM serving workloads to reveal how real users interact with many different models over time, and releases the trace for the community.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM serving workload studies are small-scale, short-term, and provide only coarse aggregate views, so they miss how workloads evolve and how real user–model interactions shape production traffic. Realistic, large, and long-duration traces are needed to design, motivate, and benchmark serving systems effectively.
AI.method: Collect and analyze a one-year production trace from the Chutes LLM serving platform, covering many models (popular and long-tail) and users. Perform a global characterization and longitudinal study from multiple viewpoints: aggregate, temporal, model-level, and user-level, to uncover evolution patterns and structural properties of the workload.
AI.result: The analysis exposes temporal evolution of LLM workloads and rich structure in user–model interactions that are not visible from aggregate statistics alone. It shows differences between popular and long-tail models and how traffic patterns and user behavior change over time, providing detailed empirical insights missing from prior work.
AI.conclusion: Real-world LLM serving workloads are complex, evolving, and structured at the model and user levels in ways that aggregate and short-term studies cannot capture. Longitudinal, full-production traces like the one from Chutes are crucial for understanding these workloads and for guiding system design and evaluation; releasing the one-year trace will enable broader, more realistic research on LLM serving systems.

title: GRPO Beyond English: A Large-Scale Study of GRPO in Non-English and Multilingual Settings
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), often optimized with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has become a central recipe for improving the reasoning capabilities of pretrained language models but current studies remain heavily English-centric. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of multilingual and non-English GRPO across a wide range of base models, training languages, and different reasoning language rewards. We find that training to reason in the native language often leaves only a small gap to training for English reasoning. We further observe strong crosslingual transfer: training in one language often improves performance in many others. However, specific trends are highly model- and language-dependent. In some cases, training in a particular language induces severe regressions on out-of-domain capabilities in other languages. Our analysis shows that RLVR beyond English can provide broad crosslingual gains, but also requires broad evaluation to detect language-specific regressions.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how well Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), optimized with GRPO, works for reasoning in many languages, not just English.
AI.motivation: Most RLVR/GRPO work focuses on English, leaving unclear whether these methods effectively improve reasoning in other languages and how training in one language affects others.
AI.method: They run a large-scale empirical study of multilingual and non-English GRPO: varying base LMs, training languages, and the language in which reasoning rewards are defined, then measuring performance and crosslingual transfer patterns.
AI.result: (1) Training models to reason in their native language nearly matches training them for English reasoning. (2) Training in one language often boosts reasoning performance in many other languages (strong crosslingual transfer). (3) The direction and magnitude of transfer are highly model- and language-dependent, and some language-specific training can cause substantial regressions in out-of-domain languages.
AI.conclusion: RLVR applied beyond English can deliver broad crosslingual reasoning gains, but its effects are uneven and sometimes harmful, so multilingual RLVR requires equally broad, language-aware evaluation to identify and mitigate regressions.

title: Agentao: A Governed Local-First Runtime for Tool-Using LLM Agents
comment: The code is publicly available at Github. We are conducting testing and analysis of this framework, and will provide experimental results and examples in future versions
summary: LLM agents increasingly operate as execution systems that invoke tools, modify local state, use persistent memory, and interact with external protocols. These capabilities make agents useful, but they also introduce risks related to over-privileged actions, weak auditability, prompt injection, tool poisoning, and uncontrolled side effects. This paper presents Agentao, a governed local-first runtime for tool-using LLM agents. Agentao separates model-generated action proposals from host-authorized execution through a layered architecture consisting of host-facing surfaces, a host contract, a runtime core, a permission-mediated tool system, and supporting subsystems for memory, replay, plugins, skills, sub-agents, and protocol integration. We describe the motivation, threat model, design goals, governance model, execution pipeline, and structured event interface of the system. Agentao does not provide formal safety guarantees; rather, it demonstrates how permissions, state, protocol boundaries, and execution traces can be made explicit runtime abstractions for building agents that are more governable, inspectable, and suitable for host-controlled local environments. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jin-bo/agentao.

AI.tldr: Agentao is a governed, local-first runtime that separates LLM agents’ proposed actions from host-authorized execution using a layered, permissioned architecture to make tool-using agents more controllable and inspectable.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents gain capabilities to call tools, change local state, persist data, and interact with external systems, they introduce security and safety risks such as over-privileged operations, prompt injection, tool poisoning, and difficult auditing of behavior. There is a need for a runtime that treats governance, permissions, and observability as first-class concerns so that agents can be safely embedded in host-controlled environments.
AI.method: The paper designs and implements Agentao, a local-first runtime that cleanly separates model-generated action proposals from actual execution via a layered architecture. It defines host-facing surfaces and a host contract, a runtime core, and a permission-mediated tool system, plus subsystems for memory, replay, plugins, skills, sub-agents, and protocol integration. The system introduces an execution pipeline and a structured event interface so that permissions, protocol boundaries, state transitions, and execution traces become explicit runtime abstractions that the host can govern and inspect.
AI.result: Agentao provides a working, publicly released runtime in which LLM agents operate under explicit permissions and governance constraints. The system shows that agent actions can be mediated, traced, and bounded by protocol and state abstractions without requiring changes to the LLM itself, improving governability and auditability relative to ad hoc tool-calling setups.
AI.conclusion: While Agentao does not offer formal safety guarantees, it demonstrates a practical architecture for governed, local-first LLM agent execution. By making permissions, state, protocol boundaries, and execution traces explicit and inspectable, Agentao enables hosts to exert finer-grained control over tool-using agents and to deploy them more safely within local, host-controlled environments.

title: CLAIR-Fin: An Adversarial Multi-Agent Framework for Claim-Level Verification and Adaptive Debate in Cross-Modal Financial QA
summary: Existing defenses against hallucination in retrieval-augmented and multi-agent pipelines remain partial: evidence is trusted despite modality disagreement, debate verifies an aggregate report rather than individual claims, and such verification occurs only after drafting, leaving inter-agent errors undetected until the final text. To close this gap, we present CLAIR-Fin, a nine-agent framework that decomposes each question into atomic claims maintained in a typed Financial Claim Ledger. Each claim is resolved through Asymmetric Evidence Authority, which conditions evidence trust on claim type rather than treating all modalities as equally reliable; Chain-of-Custody Verification, which checks grounding at the hand-off between drafting and adversarial review rather than only at the pipeline's exit; an Adaptive Rebuttal Cycle, which routes contested claims through adversarial debate whose depth scales with what that debate finds; and a terminal entailment audit paired with a continuous Hallucination Risk Index that distinguishes claims that passed scrutiny from claims never contested. We evaluate CLAIR-Fin on BB-FinQA-X, a 500-question cross-modal financial evaluation set built from Bangladesh Bank Annual Report material, stratified by query type, format, and difficulty. Relative to a single-pass retrieval-augmented generation baseline, it raises faithfulness ($0.780 \rightarrow 0.889$) while abstaining on 5.4% of questions when evidence is insufficient rather than forcing an unsupported response, and it exceeds stronger retrieval-strategy baselines such as HyDE and Graph-RAG on faithfulness ($\leq 0.874$).

AI.tldr: CLAIR-Fin is a multi-agent framework that reduces hallucinations in financial QA by decomposing questions into atomic claims, assigning modality-aware evidence authority, verifying claim grounding at each hand‑off, and adaptively debating contested claims, achieving higher faithfulness than strong RAG baselines on a new Bangladesh Bank–based benchmark.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation and multi-agent systems still hallucinate because they over-trust any retrieved evidence regardless of modality, verify only aggregate answers instead of individual claims, and perform verification only at the end of the pipeline, missing inter-agent propagation of errors. In high-stakes financial domains, these weaknesses make current defenses against hallucination insufficient and unreliable, motivating a more fine-grained, claim-centric and process-aware approach.
AI.method: The paper introduces CLAIR-Fin, a nine-agent pipeline that represents each question as a set of typed atomic claims in a Financial Claim Ledger. Claims are resolved using: (1) Asymmetric Evidence Authority, where trust in evidence is conditioned on the claim type so modalities are not treated uniformly; (2) Chain-of-Custody Verification, which checks whether each claim remains properly grounded when passed between drafting and adversarial review agents, rather than only auditing the final output; (3) an Adaptive Rebuttal Cycle, which funnels disputed claims into adversarial debates whose depth varies according to the issues surfaced; and (4) a final entailment audit combined with a continuous Hallucination Risk Index that marks which claims were rigorously vetted versus those never challenged.
AI.result: On BB-FinQA-X, a 500-question cross-modal financial QA dataset derived from Bangladesh Bank annual reports and stratified by query type, format, and difficulty, CLAIR-Fin substantially improves faithfulness from 0.780 to 0.889 relative to a single-pass RAG baseline, while abstaining on 5.4% of questions when adequate evidence is lacking. It also outperforms stronger retrieval baselines like HyDE and Graph-RAG, which achieve faithfulness no higher than 0.874.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing financial QA into typed atomic claims and enforcing modality-aware evidence authority, stepwise chain-of-custody verification, and adaptive adversarial debate can significantly reduce hallucinations in retrieval-augmented, multi-agent pipelines. CLAIR-Fin not only yields more faithful answers but also responsibly abstains when evidence is insufficient, demonstrating that structured, claim-level oversight and risk tracking offer a more robust defense against hallucinations than existing RAG strategies.

title: AI Evaluation Should Work With Humans
comment: Accepted to ICML 2026 Position Paper Track
summary: This position paper argues that the dominant paradigm of AI evaluation (which focuses on superhuman autonomous performance and so implicitly targets the goal of replacing humans) is guiding AI development in the wrong direction. Instead, the AI community should pivot to evaluating the performance of human--AI teams. We argue that this collaborative shift will foster AI systems that act as true complements to human capabilities and therefore lead to far better societal outcomes than will the current process.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques current AI evaluation practices and advocates for assessing human–AI team performance instead of solely autonomous AI performance.
AI.motivation: Current AI evaluation emphasizes superhuman, fully autonomous performance, implicitly aiming to replace humans. The authors believe this paradigm misdirects AI research and may produce worse societal outcomes, motivating a rethinking of evaluation goals and metrics.
AI.method: This is a conceptual/position paper. The authors present arguments and reasoning rather than empirical experiments, contrasting the dominant evaluation paradigm with an alternative focused on human–AI collaboration and complementary capabilities.
AI.result: The main result is a structured argument showing that focusing on human–AI team performance better aligns AI development with human complementarity, and that the existing focus on replacement risks misaligned incentives and suboptimal societal impact.
AI.conclusion: AI research and benchmarking should pivot from evaluating autonomous, superhuman AI to evaluating human–AI teams. Adopting this collaborative evaluation paradigm will encourage the design of AI systems that complement rather than replace humans, leading to better societal outcomes.

title: TeachMateGPT: A Multi-Agent Knowledge-Grounded Framework for Pedagogical Assessment Generation from Science Curriculum Materials
summary: Automatically generating textbook-grounded assessment items can reduce science teachers' workload, but existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems rely on flat retrieval, support only single-question generation, lack safeguards against weak evidence, and are ill-suited to low-resource, board-exam-structured curricula. We address these limitations with TeachMateGPT, a multi-agent system contributing four advances to curriculum-grounded science-assessment authoring. (i) COPE, a hierarchical knowledge base replacing token-window chunking with a multi-resolution index that segments documents along syllabus structure and links them at three granularities via a traversable graph-based lineage, matching evidence to each topic's instructional level. (ii) A staged, fail-closed agent pipeline replacing one-shot retrieve-then-generate: routing gates search, retrieval fuses dense and lexical evidence under a coverage gate that withholds generation on insufficient evidence, and specialist agents draft objective and constructed-response items. (iii) SAVER, a source-attributed verification protocol scoring faithfulness, relevance, and hallucination risk against retrieved evidence, applying stricter grounding checks across each creative question's four sub-parts, paired with teacher-in-the-loop evaluation rather than automatic filtering. (iv) NCTB-SciGen8, a curriculum-grounded dataset of 198 items (143 multiple-choice, 55 creative questions) spanning all 14 chapters of the NCTB Class 8 science textbook, produced by the pipeline and rated by three practicing teachers. TeachMateGPT raises faithfulness (0.68 $\rightarrow$ 0.96) and answer relevancy (0.60 $\rightarrow$ 0.89) over a vanilla RAG baseline.

AI.tldr: TeachMateGPT is a multi-agent, curriculum-grounded RAG system that builds a hierarchical syllabus-aligned index, uses a staged retrieval-and-generation pipeline with safety checks, verifies grounding via a source-attributed protocol, and provides a new teacher-rated benchmark, substantially improving faithfulness and answer relevance over vanilla RAG for science item generation.
AI.motivation: Manual creation of textbook-aligned assessment items is time-consuming for science teachers, and existing RAG-based question generation systems are poorly suited for structured, low-resource curricula: they use flat, window-based retrieval, generate only one question at a time, lack robust safeguards when evidence is weak or missing, and are not tailored to board-exam style assessment. The authors aim to automate high-quality, curriculum-grounded question authoring while reducing hallucinations and mismatches to instructional level.
AI.method: The paper proposes TeachMateGPT, a multi-agent RAG framework with four components: (i) COPE, a hierarchical, multi-resolution knowledge base that segments textbooks by syllabus structure and connects segments via a graph so retrieval can match question difficulty and topic granularity; (ii) a staged, fail-closed pipeline with routing gates, hybrid dense+lexical retrieval, a coverage gate that blocks generation when evidence is insufficient, and specialized agents for objective and constructed-response item drafting; (iii) SAVER, a source-attributed verification protocol that scores question parts for faithfulness, relevance, and hallucination risk against retrieved passages and enforces stricter checks for creative questions’ sub-parts, combined with teacher-in-the-loop review instead of automatic filtering; (iv) NCTB-SciGen8, a new dataset of 198 curriculum-grounded questions for the NCTB Class 8 science textbook, including both multiple-choice and creative items, all generated by the pipeline and rated by practicing teachers.
AI.result: TeachMateGPT is able to generate curriculum-grounded assessment items spanning all 14 chapters of the NCTB Class 8 science textbook. Empirical evaluation against a vanilla RAG baseline shows substantial gains in grounding quality: faithfulness improves from 0.68 to 0.96, and answer relevance increases from 0.60 to 0.89. The system can handle both objective (multiple-choice) and more complex, multi-part creative questions under stronger evidence and hallucination controls.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a hierarchical, syllabus-aware index combined with a guarded, multi-agent generation pipeline and explicit source-attributed verification can significantly improve the reliability and curriculum alignment of automatically generated science assessments. TeachMateGPT offers a practical, teacher-in-the-loop tool for low-resource, exam-oriented education settings and provides a new benchmark dataset to support further research on grounded question generation.

title: Stable Miscalibration in Large Language Models: A Practical View of High-Confidence Errors
comment: Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Epistemic Intelligence in Machine Learning (EIML)@ICML 2026. 7 pages, 4 figures
summary: High-confidence errors in large language models are often treated as evidence of fragile internal inference. We study a different possibility: stable miscalibration, where a confident wrong answer remains locally stable under small perturbations. We combine two diagnostics: a label-aware output-level audit score that ranks domains by confidence variation and overconfident mistakes under a forced-answer baseline, and an internal sensitivity probe that measures hidden-state movement. On a multi-domain binary factual audit set, this audit score tracks where abstention-aware self-critique reduces decision loss, although direct labeled baselines rank the same gain more strongly. Internally, self-critical prompting consistently reduces hidden-state sensitivity across layers in three open-weight models. This supports prompt-induced local stabilization rather than a purely output-level abstention pattern, but it does not imply calibration: audit-defined overconfident errors are not clearly more locally sensitive than confidently correct answers, so some high-confidence errors may be stable and miscalibrated rather than simply fragile.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether large language models’ confident mistakes come from fragile reasoning or from stable miscalibration, using both output-level audits and internal hidden-state sensitivity probes.
AI.motivation: Large language models sometimes give highly confident but wrong answers. Many interpret this as evidence that their internal reasoning is brittle, but it could also be that some wrong beliefs are stable and systematically miscalibrated. Understanding which is true matters for improving reliability and designing better mitigation strategies such as abstention or self-critique.
AI.method: The authors define a label-aware, output-level audit score that captures variation in confidence and overconfident errors across domains under a forced-answer baseline. They also design an internal sensitivity probe that measures how much hidden states move under perturbations (e.g., self-critical prompting). They apply these diagnostics to a multi-domain binary factual audit set and test three open-weight models, comparing behavior with and without abstention-aware self-critique prompts and tracking layer-wise sensitivity changes.
AI.result: The audit score correlates with where abstention-aware self-critique reduces decision loss, but simple supervised (labeled) baselines identify the same gains more strongly. At the representation level, self-critical prompting reliably reduces hidden-state sensitivity across layers in all three models, indicating local stabilization of internal states. However, overconfident errors, as defined by the audit, are not consistently more sensitive than confidently correct answers.
AI.conclusion: Self-critique and abstention change not only output patterns but also stabilize internal representations, suggesting that some improvements come from prompt-induced local stabilization rather than just output-level filtering. Yet this stabilization does not automatically yield better calibration: some high-confidence errors appear stable and not especially sensitive, supporting the view that a subset of errors are genuinely miscalibrated rather than just artifacts of fragile inference.

title: StreamHear: Domain-Adapted Pseudo-Labeling for Semi-Supervised Streaming Speech Recognition
summary: Streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR) underperforms on domain-shifted target audio, where labeled in-domain data is costly to prepare while unlabeled audio is abundant. We present StreamHear, a semi-supervised pipeline that adapts a pretrained streaming student by fine-tuning an offline transducer teacher on the labeled training set, generating pseudo-labels on the unlabeled portion, and fine-tuning the student on the mixture. We further introduce a prior-regularized dynamic-programming realignment step that fixes chunk-level word placement using an ASR-hypothesis anchor. Across four datasets spanning financial calls, prepared read speech, and phone-quality dialogue, StreamHear consistently outperforms supervised student fine-tuning and narrows the gap to the offline teacher.

AI.tldr: StreamHear is a semi-supervised method to adapt streaming ASR models to new domains using a stronger offline teacher, pseudo-labels, and a realignment step to improve chunk-level word placement.
AI.motivation: Streaming ASR models suffer accuracy degradation when deployed on audio from domains different from their training data, yet collecting labeled in-domain streaming data is expensive while unlabeled audio is plentiful. There is a need for an adaptation approach that effectively leverages unlabeled in-domain audio to close the performance gap between fast streaming models and more accurate offline models.
AI.method: The authors propose StreamHear, a semi-supervised teacher–student framework. First, an offline transducer teacher model is fine-tuned on the available labeled in-domain data. Second, this teacher generates pseudo-labels for the large pool of unlabeled in-domain audio. Third, the original streaming student ASR model is fine-tuned on a mixture of true labels (from the labeled subset) and pseudo-labels (from unlabeled audio). Additionally, they introduce a prior-regularized dynamic-programming realignment algorithm that, using an existing ASR hypothesis as an anchor, adjusts the chunk-level timing and placement of words to better match streaming constraints.
AI.result: On four datasets covering financial call-center speech, prepared read speech, and telephone-quality conversational dialogue, StreamHear delivers consistent gains over a baseline that only performs supervised fine-tuning of the streaming student on labeled data. The method also reduces the performance gap between the streaming student and the more accurate offline teacher model.
AI.conclusion: StreamHear is an effective semi-supervised adaptation pipeline for streaming ASR under domain shift. By exploiting unlabeled in-domain audio with a pseudo-labeling teacher and incorporating a realignment step to correct chunk-level word placement, it improves recognition accuracy beyond purely supervised fine-tuning and brings streaming performance closer to that of an offline teacher across multiple speech domains.

title: Measuring Cross-Task Behavioral Consistency in Language Model Agents
summary: Agent evaluation relies almost entirely on outcome metrics such as success rate, which capture whether an agent succeeds but not how consistently it behaves. We argue that behavioral consistency across tasks is a distinct and measurable property, and we introduce the Behavioral Consistency Metric (BCM) to quantify it. BCM trains a model to predict task success from behavioral features of agent execution traces, derives a per-trajectory feature-attribution vector, and measures the mean pairwise similarity of these vectors within an agent system. Across roughly 9,000 trajectories from six language model agents on software engineering tasks, our central finding is that cross-task and within-task consistency are distinct axes that can diverge: some systems are locally reproducible, behaving similarly on repeated attempts at one task, yet globally fragmented, with no stable strategy across different tasks, while others are consistent at both scales. Prior work measures only same-task reproducibility and so cannot observe this separation. We further find that consistency is not reducible to success rate, since systems with comparable success can differ sharply in consistency, and that the frontier-versus-open-source consistency gap persists under a within-task control that holds task difficulty constant. We position BCM as a process-level reliability signal that complements outcome metrics, and we are explicit about the conditions under which it is meaningful.

AI.tldr: Introduces Behavioral Consistency Metric (BCM) to measure how consistently language model agents behave across and within tasks, beyond simple success rate.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of agents almost exclusively use outcome metrics like success rate, which ignore how consistently an agent behaves across runs and tasks. This misses important aspects of reliability, such as whether an agent has a stable strategy, behaves reproducibly, or fragments into different behavior modes depending on the task. There is also a need to understand whether more advanced (frontier) models are not just more successful but more behaviorally consistent than open-source alternatives.
AI.method: Define Behavioral Consistency Metric (BCM) as a process-level measure. For a given agent, collect execution traces (trajectories) over many tasks and runs. Extract behavioral features from each trajectory, train a predictive model that maps these features to task success, then compute per-trajectory feature-attribution vectors from this model. Measure behavioral consistency as the mean pairwise similarity between these attribution vectors within the same agent system, considering both cross-task and within-task groupings. Apply BCM to roughly 9,000 trajectories from six language model agents on software engineering tasks, comparing within-task reproducibility and cross-task strategy consistency and analyzing relationships with success rates and model type (frontier vs open-source).
AI.result: Finds that behavioral consistency has at least two distinct axes: cross-task consistency (stable strategies across different tasks) and within-task consistency (reproducibility on repeated runs of the same task). Some systems are reproducible within a task but fragmented across tasks, while others are consistent at both levels. Prior work that only measures same-task reproducibility misses this divergence. Consistency is not simply a function of success rate: agents with similar success can have very different consistency profiles. Additionally, the gap between frontier and open-source systems in terms of consistency remains even when controlling for task difficulty within tasks.
AI.conclusion: BCM provides a new, process-level reliability metric that captures behavioral consistency beyond traditional success-based evaluation. It reveals that within-task reproducibility and cross-task strategy stability are separable properties, and that success rate alone cannot characterize agent reliability. BCM can therefore complement outcome metrics in evaluating and comparing agent systems, especially when judging their robustness and trustworthiness, as long as the stated conditions for its meaningful application are respected.

title: BM25-Augmented Many-Shot Translation for Low-Resource North-Eastern Indian Languages
summary: This paper describes the University of Florida Gators submission to the WMT26 Low-Resource Indic Language Translation shared task. We adapt the retrieval-augmented many-shot translation pipeline from our AmericasNLP 2026 system to translate between English and eleven North-Eastern Indian languages in both directions. At inference time, BM25 retrieves the most similar parallel examples from a language-specific training bank, and Gemini 2.5 Flash translates the input conditioned on these examples. No model fine-tuning is involved. Training banks combine official WMT26 data with publicly available corpora such as Samanantar and prior WMT shared task releases. A grid search over retrieval count r and development exemplar count d across all 22 language-direction pairs selects the best configuration for each submission.

AI.tldr: Many-shot, retrieval-augmented machine translation system for low-resource Indic languages using Gemini 2.5 Flash without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To participate in the WMT26 Low-Resource Indic Language Translation task and improve translation quality for eleven low-resource North-Eastern Indian languages using scalable methods that avoid model fine-tuning.
AI.method: Use a retrieval-augmented many-shot translation pipeline where, at inference, BM25 retrieves similar parallel sentence pairs from a language-specific training bank. These examples, coming from WMT26 data plus external corpora like Samanantar and prior WMT tasks, are provided as in-context exemplars to Gemini 2.5 Flash, which performs the translation. A grid search over the number of retrieved examples (r) and the number of development exemplars (d) is run for each of the 22 translation directions to select best-performing configurations.
AI.result: The abstract does not provide numerical results, but indicates that the system configurations for each of the 22 language directions are selected via grid search optimizing performance on development data.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-augmented many-shot prompting with a large language model and no fine-tuning is a viable approach for low-resource Indic language translation, especially when leveraging a mixture of official shared-task data and publicly available parallel corpora.

title: Cross-Disciplinary Taxonomy and Modeling of Misunderstanding Generation, Amplification, and Detection, from Pragmatics to AI Agents
comment: 49 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables, 94 references. Cross-disciplinary conceptual synthesis across multiple fields. Includes a source-by-source evidence matrix in Appendix A and a coding manual in Appendix B for independent application of the taxonomy
summary: Detection of misunderstanding is an urgent problem to solve because communication has moved away from real-time, in-person interaction and is increasingly handled by AI-mediated channels. This shift cuts communicators off from the resources repair depends on faster than new means of detection are being built. In this paper we analyse misunderstanding as a layered process in which a divergence is generated, may then be amplified, and is either detected and repaired or left to persist unnoticed. Consolidating accounts from nine fields of research that do not ordinarily cite one another, we identify eleven exact failure modes and show that each operates at a specific point in a communicative process rather than anywhere within it. Those points give eight analytical layers, derived from the literature rather than adopted from an existing model. Eight of the mechanisms primarily generate a divergence, two primarily amplify one already present, and one governs whether a divergence is detected and repaired. We model the eight layers formally, extending information and communication theory from the transmission of signals to the reconstruction of meaning, and we supply a source-by-source evidence matrix that makes every rating auditable, a coding manual, and nine analysed dialogue cases. No prior classification of misunderstanding both locates mechanisms at points in the process and types them by function.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a layered, formally modeled classification of how misunderstandings arise, get amplified, and (fail to) get repaired in AI-mediated and other non-face-to-face communication.
AI.motivation: As communication increasingly occurs via AI-mediated and other non-real-time channels, traditional cues for detecting and repairing misunderstandings (e.g., facial expressions, immediate back-and-forth) are diminished. Existing research on misunderstanding is fragmented across many disciplines and lacks an integrated, process-based classification that pinpoints where and how misunderstandings occur. This makes it hard to systematically detect, prevent, and repair misunderstandings in modern communication environments.
AI.method: The authors conduct a cross-disciplinary synthesis of accounts from nine different research fields that typically do not cite one another. From this literature, they identify eleven distinct failure modes in communication and map each to its specific position in the communicative process. Based on these mappings, they derive eight analytical layers of communication, not imported from an existing model but grounded in the evidence. They then formally model these eight layers by extending classical information and communication theory beyond signal transmission to include reconstruction of meaning. They also build an evidence matrix, a coding manual, and apply their framework to nine detailed dialogue case analyses to validate and illustrate the model.
AI.result: They identify eleven precise failure modes of misunderstanding, each tied to a specific point in the communicative process. These are grouped into eight analytical layers: eight mechanisms that primarily generate divergence in meaning, two that primarily amplify an existing divergence, and one that controls whether a divergence gets detected and repaired. They produce formal models of the eight layers, a fully auditable source-by-source evidence matrix for their ratings, a coding manual for applying the framework, and nine analysed dialogue cases demonstrating the model in practice.
AI.conclusion: Misunderstanding can be systematically described as a layered process in which divergences in meaning are generated, possibly amplified, and either repaired or left undetected. Each mechanism of failure operates at a specific, identifiable point in the communicative process, and can be typed by its functional role (generation, amplification, detection/repair). The authors claim this is the first classification that both situates mechanisms at precise process points and categorizes them by function, extending communication theory from signal transmission to meaning reconstruction and providing tools (models, coding manual, evidence matrix, case analyses) to study and manage misunderstanding more rigorously.

title: GALA: Generation-Aware Cross-Modal Alignment for Text-to-Time-Series Synthesis
summary: Synthesizing time series from natural language is emerging as the most expressive form of controllable time series generation. However, existing text-conditioned generators either take caption embeddings frozen from off-the-shelf text encoders, or adapt the encoder end-to-end, letting the denoising loss shape the embeddings only as a by-product. In either case, the conditioning representation is never deliberately matched to the signal modality, leaving it ill-suited to guide generation. We address this by introducing GALA: Generation-Aware cross-modaL Alignment for text conditional time series generation. GALA is a two-stage approach that first contrastively couples a pretrained text encoder with a time-series foundation model into a shared embedding space with both encoders adapted to generation by an auxiliary generative loss, and then freezes the resulting caption embedding to drive a flow-matching generator.
