On TSFragment-600K, spanning four domains and three fragment lengths, GALA sets a new state of the art, ranking first in 30 of 36 metric columns and reaching an average rank of 1.08/1.08/1.42 at lengths 24/48/96 against 1.92/2.00/1.75 for the strongest baseline. We further find that generator-internal text encoders force a trade-off between fidelity and caption adherence, whereas conditioning on the aligned embedding breaks it: FID, CTTP, and JFTSD all improve at once. Ablating the auxiliary loss degrades FID, CTTP and JFTSD together, it indicates the generative term is a necessary component of the alignment rather than an add-on.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GALA, a two-stage method that aligns text and time-series representations for better text-conditional time series generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a large benchmark and showing that generation-aware alignment improves both fidelity and text adherence simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Existing text-conditioned time series generators rely on text embeddings that are not explicitly aligned with the time-series modality. Either they freeze off-the-shelf text encoders or adapt them only indirectly via denoising losses. As a result, the text conditioning is suboptimal for guiding generation, often forcing a trade-off between realism and adherence to the caption. The authors want a conditioning representation that is purposefully aligned with time-series generation needs.
AI.method: GALA (Generation-Aware cross-modaL Alignment) is a two-stage framework. In stage one, it uses contrastive learning to couple a pretrained text encoder and a time-series foundation model into a shared embedding space, while simultaneously adapting both encoders with an auxiliary generative loss so that the embeddings are tuned for generation. In stage two, the resulting aligned caption embeddings are frozen and used as conditioning inputs to a flow-matching time-series generator. The design explicitly separates learning good, generation-aware cross-modal embeddings from the downstream generative modeling, and tests variants with and without the auxiliary generative term.
AI.result: On the TSFragment-600K benchmark, which covers four domains and three fragment lengths (24, 48, and 96), GALA achieves state-of-the-art performance. It ranks first in 30 out of 36 evaluation metrics and attains average ranks of 1.08/1.08/1.42 at lengths 24/48/96, compared to 1.92/2.00/1.75 for the strongest competing baseline. Experiments also show that standard generator-internal text encoders suffer from a fidelity–caption-adherence trade-off, whereas conditioning on GALA’s aligned embeddings improves multiple metrics simultaneously: FID, CTTP, and JFTSD all get better. Removing the auxiliary generative loss in the alignment stage consistently worsens these metrics.
AI.conclusion: Deliberately learning a generation-aware, cross-modal alignment between text and time series yields better conditioning embeddings than using off-the-shelf or passively adapted text encoders. GALA’s two-stage contrastive plus generative alignment enables a flow-matching generator to produce time series that are both more realistic and more faithful to textual descriptions, avoiding the usual trade-off between fidelity and caption adherence. The auxiliary generative loss is an essential part of successful alignment rather than a minor enhancement.

title: Active Perception for Embodied Disambiguation
summary: Natural language provides robots with a flexible task interface, but target ambiguity in embodied environments arises not only from user intent; it can also result from missing taskrelevant physical evidence in the current observation. Existing interactive disambiguation methods primarily obtain additional information by asking the user, whereas occlusion, restricted viewpoints, unreadable text, and unobserved targets require the robot to actively change its observation. We propose an active-perception framework for embodied target disambiguation that uses active observation as the backbone for information acquisition and uses a vision-language model to decide, on the basis of accumulated visual evidence and interaction information, whether to continue observing, request clarification, or complete target selection. Active observation can both directly recover missing discriminative evidence and reveal object names, labels, and semantic attributes, thereby improving user clarification when it remains necessary. Real-robot experiments show that the framework combines physical information acquisition and userintent clarification within a unified embodied disambiguation process.

AI.tldr: Active-perception framework that lets a robot move its sensors and/or ask questions to resolve ambiguous natural-language target descriptions.
AI.motivation: In real-world, embodied settings, language instructions like “pick up the red mug” can remain ambiguous even after a user clarifies, because the robot’s current viewpoint may hide key evidence (occlusions, unseen objects, unreadable labels). Existing methods mainly rely on further user interaction and neglect that robots can physically move to acquire better observations, limiting robustness in realistic environments.
AI.method: They design an active-perception framework where the robot repeatedly: (1) takes actions to change its viewpoint (active observation), (2) feeds accumulated visual observations and any dialog history into a vision-language model, and (3) lets the model decide among three options: keep observing, ask the user for clarification, or finalize the target choice. Active observation is used not just to better see objects but also to reveal text (names, labels) and semantic attributes that disambiguate the target.
AI.result: In real-robot experiments, the framework successfully resolves target ambiguities caused by missing or occluded visual evidence and achieves better, more reliable target selection by combining physical exploration with language-based clarification.
AI.conclusion: An integrated active-perception and interaction framework enables robots to disambiguate language-specified targets more effectively by deciding when to move, when to ask, and when to act, unifying physical evidence gathering with user-intent clarification in embodied environments.

title: Amplified Does Not Mean Predictive: Reasoning Behaviors in Thinking Models
summary: Which reasoning behaviors are associated with correct answers in reasoning models, and does reasoning-oriented training amplify those behaviors? This distinction is important because reasoning-oriented training can make traces look more deliberative without amplifying the behaviors most tied to model correctness. We quantify this mismatch with Behavioral Lift, a metric that measures how much correctness changes when a behavior is present versus absent in a model's reasoning trace. Across 15 models and 6 benchmarks spanning text-only and vision-language reasoning, we annotate 15,282 traces with a taxonomy whose core behaviors are defined for both LLM and VLM traces. We find evidence for an Amplification-Lift Gap, in which thinking models strongly amplify self-correction, hypothesis testing, and uncertainty acknowledgment, while the highest-lift behaviors are confidence calibration, knowledge alignment, and self-awareness. Confidence calibration is among the strongest positive signals of correctness in both modalities, yet is barely amplified; uncertainty acknowledgment is amplified by 3--7$\times$, yet is weakly or negatively associated with correctness. We find that reasoning-oriented training does not preferentially amplify the highest-Lift behaviors, motivating process-level objectives that reward calibrated and grounded reasoning rather than surface form alone.

AI.tldr: The paper studies which observable reasoning behaviors in model traces are truly predictive of correct answers and whether current reasoning-focused training actually strengthens those high-value behaviors.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models often appear more deliberative after reasoning-oriented training, but it is unclear whether the behaviors shown in their traces are the ones most responsible for correct answers. There may be a mismatch between behaviors that are visually amplified (e.g., more steps, more uncertainty expressions) and those that actually correlate with correctness. Understanding this gap is important for designing better training objectives.
AI.method: The authors introduce Behavioral Lift, a metric that quantifies how much a model’s accuracy changes when a specific behavior is present versus absent in its reasoning trace. They construct a behavior taxonomy that applies to both text-only LLMs and vision-language models (VLMs), and annotate 15,282 reasoning traces from 15 models across 6 reasoning benchmarks. They then measure both (a) how strongly each behavior is amplified by reasoning-oriented training and (b) the Lift of each behavior with respect to correctness.
AI.result: They identify an Amplification-Lift Gap: reasoning-oriented training substantially amplifies behaviors such as self-correction, hypothesis testing, and explicit acknowledgment of uncertainty, but the behaviors most predictive of correctness (high Lift) are confidence calibration, knowledge alignment with the ground truth, and self-awareness of one’s own limitations. Confidence calibration is consistently one of the strongest positive predictors of correctness across text and vision-language models but is barely increased by current training, while uncertainty acknowledgment is amplified 3–7x despite having weak or even negative association with correctness.
AI.conclusion: Current reasoning-oriented training methods mostly improve the surface appearance of deliberation rather than the behaviors that truly underlie correct reasoning. Because amplification does not focus on the highest-Lift behaviors, the authors argue for new process-level objectives that directly reward calibrated confidence, alignment with correct knowledge, and genuine self-awareness, instead of simply rewarding longer or more hedged reasoning traces.

title: MobileMem: Learning from a Year of Mobile Experiences
summary: The next generation of AI agents is increasingly moving beyond systems that answer isolated questions toward persistent personal assistants that can understand, remember, and continuously learn from users' experiences. Such assistants require long-term memory to accumulate and leverage user-specific experiences over time, yet existing benchmarks remain inadequate for realistic mobile settings, where experiences are heterogeneous, multimodal, evolving, and deeply personal. We introduce MobileMem, a benchmark and framework for studying on-device long-term memory, grounded in a year-scale collection of mobile experiences. MobileMem employs a knowledge-grounded synthesis pipeline to construct coherent and temporally consistent long-horizon trajectories from user-app sessions. It provides complementary text and multimodal settings covering multi-hop and temporal reasoning, knowledge updating, and implicit preference inference. Specifically, MobileMem enables agents to remember the past, understand the present, and adapt to the future. By modeling experiences rather than isolated facts, MobileMem moves memory beyond information retrieval toward experiential intelligence for continuous personal learning.

AI.tldr: Introduces MobileMem, a benchmark and framework for evaluating long-term, on-device memory in mobile AI assistants using realistic, year-long multimodal user experiences.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents are evolving into persistent personal assistants that must understand and learn from heterogeneous, long-term, deeply personal user experiences on mobile devices. Existing benchmarks are insufficient because they typically focus on short, isolated queries and lack realistic, multimodal, temporally extended and user-specific data, especially in mobile contexts.
AI.method: The authors build MobileMem, a benchmark and framework based on year-scale mobile user experiences. They design a knowledge-grounded synthesis pipeline that converts raw user-app sessions into coherent, temporally consistent long-horizon trajectories. The benchmark includes both text-only and multimodal tasks that test multi-hop and temporal reasoning, knowledge updates over time, and inference of implicit user preferences. The framing emphasizes on-device long-term memory for mobile agents.
AI.result: MobileMem yields a structured evaluation setting where AI agents can be tested on remembering past events, interpreting current context, and anticipating or adapting to future needs using long-term experiential memory. It offers realistic, heterogeneous trajectories that go beyond standard factual question answering, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: By focusing on modeled experiences instead of isolated facts, MobileMem shifts the study of memory for AI assistants from simple information retrieval to experiential intelligence and continuous personal learning. This benchmark is intended to support the development and evaluation of persistent, on-device personal assistants with robust long-term memory in real-world mobile environments.

title: When Lexical Change Misleads: Rethinking Dynamic Topic Model Evaluation with Traditional and LLM-Based Metrics
summary: Dynamic topic models capture evolving word distributions, but traditional coherence metrics may fail when vocabulary changes while semantic meaning persists. We evaluate 120 topics from CoNTM and DLDA across NYT, DBLP, and arXiv, using three human annotators and Low, Medium, and High lexical-change categories. Traditional temporal coherence shows highly variable agreement with human judgments ($ρ$=-0.256 to 0.614). In contrast, LLM-based semantic similarity agrees strongly with human semantic judgments for CoNTM on NYT ($ρ$=0.609), DBLP ($ρ$=0.721), and arXiv ($ρ$=0.502), but is less consistent for DLDA. Lexical-change stratification reveals variation hidden by aggregate evaluation. We therefore advocate lexical-change-aware evaluation, jointly reporting traditional coherence and LLM-based semantic measures as complementary rather than interchangeable signals.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well traditional and LLM-based coherence measures capture topic quality in dynamic topic models, especially when vocabularies change but semantics stay similar, and argues for lexical-change-aware, dual-metric evaluation.
AI.motivation: Dynamic topic models allow topics to evolve over time, but standard coherence metrics rely heavily on surface word overlap. When vocabulary shifts (e.g., new jargon) while underlying semantics remain stable, these metrics can misjudge topic quality. The authors aim to understand whether newer LLM-based semantic similarity measures better reflect human judgments, and how vocabulary change levels affect evaluation reliability.
AI.method: They analyze 120 topics produced by two dynamic topic models (CoNTM and DLDA) on three corpora (NYT, DBLP, arXiv). Topics are manually annotated by three human judges, including categorization into Low, Medium, and High lexical-change levels. They compute traditional temporal coherence scores and LLM-based semantic similarity scores and correlate these with human judgments using Spearman’s ρ, both overall and within lexical-change strata.
AI.result: Traditional temporal coherence shows inconsistent correlation with human judgments, with Spearman correlations ranging from negative (-0.256) to moderately positive (0.614). LLM-based semantic similarity correlates strongly with human semantic judgments for CoNTM across NYT (ρ=0.609), DBLP (ρ=0.721), and arXiv (ρ=0.502), but yields less consistent results for DLDA. Stratifying topics by lexical-change levels reveals important variability that is obscured when evaluations are aggregated.
AI.conclusion: Traditional coherence and LLM-based semantic similarity capture complementary aspects of topic quality and should not be treated as interchangeable. Because vocabulary dynamics significantly affect evaluation behavior, the authors recommend lexical-change-aware evaluation protocols that always report both traditional word-based coherence and LLM-based semantic measures, analyzed across different lexical-change regimes.

title: No Universal Signal Predicts Sample-Level LLM Regression under Version Updates
summary: Frontier LLMs are updated frequently and typically outperform their predecessors in aggregate. But aggregate gains say little about individual samples: an update can still cause sample-level regression, where a response correct under the old model becomes incorrect under the new one. This paper studies how to predict such regressions from signals available at inference time. We compare single-model signals (confidence, logit margin, attention entropy) against cross-version signals (output KL divergence, likelihood drift, token-level KL, representation drift) under a unified added-value test that isolates each signal's gain over a confidence baseline. Across six benchmarks in three task families (multiple-choice question answering, or MCQ; math reasoning; code generation) and six model update pairs, we find that (1) signal effectiveness is task-dependent: confidence is strongest on MCQ and simpler math, while likelihood/KL signals give the most frequent gains on harder math and code; (2) no signal is universally best across model updates either; and (3) some cross-version signals stay informative even when confidence fails, including without labels, which supports a proof-of-concept selective fallback that routes high-risk samples back to the old model. Practitioners can use these task-level patterns to choose which regression signal to trust for a given update. Code is available at https://github.com/jiashengsally/llm-regression-signals.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how to predict when a newer LLM will perform worse than its predecessor on specific inputs, using various confidence and cross-model divergence signals, and shows which signals work best by task to enable selective fallback to older models.
AI.motivation: Although newer frontier LLMs generally outperform previous versions on aggregate benchmarks, they can still degrade on individual samples, turning previously correct outputs into incorrect ones. This kind of sample-level regression is problematic for reliability, safety, and user trust, especially in high-stakes or production settings. There is a practical need for methods that can, at inference time and without ground-truth labels, flag inputs where a model update is likely to regress, so that systems can selectively fall back to older models or otherwise mitigate risk.
AI.method: The authors frame the problem as predicting sample-level regression between an old and a new LLM version using only inference-time signals. They evaluate two broad categories of signals: (1) single-model signals from the new model alone, such as confidence, logit margin, and attention entropy; and (2) cross-version signals comparing old and new models, such as output KL divergence, likelihood drift, token-level KL divergence, and representation drift. Under a unified "added-value" evaluation protocol that measures each signal’s incremental benefit over a confidence-only baseline, they run experiments across six benchmarks spanning three task families (multiple-choice QA, math reasoning, and code generation) and six different model-update pairs. They analyze how well each signal predicts regressions and in what settings it adds value beyond confidence.
AI.result: Empirically, the authors find that the usefulness of regression signals depends strongly on the task type and the specific model-update pair. Confidence-based signals perform best for multiple-choice QA and simpler math tasks, whereas likelihood-based and KL divergence-based cross-version signals provide more consistent improvements for harder math and code generation. No single signal dominates across all model updates. Importantly, some cross-version signals remain informative even when confidence is unreliable, and they can operate without access to labels. The authors demonstrate a proof-of-concept selective fallback mechanism that uses these signals to route high-risk samples back to the older model, reducing regressions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that sample-level regressions are a real and nuanced issue in LLM updates, but inference-time signals can help predict and mitigate them. Different tasks and model-update pairs favor different regression indicators: confidence is often sufficient for MCQ and easier math, while cross-version likelihood and KL-based signals are more valuable for challenging math and code. Since no single signal is universally best, practitioners should select regression predictors based on task characteristics and model behavior. Cross-version signals, in particular, enable label-free detection of risky inputs and support practical strategies like selective fallback to older models, improving reliability of model updates in deployed systems.

title: ASSERT: A Measurement Pipeline for GenAI Audits
summary: Audits of generative AI (GenAI) systems often summarize behavior as a reported rate: how often the audited system complies with policy. Researchers and stakeholders use that rate to compare systems, track regressions, and gate deployment. A reported rate reflects both the system under audit and the measurement choices behind it, so a change in the rate can leave it unclear whether the system or those choices moved. We introduce ASSERT, a specification-driven measurement pipeline for GenAI audits that ties each reported rate to a written specification of the measurement choices used to produce it. ASSERT helps draft a behavioral rubric and test cases, then runs the audit against a GenAI system and returns a reported rate. In a case study on conversational deception, we observe that the reported rate moves substantially with the dialogue setup, the simulated user, the judge, and the evidence bar for non-compliance. These measurement choices substantially change the reported rate and can reorder GenAI system rankings. Because each reported rate is tied to an explicit specification, differences across audits are easier to attribute and interpret.

AI.tldr: ASSERT is a specification-driven pipeline that makes GenAI audit results (reported compliance rates) explicitly tied to the measurement choices that generated them, improving interpretability and comparability across audits.
AI.motivation: Current audits of generative AI systems typically report a single compliance rate, which is then used to compare systems and make deployment decisions. However, this rate conflates properties of the model with properties of the audit design (prompting style, judges, definitions of non-compliance, etc.), so changes in the rate are ambiguous: it is unclear whether the model, the measurement procedure, or both changed. This ambiguity can mislead stakeholders and obscure regressions or improvements.
AI.method: The authors propose ASSERT, a specification-driven measurement pipeline. ASSERT requires auditors to write an explicit measurement specification that encodes all key choices behind an audit: behavioral rubric, dialogue setup, simulated users, judges, and evidentiary thresholds for non-compliance. The pipeline helps draft the rubric and test cases, executes the audit on a target GenAI system according to the specification, and outputs a reported compliance rate that is cryptographically or structurally linked to that specification so that each rate can be traced back to its underlying design choices.
AI.result: Using ASSERT in a case study on conversational deception, the authors show that the measured compliance rate of GenAI systems varies substantially when they change elements of the specification: dialogue setup, simulated user behavior, judging protocol, or the bar for determining non-compliance. These changes not only shift absolute reported rates but can also reorder the relative ranking of different GenAI systems under audit.
AI.conclusion: Reported compliance rates for GenAI audits are highly sensitive to measurement design choices, so interpreting them without an explicit specification is unreliable. By tying each reported rate to a clear, written measurement specification, ASSERT makes cross-audit comparisons and changes over time more interpretable and trustworthy, enabling more rigorous, transparent evaluation and governance of GenAI systems.

title: Evaluating Agentic Learning Harness Capabilities Without Labels via the Scaling Hypothesis
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at CAMLIS 2025 (Conference on Applied Machine Learning for Information Security)
summary:
Agentic "Continual Learning Harnesses", systems that pair an LLM with retrieval or memory to improve from feedback without retraining, have shown growing value in cybersecurity. But their value is conventionally measured by gains against labeled benchmarks, an approach that often fails in operational security settings. Benchmark labels are scarce, stale, and unrepresentative, so a practitioner often cannot tell whether a given harness helps at all or which of two is better for their task. Traditional LLM-as-a-judge offers little signal because it is no stronger than the agent it evaluates, and distillation is unreliable on scarce, sporadic, and biased labels.
  We propose a framework for evaluating learning harnesses end-to-end without a labeled benchmark, grounded in the scaling hypothesis. A stronger teacher model provides sparsely sampled corrections to a smaller student with a continual learning harness. We score a harness by how much its student converges toward the teacher over time. Across security tasks, model families, and harness designs, we show that improvement relative to the teacher correlates with improvement relative to a held-out gold standard, validating teacher-relative lift as a proxy for true harness uplift when labels are absent. We further show that LLM-as-a-judge between similarly powered models yields no usable signal. These results suggest that a teacher-sized model can be improved through the same harness when humans provide the same kind of sparse, high-precision corrections.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a way to evaluate continual-learning “harnesses” for LLM agents in cybersecurity without needing labeled benchmarks, by measuring how much a smaller student model with a harness converges toward a stronger teacher model over time.
AI.motivation: In cybersecurity, agentic continual-learning systems that pair LLMs with retrieval or memory show promise, but their benefits are hard to measure in real-world settings. Standard evaluations rely on labeled benchmarks, which are often scarce, outdated, and not representative of operational environments. As a result, practitioners cannot reliably tell whether a specific harness helps or which harness works best for their task. Existing alternatives like LLM-as-a-judge and distillation also break down when labels are sparse, sporadic, or biased, giving weak or misleading signals about true performance gains.
AI.method: The authors introduce an evaluation framework that replaces benchmark labels with guidance from a stronger teacher model. A smaller student LLM is equipped with a continual learning harness (e.g., retrieval or memory mechanism) and interacts with tasks, while a stronger teacher occasionally provides sparse corrective feedback. The key metric is how much the student model’s behavior converges toward the teacher over time, i.e., the teacher-relative lift. This metric is then compared to performance against a held-out gold standard where available, across different security tasks, model families, and harness designs, to assess whether teacher-relative lift is a valid proxy for true harness uplift.
AI.result: Experiments show that students using more effective continual-learning harnesses move closer to the teacher’s outputs over time and that this teacher-relative improvement correlates well with gains on a held-out gold-standard evaluation. In contrast, using LLM-as-a-judge between models of similar capability provides almost no actionable signal about harness quality. The results hold across multiple cybersecurity tasks, different base models, and various harness architectures.
AI.conclusion: Teacher-relative lift—how much a student model with a continual-learning harness converges toward a stronger teacher—serves as a practical, label-free proxy for evaluating harness effectiveness in real-world cybersecurity settings. Since LLM-as-a-judge is ineffective when models are similarly strong and labeled benchmarks are unreliable or unavailable, practitioners can instead rely on sparse corrections from a stronger teacher to assess harness uplift. The findings also imply that models as large as the teacher could benefit from the same harness mechanisms if humans play the role of the teacher by providing sparse, high-precision feedback.

title: Bootstrapping Niche Multilingual Code Translation via Reinforcement Learning with Execution-Based Verifiable Supervision
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Preprint under review
summary: Code translation must preserve executable behavior across many programming languages, yet neural code translation has largely focused on a few popular languages such as C++, Java, and Python. This leaves a niche, many-to-many setting where parallel supervision is sparse, producing plausible but non-executable translations. We address this setting with preference-based reinforcement learning driven by execution-based supervision. Our pipeline firstly expands verifiable seed Python programs into a multilingual pool of execution-validated codes. Using the pool, a base LLM generates translation candidates across language pairs, which we label by their execution outcomes. The resulting preferences are used to train a reward model that scores cross-language translation quality. Finally, we optimize our base LLMs with GRPO over 600 directed language pairs (25 x 24) using the reward model as a signal. To evaluate the niche translation capability, we introduce HumanEval-X++, an execution-based benchmark that extends HumanEval-X to a broad many-to-many language space. We evaluate our approach using Qwen-3.5 4B and 9B models. On HumanEval-X++ and existing benchmarks, it yields consistent gains over the untrained baselines. In particular, the 4B model achieves an average improvement of 13% across all languages on HumanEval-X++, with a gain of 21% on mid-tier languages. Our study establishes a reliable approach of data generation, training, and benchmarking, paving the way toward further bootstrapping the quality of many-to-many translation for programming languages.

AI.tldr: They propose a reinforcement-learning-based pipeline to improve many-to-many code translation between many programming languages using execution-based feedback, and introduce a new benchmark (HumanEval-X++) to evaluate it.
AI.motivation: Existing neural code translation focuses on a few popular languages and mostly one-to-one or limited language pairs. In low-resource, many-to-many settings, there is sparse parallel supervision, so models often produce syntactically plausible but non-executable translations. There is a need for a scalable method that can improve translation quality across many languages using reliable supervision and a benchmark that properly evaluates this niche capability.
AI.method:
1) Start from a set of verifiable Python seed programs.
2) Automatically translate and expand them into multiple programming languages, retaining only those variants whose behavior is execution-validated, forming a multilingual, executable code pool.
3) Use a base LLM to generate translation candidates between many language pairs.
4) Execute these candidates and label them by success/failure, turning execution outcomes into preference data.
5) Train a reward model on these preferences to score cross-language translation quality.
6) Use GRPO (a preference-based RL optimization method) to fine-tune the base LLM on 600 directed language pairs (25 source x 24 target languages) using the reward model as the optimization signal.
7) Build HumanEval-X++, a new benchmark extending HumanEval-X to evaluate many-to-many execution-based code translation.
8) Evaluate Qwen-3.5 4B and 9B models on HumanEval-X++ and other benchmarks.
AI.result: The RL-trained models consistently outperform their untrained baselines on HumanEval-X++ and other existing benchmarks. Specifically, the Qwen-3.5 4B model gains on average 13% performance across all languages on HumanEval-X++ and 21% improvement on mid-tier languages, indicating substantial gains especially for languages that are not top-tier or extremely low-resource.
AI.conclusion: Execution-based, preference-driven reinforcement learning is an effective way to improve many-to-many code translation across a broad language set. The proposed pipeline provides a robust way to generate supervision signals, train models, and evaluate performance. The new HumanEval-X++ benchmark and demonstrated gains on Qwen-3.5 models suggest that this approach can reliably bootstrap and scale translation quality beyond a few popular languages toward a richer multilingual programming ecosystem.

title: SemPlan: Benchmarking Structured Semantic Planning for LLM-Based Queries over Enterprise Data
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Natural-language interfaces to enterprise data must translate underspecified requests into governed, executable behavior while controlling invalid queries, policy failures, cost, and nondeterminism. SemPlan Benchmark evaluates this architectural design space with a deterministic synthetic bilingual benchmark containing 1,800 cases in English and Brazilian Portuguese; 1,200 cases form the frozen scientific evaluation subset. Four architectures are compared under the same model configuration: direct SQL generation (A1), a bounded tool-agent baseline (A2), structured semantic-request generation followed by deterministic planning and execution (A3), and a clarification/stateful semantic-plan variant (A4). Across 4,800 primary records, answer correctness was low in absolute terms: 22.25% for A1, 22.58% for A2, 25.67% for A3, and 24.25% for A4. A3 had the highest observed correctness and significantly exceeded A1, A2, and A4 in the pre-specified paired correctness analysis, while A1 retained the highest policy-correct rate and the lowest unsafe-or-invalid rate. A4 had the lowest mean API cost and lowest false-refusal rate. On a preselected 150-case stability subset, answer-correct repeatability ranged from 92.00% to 98.67%. The results support a trade-off interpretation rather than a universal ranking: additional structural constraints changed failure modes and efficiency, but did not monotonically improve correctness or solve ambiguity and multi-turn state consistency.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SemPlan Benchmark, a deterministic bilingual benchmark to evaluate architectures for natural-language interfaces to enterprise data, revealing trade-offs between correctness, safety, cost, and robustness across four system designs.
AI.motivation: Natural-language access to enterprise data is attractive but challenging: user requests are underspecified and must be mapped to safe, policy-compliant, efficient executable queries while handling ambiguity, invalid requests, and nondeterminism. There is a lack of systematic, controlled benchmarks to compare different architectural approaches (e.g., direct SQL generation vs. mediated semantic planning) under identical model conditions. The authors aim to fill this gap and quantify how different architectural constraints affect correctness, safety, cost, and stability.
AI.method: The authors construct SemPlan Benchmark, a synthetic but deterministic dataset with 1,800 bilingual (English and Brazilian Portuguese) cases, of which 1,200 belong to a frozen evaluation subset. They then instantiate four distinct architectures, all with the same underlying model configuration: (A1) direct natural-language-to-SQL generation; (A2) a bounded tool-agent baseline; (A3) a two-step pipeline that first generates a structured semantic request and then uses deterministic planning and execution; and (A4) a clarification- and stateful-variant of semantic planning. They run 4,800 primary records through these setups, measure answer correctness, policy correctness vs. unsafe/invalid behavior, API cost, false refusals, and repeatability on a 150-case stability subset, and perform pre-specified paired correctness analyses between architectures.
AI.result: Absolute answer correctness is low for all methods, with A3 (semantic-request plus deterministic planning) achieving the highest correctness at 25.67%, compared to 22.25% (A1), 22.58% (A2), and 24.25% (A4). A3 significantly outperforms A1, A2, and A4 in paired correctness analyses. A1 (direct SQL) yields the highest rate of policy-correct behavior and the lowest unsafe-or-invalid rate. A4 provides the lowest average API cost and lowest false-refusal rate. Across a 150-case stability subset, answer-correct repeatability is high, between 92.00% and 98.67%, indicating that when a system is correct once, it tends to remain correct across repeats.
AI.conclusion: No single architecture dominates: instead there are trade-offs between correctness, safety, cost, and failure modes. Introducing more structure, such as semantic planning and clarification turns, changes how systems fail and can improve certain aspects like average correctness or cost, but does not monotonically improve overall accuracy nor fully resolve ambiguity or multi-turn state consistency. SemPlan thus serves as an evaluation framework showing that architectural choices should be driven by specific enterprise priorities (e.g., safety vs. cost vs. accuracy) rather than expecting a universally best design.

title: Scaling Creative Writing Beyond Story-Centric Data with Attribute-Guided Genre Expansion
summary: High-quality creative writing data for large language models (LLMs) remains dominated by story-centric data, limiting models' ability to follow the structural and functional conventions of diverse creative formats. We propose an attribute-guided genre expansion framework for scaling creative writing data beyond story generation. By separating thematic breadth from genre-form control, our framework leverages human-authored story prompts as diverse creative seeds, while utilizing manually curated genre attributes to enforce distinct structural, stylistic, and formatting conventions. We combine these to prompt strong LLMs for genre-faithful query-response pairs, which are then quality-filtered. Applying this framework, we construct the Multi-Genre Collection, a 50K-example corpus spanning 13 creative genres, including story, rap, lyrics, scripts, game design, character design, and other creative formats. Experiments across out-of-distribution writing benchmarks and held-out genre diagnostics demonstrate that models fine-tuned on our data consistently surpass not only base models and writing-specialized baselines, but also models trained on existing writing corpora. Genre-count ablations further indicate that controlled genre expansion, rather than story-centric scaling alone, is a key driver of robust creative writing capability.

AI.tldr: They introduce a method to generate high-quality, diverse creative-writing datasets across many genres (not just stories) by guiding LLMs with explicit genre attributes, and show that fine-tuning on this multi-genre data improves creative performance and robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM creative writing data is heavily skewed toward narrative stories, so models are good at storytelling but weaker at following the specific structural, stylistic, and formatting conventions of other creative formats like scripts, lyrics, or game design documents. There is a need for scalable methods to build high-quality, genre-faithful datasets that cover many creative formats without requiring massive human annotation for each genre.
AI.method: They design an attribute-guided genre expansion framework that decouples thematic content from genre form. Human-authored story prompts are used as seeds for diverse themes, while a manually crafted set of genre attributes encodes the structure, style, and formatting rules for different creative genres. Strong LLMs are then prompted with combinations of prompts and genre attributes to generate genre-faithful query–response pairs. The generated outputs are quality-filtered and compiled into a corpus covering multiple creative genres.
AI.result: Using this framework, they build the Multi-Genre Collection: about 50,000 examples across 13 creative genres (stories, rap, lyrics, scripts, game design, character design, and others). Models fine-tuned on this dataset outperform base LLMs, writing-specialized baselines, and models trained on existing writing corpora on out-of-distribution creative writing benchmarks and held-out genre-specific evaluations. Ablation studies on the number of genres show that adding controlled genre diversity yields more robust creative capabilities than simply adding more story data.
AI.conclusion: Systematic, attribute-guided expansion of creative genres is an effective strategy for improving LLM creative writing ability. Explicit control over genre-specific structural and stylistic attributes, combined with diverse thematic prompts, produces a scalable multi-genre corpus that leads to better generalization and genre adherence than story-centric data scaling alone.

title: How Compliant is Sepsis Treatment? An Expert-Guided Neuro-symbolic Pipeline for Generating Clinical Compliance Insights
comment: This has been submitted and accepted in NeSy 2026 (https://2026.nesyconf.org/)
summary: Verifying whether clinical care follows evidence-based protocols is a natural neuro-symbolic problem, yet the safety-critical setting defeats either paradigm alone. We present an expert-guided pipeline that constrains a large language model strictly to semantic normalization, mapping messy drug and microbiology strings onto a fixed clinical vocabulary, while a Sugeno fuzzy inference system reasons over the normalized events. The fuzzy layer encodes eight Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundle rules and replaces binary judgments with graded scores in [0,1]. Applied to 2,438 MIMIC-IV v3.1 sepsis episodes, it surfaces antibiotic timing as the most critical breakdown (mean 0.24, 13% within one hour), Hour-1 underperformance (mean 36.7%), a 51% elevated-lactate drop-off, and descriptive differences in ICU stay across compliance groups (3.8 versus 5.1 days).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a neuro-symbolic pipeline that uses a constrained large language model for clinical text normalization and a Sugeno fuzzy inference system to check sepsis guideline adherence, revealing key gaps in antibiotic timing and overall Hour‑1 bundle performance in ICU data.
AI.motivation: Ensuring that real-world clinical care follows evidence-based protocols, such as the Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundles, is crucial but difficult: clinical data are messy free-text and existing methods either rely purely on symbolic rules, which struggle with noisy inputs, or on black-box machine learning, which lacks safety and transparency. The authors aim to build a robust, interpretable system that can work on large ICU datasets and reliably assess adherence to sepsis care bundles.
AI.method: The authors design an expert-guided neuro-symbolic pipeline. First, they tightly constrain a large language model to perform only semantic normalization, converting unstructured drug and microbiology text strings into a standardized, fixed clinical vocabulary. Second, they feed these normalized clinical events into a Sugeno-type fuzzy inference system. This system encodes eight rules derived from the Surviving Sepsis Campaign sepsis treatment bundles and outputs graded compliance scores in the continuous range [0,1] instead of binary yes/no judgments.
AI.result: Using 2,438 sepsis episodes from the MIMIC-IV v3.1 ICU database, the system evaluates compliance with the sepsis bundle rules. It identifies antibiotic timing as the main point of failure, with a mean compliance score of 0.24 and only 13% of episodes meeting the one-hour administration target. Overall Hour-1 bundle performance is low, with an average compliance of 36.7%. The analysis also shows a 51% drop-off in adherence when elevated lactate is present and documents clear descriptive differences in ICU length of stay between higher- and lower-compliance groups (3.8 vs. 5.1 days).
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a carefully constrained LLM combined with fuzzy rule-based reasoning can safely and interpretably evaluate adherence to complex clinical protocols from messy ICU data. The fuzzy neuro-symbolic approach captures gradations of compliance, highlights key breakdowns—especially in timely antibiotic delivery—and links these to clinically relevant outcomes such as ICU length of stay, suggesting its potential as a practical auditing and quality-improvement tool for evidence-based sepsis care.

title: Repair, Not Improvement: Decomposing Constrained Decoding in Tool-Call Abstention
summary: Function calling is what the recent accounting of constrained generation explicitly sets aside: it finds the decoder's contribution small for format constraints, then warns in its Section 7 against extrapolating where a constraint encodes a correctness requirement, and names function calling as one. Tool abstention is that case at its sharpest: an enum leaves the wording of an answer alone and narrows the set of answers there are, and declining to call anything is the first it drops. We measure the excluded case. Three conditions over one byte-identical prompt separate a grammar's two jobs: it fixes where generation stops as well as which tokens may be emitted. We evaluate open-weight models from 0.6B to 4B on matched English and Korean items, so the language comparison is made within item. Against an unconstrained decoder, prior work's contrast is negative on abstention in four of six cells with intervals excluding zero, worst -29.5 points, and positive with an interval excluding zero in none. The total is a sum with opposite signs: on the smallest model in Korean the stop token costs -20.0, the enum returns +19.5, and the two leave -0.5. What it recovers is form: of 698 abstentions repaired, 545 had no readable answer and 0 were judgements the scorer refused. On tool-needed items it is positive throughout; abstention leads because it is the preregistered measure, and the pooled number being kinder to the intervention makes moving to it worse rather than better. Both preregistered language claims fail.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies how grammar-based constrained decoding affects tool abstention behavior in function-calling scenarios, disentangling the impact of stop conditions from output token constraints, across English and Korean and multiple model sizes.
AI.motivation: Prior work on constrained generation suggests that format-enforcing grammars contribute little beyond the base model, and explicitly warns against extrapolating these results to constraints that encode correctness, such as function calling. Tool abstention—deciding when not to call a tool—is a particularly sharp case where a grammar restricts the allowable outputs. Yet, the concrete impact of such constraints on abstention accuracy and behavior, especially across languages and model scales, is not well quantified. This paper aims to fill that empirical gap and test preregistered hypotheses about language effects.
AI.method: The authors construct a setting where the same byte-identical prompt is decoded under three conditions that separate a grammar’s two roles: (1) unconstrained decoding, (2) constrained stopping condition (where generation must end at a specific token), and (3) full grammar constraints (fixing both where generation stops and which tokens are allowed, e.g., via an enum that includes an explicit abstain option and tool choices). They focus on tool-calling / tool-abstention decisions, including items where a tool is actually needed, and evaluate open-weight language models ranging from 0.6B to 4B parameters. Matched English and Korean versions of each item enable within-item cross-lingual comparison. Performance differences between decoding regimes are quantified, including confidence intervals, for abstention accuracy and downstream task outcomes.
AI.result: Relative to an unconstrained decoder, the prior work’s aggregate contrast is often negative for abstention: in four of six evaluated cells the constrained setup reduces abstention performance, with confidence intervals excluding zero and the worst decline at -29.5 percentage points. No cell shows a clearly positive effect with an interval excluding zero. Decomposing the grammar’s roles shows that the forced stop token can substantially hurt performance (e.g., -20.0 points for the smallest model in Korean), while the enumeration constraint on allowed outputs yields a nearly offsetting gain (+19.5), netting -0.5 overall. The main benefit recovered by constraints is formal correctness: among 698 abstentions that constraints “repaired,” 545 originally had no readable answer and none were flagged as unscorable judgments. On items where a tool is needed, constrained setups yield consistently positive effects, and abstention remains the preregistered primary measure. However, the pooled estimates, which might seem more favorable to the intervention, actually make the constrained setup look worse when switching to them. Both preregistered claims about language-specific effects are not supported by the data.
AI.conclusion: Grammar-based constrained decoding in function-calling and tool-abstention settings has nuanced effects: enforcing stop tokens can significantly harm abstention accuracy, while constraining the allowed output set via enums can partially compensate by improving formal correctness and recovering unusable outputs. Overall improvements relative to unconstrained decoding are weak or negative in many conditions, and supposed language-specific advantages do not hold under preregistered analysis. The primary gain from these constraints is structural well-formedness, not clearly better abstention judgments, suggesting that care is needed when extrapolating from format-only constraints to correctness-encoding grammars in tool-calling scenarios.

title: Algorithm Design and Physician Liability
comment: 65 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables; includes online appendix (pp. 51-65)
summary: A single clinical algorithm can deliver unequal accuracy across patient groups, and concern about such disparity has grown as artificial intelligence (AI) spreads through clinical decision-making. In response, a liability rule introduced in the United States holds healthcare providers responsible when their reliance on disparate algorithms contributes to erroneous clinical decisions. We examine how such liability considerations reshape (i) an AI firm's algorithm design decisions that drive group-specific accuracy and (ii) a physician's decisions to use AI in healthcare delivery. The AI firm designs an algorithm for two patient groups, and improving accuracy for the disadvantaged group is more costly. The physician (who remains the accountable decision-maker) then decides whether to consult AI, weighing the reduction in clinical uncertainty against expected liability exposure when AI errors disproportionately affect the disadvantaged group. We find the liability rule can induce disparate use of AI: the physician may reduce AI use overall and, over an intermediate range of liability, rely on AI less for disadvantaged patients. The effect is non-monotone. As liability increases, the physician's use of AI for disadvantaged patients first declines, then rises as the firm reallocates investment toward reducing disparity or switches to an equal-accuracy design. Mandating equal algorithmic accuracy across patient groups can then inadvertently harm both groups, because a uniform accuracy requirement distorts the firm's investment incentives and the physician's equilibrium AI-use decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how liability rules for inaccurate clinical AI affect algorithm design, physician adoption, and fairness between patient groups, and shows that well‑intentioned rules can backfire and harm both groups.
AI.motivation: As AI tools become integrated into clinical decision-making, their accuracy often differs across patient groups, raising fairness concerns. A new U.S. liability rule makes providers responsible when using algorithms that exhibit disparate performance leads to errors, but it is unclear how this legal pressure changes the behavior of AI developers and physicians, and whether it actually reduces disparities or instead produces unintended negative consequences.
AI.method: The authors build a theoretical model with two strategic agents: an AI firm that selects accuracy levels for two patient groups subject to different marginal costs of improving accuracy, and a physician who decides when to consult AI given clinical uncertainty and potential legal liability. They analyze the equilibrium outcomes in terms of group-specific AI accuracy, AI adoption rates by group, and overall welfare, and then compare regimes with and without liability rules and with or without mandated equal accuracy across groups.
AI.result: The model shows that the liability rule can lead physicians to use AI less overall, and in a certain liability range, to use it less specifically for the disadvantaged group whose accuracy is initially lower and costlier to improve. This effect is non-monotone: as liability tightens, AI use for disadvantaged patients first falls, but then rises once the firm optimally reallocates investment toward that group or switches to designing an algorithm with equal accuracy across groups. Additionally, imposing a regulatory requirement of equal accuracy across groups can reduce welfare for both groups by distorting how the firm allocates investment and how physicians respond in their AI-use decisions.
AI.conclusion: Liability rules aimed at curbing reliance on disparate clinical algorithms can unintentionally create disparate AI use and reduce the overall adoption of beneficial AI tools, particularly harming disadvantaged patients over some liability ranges. Furthermore, simple mandates for equal algorithmic accuracy across groups may backfire by misaligning incentives for both AI developers and physicians. Effective policy design must account for the strategic responses of both firms and clinicians, rather than assuming that liability or equal-accuracy requirements will automatically improve fairness and outcomes.

title: Batch-wise Adaptive Pruning: Periodic Neuron Activation-Aware Weight Pruning for Language Reasoning Model
comment: Accepted at COLM 2026. 28 pages, 12 figures, 18 tables. Code: https://github.com/matsuolab/batch-wise-prune
summary:
Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks through extended chain-of-thought generation, but incur substantial computational costs during inference. In production settings, batched inference is essential for high throughput, yet the existing training-free adaptive pruning methods we evaluate severely degrade in this regime. Because a batch must share a single pruning mask, these methods aggregate activations across samples and then apply threshold-based selection; the threshold, calibrated offline on unaggregated activations, no longer matches the aggregated distribution, so the realized sparsity ratio drifts and accuracy on reasoning tasks collapses under batched inference.
  In this work, we propose a training-free adaptive pruning method designed specifically for batched inference in LRMs, built on two components. First, we replace threshold-based selection with periodic top-k selection over the aggregated importance scores, which is unaffected by the shift that aggregation induces in the activation distribution, and which runs selection once per update period rather than at every token, preserving the speedup. Second, based on the observation that important neurons re-fire periodically during long reasoning generation, we introduce an activation memory that accumulates importance across update phases so that recurring neurons are retained.
  Experiments on diverse reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art adaptive pruning method by 39.7 percentage points in average accuracy at batch size 4 with 50% target sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and reaches 1.40x speedup over dense inference at 50% actual sparsity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a training-free pruning scheme tailored for batched inference in Large Reasoning Models that preserves accuracy while delivering speedups via adaptive, memory-augmented top-k neuron selection.
AI.motivation: Large Reasoning Models use long chain-of-thought generation, which makes inference computationally expensive. Practical deployments require batched inference for throughput, but existing adaptive pruning methods break down in this regime because they rely on shared, threshold-based pruning masks whose calibration fails once activations are aggregated across samples, causing sparsity ratio drift and major accuracy loss.
AI.method: The authors design a training-free adaptive neuron pruning algorithm specifically for batched inference. Instead of offline-calibrated thresholds, they periodically perform top-k selection on aggregated importance scores to determine a shared pruning mask for the batch, avoiding distribution-shift issues and reducing selection overhead by updating only every few tokens. Additionally, they introduce an activation memory that accumulates and carries forward neuron importance across update phases, leveraging the observation that key neurons tend to re-fire periodically during long reasoning chains so that such neurons are preferentially retained.
AI.result: Across multiple reasoning benchmarks with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the proposed method significantly outperforms prior adaptive pruning: at batch size 4 and a 50% target sparsity, it improves average accuracy by 39.7 percentage points relative to the previous state of the art, and at 50% realized sparsity it achieves a 1.40x inference speedup over dense execution.
AI.conclusion: By rethinking adaptive pruning around the constraints of batched inference—using batch-level top-k selection and an activation memory—the method avoids sparsity drift, preserves important recurrent neurons, and delivers substantial speedup with far less accuracy degradation on complex reasoning tasks, making LRMs more practical for high-throughput deployment.

title: Your Probabilistic JEPA Is Secretly a Hidden Markov Model: A State-Space Interpretation of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning
summary: A hidden Markov model (HMM) combines three roles: inference of a hidden-state belief from observations, propagation through a Markov transition, and emission back to observation space. We show that full, time-indexed Predictive Information Bottleneck VJEPA (PIB-VJEPA) exposes the same computational structure: a stochastic context encoder plays the role of an amortized filtering distribution, a probabilistic predictor defines latent-state dynamics, and a decoder, inverse target encoder, or induced implicit conditional supplies the emission direction. We distinguish 4 progressively stronger levels of correspondence and give sufficient conditions for exact sequence-level HMM equivalence. To make the connection concrete, we introduce Markov-Chain JEPA (MCJEPA), which replaces the latent predictor by a learned transition matrix; in the finite time-homogeneous case, matrix powers guarantee exact multi-horizon Chapman--Kolmogorov consistency. Conditioned discrete-state transitions, continuous-state Markov kernels, and continuous-time dynamics extend this construction, while deterministic temporal JEPA appears as a degenerate Dirac-kernel special case. We further interpret predictive information-bottleneck learning as seeking a compact predictive state: compression promotes minimality, while residual predictability tests sufficiency. Controlled experiments support transition composition, the filtering interpretation, predictive Markovization in a known synthetic process, and the distinction between JEPA latent prediction and HMM-style sequence learning. Together, these results give temporal JEPA a principled state-space interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a temporal JEPA trained with the predictive information bottleneck is computationally equivalent to a Hidden Markov Model under certain conditions, giving JEPA a principled state-space interpretation.
AI.motivation: Temporal JEPA models are powerful for self-supervised representation learning but lack a clear probabilistic state-space interpretation. Meanwhile, Hidden Markov Models have a well-understood structure for latent-state inference, transition, and emission. The authors aim to bridge these views, clarifying when and how JEPA behaves like an HMM, and to ground predictive information bottleneck learning in the theory of compact predictive state representations.
AI.method: They analyze the computational structure of full time-indexed PIB-VJEPA and map its components onto the three HMM roles: (1) the stochastic context encoder as an amortized filtering distribution, (2) a probabilistic latent predictor as latent-state dynamics, and (3) a decoder/inverse target encoder/implicit conditional as the emission model. They formalize four levels of correspondence between PIB-VJEPA and HMMs and derive sufficient conditions for exact sequence-level equivalence. To instantiate this, they introduce Markov-Chain JEPA (MCJEPA), replacing the generic latent predictor by a learned transition matrix whose powers enforce Chapman–Kolmogorov consistency over multiple horizons. They further generalize to conditioned discrete transitions, continuous Markov kernels, and continuous-time dynamics, and analyze deterministic temporal JEPA as a Dirac-kernel limiting case. Finally, they run controlled experiments to test transition composition, filtering behavior, predictive Markovization on synthetic data, and differences between JEPA latent prediction and full HMM sequence learning.
AI.result: They demonstrate that PIB-VJEPA has the same three-part computational structure as an HMM and identify conditions under which a temporal JEPA can be exactly equivalent to an HMM at the sequence level. MCJEPA provides a concrete instantiation where the learned transition matrix yields exact multi-step Chapman–Kolmogorov consistency via matrix powers. Experiments confirm that JEPA can implement proper transition composition, behaves like a filter over latent states, can recover Markov structure in a known synthetic process (predictive Markovization), and that there are meaningful differences between JEPA-style one-step latent prediction and classical HMM sequence learning.
AI.conclusion: Temporal PIB-VJEPA can be understood as a probabilistic state-space model closely analogous to an HMM, with its encoder, predictor, and decoder corresponding to filtering, transition, and emission components. Under suitable assumptions, JEPA can be made exactly sequence-equivalent to an HMM, and MCJEPA provides a Markov-chain-based realization with strong multi-horizon consistency. Predictive information bottleneck training can be interpreted as learning a compact, sufficient predictive state: compression enforces minimality of the state, while residual predictability tests its sufficiency. This grants temporal JEPA a principled state-space and predictive-state interpretation, clarifying its behavior and guiding future model design.

title: S2Dialog: Multimodal Dialogue Retrieval with Semantic and Acoustic-Style Modeling
summary: Multimodal dialogue retrieval aims to retrieve dialogues from multimodal dialogue banks that are similar to a target dialogue in terms of both textual semantics and acoustic conversational styles. Such dialogue-level retrieval is crucial for many dialogue-related tasks, including Emotion Recognition in Conversation, Spoken Dialogue Systems, and Conversational Speech Synthesis, where external dialogue examples can provide valuable semantic and stylistic references. However, existing retrieval methods are still largely limited to utterance-level or unimodal matching, and often fail to capture the global semantic coherence and stylistic consistency of an entire dialogue. To address this gap, we propose S2Dialog, a unified framework for dialogue-level semantic-style retrieval from multimodal dialogue banks. Specifically, S2Dialog consists of a Dialogue-level Textual Retriever and a Dialogue-level Acoustic Retriever, which encode the textual and acoustic modalities of a dialogue into dialogue-level representations, respectively. To further enhance multimodal retrieval, we introduce Dialogue-level Textual-Acoustic Contrastive Learning, which aligns semantically and stylistically similar dialogues while distinguishing unrelated ones. Extensive experiments on the multimodal dialogue dataset DailyTalk demonstrate that S2Dialog achieves outstanding retrieval performance.

AI.tldr: They propose S2Dialog, a framework that retrieves whole dialogues from multimodal dialogue banks by considering both textual semantics and acoustic conversational styles, using dialogue-level representations and contrastive learning to outperform prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval systems mostly work at the utterance level or on a single modality (usually text), so they miss the global semantic coherence and consistent speaking style that span an entire dialogue. Many downstream tasks like emotion recognition in conversation, spoken dialogue systems, and conversational speech synthesis benefit from retrieving whole dialogues that are both semantically similar and stylistically aligned to a target dialogue. There is a clear gap in methods that perform such dialogue-level, multimodal semantic-style retrieval.
AI.method: They introduce S2Dialog, a unified multimodal retrieval framework with two main components: (1) a Dialogue-level Textual Retriever that encodes the textual content of an entire dialogue into a single dialogue-level representation capturing global semantics, and (2) a Dialogue-level Acoustic Retriever that encodes the acoustic features of the whole dialogue into a dialogue-level representation capturing conversational style. On top of these, they design Dialogue-level Textual-Acoustic Contrastive Learning, which jointly trains the two retrievers by pulling together representations of dialogues that are semantically and stylistically similar and pushing apart those of unrelated dialogues, thereby aligning textual and acoustic spaces for improved multimodal retrieval.
AI.result: On the DailyTalk multimodal dialogue dataset, S2Dialog achieves significantly better dialogue-level retrieval performance compared with existing utterance-level or unimodal baselines, showing stronger ability to retrieve dialogues that are coherent in meaning and consistent in acoustic style with a target dialogue. The experiments are extensive, validating the framework's effectiveness across multiple retrieval metrics.
AI.conclusion: Dialogue-level multimodal retrieval that jointly accounts for semantics and acoustic style is both feasible and beneficial. S2Dialog, with its dual dialogue-level retrievers and contrastive learning across text and audio, effectively captures global semantic coherence and stylistic consistency, leading to improved retrieval quality. This makes it a strong foundation for enhancing downstream tasks such as emotion recognition in conversation, spoken dialogue systems, and conversational speech synthesis that rely on high-quality example dialogues.

title: ARC: Fair Relative Advantage Comparison in Open-Ended Real-World Interaction
summary: Open-ended real-world interaction admits multiple valid behaviors: an agent may answer directly, ask for clarification, provide progress updates, or confirm before acting. This flexibility breaks a core assumption behind group-based RL: rollouts compared within a group are no longer guaranteed to be behaviorally comparable. As a result, reward-model preferences over interaction style can distort relative advantages and steer optimization toward reward-preferred behaviors rather than context-appropriate ones. We formalize this as a \textit{reward fairness problem} and propose \textbf{ARC} (Advantage Regularization via Conditioning), a training recipe that restores fairer relative comparison through strategy-conditioned rollout grouping, together with hybrid rewards and entropy regularization. We study ARC in our proposed \inter, a novel paradigm for responsive, steerable, and execution-aware user-agent interaction that decouples user-visible communication from latent reasoning and tool use. \inter\ also provides the annotation and distillation pipeline for constructing \inter-86K, our strategy-annotated training corpus for supervised and RL training. Empirically, ARC substantially strengthens the core $τ/τ^2$ tool-use benchmarks, while \inter\ reduces time-to-first-token from 4.91s to 1.27s relative to a think-style baseline. Together, these results suggest that a central bottleneck in open-ended interactive learning is not only how agents are rewarded, but whether their behaviors are compared fairly in the first place. The ARC implementation and \inter-86K training data will be released.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and addresses a reward fairness problem in RL for open-ended interactions, proposing ARC and the INTER framework to fairly compare different valid interaction styles and improve tool use and responsiveness.
AI.motivation: In open-ended, real-world user-agent interactions, there are often multiple valid behaviors (e.g., answering, asking clarifying questions, confirming actions). Traditional group-based RL assumes rollouts in a comparison group are behaviorally comparable, which breaks under such diversity. This leads reward models to favor particular interaction styles rather than truly better, context-appropriate behaviors, skewing learning and harming performance. The authors are motivated to fix this unfair comparison problem so that RL optimization reflects genuine advantages rather than stylistic biases, and to design a practical interaction paradigm and dataset that support such fair training.
AI.method: The authors formalize the mismatch as a reward fairness problem and introduce ARC (Advantage Regularization via Conditioning), a training recipe that conditions rollout grouping on strategy, so that comparisons are made among behaviorally similar trajectories. ARC combines: (1) strategy-conditioned grouping of rollouts for fairer advantage estimation, (2) hybrid rewards, and (3) entropy regularization to maintain behavioral diversity. They also propose INTER, an interaction paradigm that separates user-visible communication from latent reasoning and tool use, enabling responsive, steerable, execution-aware interactions. INTER provides an annotation and distillation pipeline used to construct INTER-86K, a strategy-annotated corpus for supervised and RL training.
AI.result: Empirically, applying ARC significantly improves performance on τ/τ² tool-use benchmarks, indicating stronger tool-use capabilities under the proposed training scheme. Using INTER reduces time-to-first-token from 4.91 seconds to 1.27 seconds compared with a think-style baseline, showing much faster responsiveness while preserving reasoning and tool-use capacity. These results collectively support that fairer comparison of behaviors in RL improves both capabilities and user experience metrics like latency.
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that in open-ended interactive learning, a key bottleneck is not just the reward signal itself but the fairness of behavior comparisons during RL optimization. By conditioning comparisons on strategy and using the INTER paradigm with annotated data, they can mitigate reward-style biases, leading to fairer, more effective training and better real-world interaction performance. They plan to release the ARC implementation and INTER-86K dataset to facilitate further research.

title: HERMES: a multi-agent framework for structured knowledge extraction from ultra-long documents in geoscience
comment: 31-page main manuscript with 6 figures and 3 tables; supplementary information included
summary: Authoritative scientific knowledge in geoscience remains largely trapped in legacy monographs and historical literature, where unstructured text and complex layouts hinder computational access. We introduce HERMES, a scalable multi-agent framework that extracts structured data from ultra-long scientific documents. Using a coordinating large language model, HERMES integrates domain constraints, validation rules and evidence tracing within a unified document-level extraction process that incorporates parsed text, tables, figures and captions. Applied to the 55-volume Treatise on Invertebrate Paleontology, the system produced a structured database of 32,277 fossil taxonomic entities and 451,878 attributes, released online at https://treatise.geolex.org. Extraction performance remained stable across fossil groups (average F1 scores of approximately 0.90 for entities and 0.91 for attributes), improving per-volume efficiency approximately sixfold relative to the tested fully manual baseline. Evaluation in palaeomagnetism and geochemistry, conducted without additional model training, demonstrated transfer across distinct geoscience domains. This work provides a practical pathway to transform historical scientific literature into FAIR-oriented structured data, offering a sustainable infrastructure for data-intensive disciplines and large-scale knowledge integration.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HERMES, a scalable multi-agent LLM-based framework to convert ultra-long, complex scientific monographs into structured, FAIR-ready databases, demonstrated on invertebrate paleontology and transferred to other geoscience domains.
AI.motivation: Authoritative geoscience knowledge is locked in legacy monographs and historical literature with unstructured text and complex layouts, making it difficult to access computationally, integrate into databases, and reuse for data-intensive research. Manual extraction is slow, expensive, and not scalable across thousands of pages and heterogeneous document formats. There is a need for a robust, scalable method to automatically extract high-quality structured data from such ultra-long, complex documents spanning text, tables, and figures while ensuring validation and traceability.
AI.method: The authors design HERMES, a multi-agent framework orchestrated by a coordinating large language model. The system processes entire ultra-long documents and integrates multiple inputs: parsed main text, tables, figures, and captions. Domain constraints and validation rules are encoded into the workflow to enforce consistency and correctness, and evidence tracing links each extracted item back to its source in the document. Multiple specialized agents collaborate under LLM coordination to perform document understanding, candidate extraction, validation, and consolidation into a structured schema. The pipeline is evaluated on the Treatise on Invertebrate Paleontology and additionally tested, without retraining, on documents from palaeomagnetism and geochemistry.
AI.result: On the 55-volume Treatise on Invertebrate Paleontology, HERMES generated a structured database containing 32,277 fossil taxonomic entities and 451,878 associated attributes, made publicly available online. Extraction quality was high and consistent across different fossil groups, with average F1 scores of about 0.90 for entities and 0.91 for attributes. Compared to a fully manual extraction baseline, the system improved per-volume efficiency by roughly a factor of six. Zero-shot tests on palaeomagnetism and geochemistry literature showed that the framework can transfer to other geoscience domains without additional model training.
AI.conclusion: HERMES demonstrates that a coordinated multi-agent LLM framework can reliably and efficiently convert complex, ultra-long scientific monographs into high-quality structured data. The approach scales across fossil groups and generalizes to other geoscience subfields, providing a practical route for transforming historical scientific corpora into FAIR-compliant resources. This creates sustainable infrastructure for data-intensive geoscience, facilitates large-scale knowledge integration, and offers a template for similar efforts in other scientific disciplines that rely on legacy literature.

title: Reward Machines for Signal Temporal Logic
summary: Signal temporal logic (STL) provides a formal language for specifying real-time properties of real-valued observations, along with a quantitative robustness score for monitoring satisfaction. Control synthesis from STL specifications is of interest since manual controller design becomes infeasible as real-world systems grow in complexity. Moreover, many modern autonomous and AI-enabled systems lack accurate and complete system models, which makes optimization-based synthesis approaches unsuitable and motivates learning-based control. Prior work uses STL robustness scores as rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) to obtain control policies satisfying given specifications; however, robustness depends on execution history, leading to intractable state space expansion for general long-horizon specifications with arbitrarily nested temporal operators. This work introduces a novel automata-based approach that provides an efficient memory mechanism and associated Markovian rewards suitable for RL frameworks. Our approach constructs a timed alternating automaton from the given STL specifications, augments the state space with automaton locations and clock valuations, and derives rewards from the automaton acceptance condition. We empirically demonstrate that our approach learns policies that achieve higher robustness scores and satisfaction rates than those learned by existing approaches using robustness-based rewards.

AI.tldr: They propose an automata-based reinforcement learning framework that turns Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications into Markovian rewards via timed alternating automata, enabling efficient learning of controllers that better satisfy complex temporal specifications.
AI.motivation: Designing controllers that satisfy complex real-time STL specifications is hard, especially when system models are inaccurate or unavailable. Existing reinforcement learning approaches directly use STL robustness as a reward, but robustness depends on full execution history, which makes the state space explode for long and nested temporal properties and becomes computationally intractable.
AI.method: They translate an STL specification into a timed alternating automaton that compactly encodes the temporal structure and necessary memory.
