The RL agent’s state is augmented with the automaton location and clock valuations, turning the problem into a Markov decision process. Rewards are derived from the automaton’s acceptance condition, yielding Markovian rewards instead of history-dependent robustness signals.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations (on benchmark control tasks) show that policies trained with the proposed automata-based Markovian rewards achieve higher STL robustness and higher satisfaction rates than policies trained with conventional robustness-based rewards, demonstrating more reliable satisfaction of the temporal logic specifications.
AI.conclusion: Automata-based shaping of STL specifications into Markovian rewards is an effective way to enable reinforcement learning of controllers under complex temporal constraints, outperforming direct robustness-based reward designs and providing a scalable memory mechanism for long-horizon STL tasks.

title: The conditional superiority of fast silicon sampling
summary: Silicon sampling can produce surprisingly good population estimates at times. Does doing it fast attenuate such fidelity? In this study, we extend and assess ongoing work in silicon sampling by comparing the algorithmic fidelity of "fast" and "slow" modes of silicon sampling among a nationally representative sample of Singaporean survey respondents. We find that silicon sampling with contemporary frontier models remains a method in early development to be used only with great caution. While silicon samples are able to produce moderately faithful estimates of population means, they continue to understate opinion variance and distort the latent contextual space behind human opinions. Conditional on such limitations, we find "fast" modes of silicon sampling to be relatively superior to traditional "slow" modes of silicon sampling. Fast silicon sampling is significantly more efficient in compute resources and run-time while being monotonically superior to slower modes of sampling in algorithmic fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates fast vs. slow modes of silicon sampling, finding that fast modes are more efficient and at least as accurate, but overall the method is still immature and should be used cautiously.
AI.motivation: To understand whether performing silicon sampling in a faster, more computationally efficient way degrades the quality of population-level estimates compared to slower, traditional modes.
AI.method: The authors compare the algorithmic fidelity of fast and slow silicon sampling modes using contemporary frontier models, benchmarking them against a nationally representative survey of Singaporean respondents. They examine how well each mode recovers population means, opinion variance, and the latent contextual structure of human opinions.
AI.result: Silicon sampling can produce moderately accurate estimates of population means but systematically understates opinion variance and distorts the underlying opinion space. Within these limitations, fast silicon sampling outperforms slow sampling: it is more compute- and time-efficient and shows monotonically better algorithmic fidelity across evaluated metrics.
AI.conclusion: Silicon sampling remains an early-stage, high-risk method that should be applied with great caution due to its biases in variance and latent structure. However, when it is used, fast silicon sampling is preferable to traditional slow modes because it is both more efficient and at least as, if not more, faithful to actual survey data.

title: A Calibrated Test of Internal Action Maps: State Signals Without Global Affine Closure
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; includes supplementary results and ancillary reproducibility files
summary: A hidden state signal can be decodable or causally usable without supporting a reusable action map. We test whether action maps fitted without a source reach its natural post-action activation and compose. We organize the tests as an evidence lattice and validate the geometric branch on a known affine S_5 carrier: all held-source folds pass one-step, composition, inverse, decoding, and commutativity gates. Structured curvature and held-domain conjugacy raise error monotonically, but only 23/30 strongest cells flip a closure gate, bounding rather than universalizing calibration. In post-trained Qwen/Qwen3-4B, frozen final-token h28 affine maps have mean held-entity error .519, versus .398 for within-test-domain cross-fit. Seven randomized entity splits and map geometry do not support a purely entity-specific account. Earlier h4/h16 layers fit one-step transitions better, but h4 conflict-state decoding is weak and lexical controls remain unresolved. Three matched intervention datasets regenerated from one frozen checkpoint show causal effects only at h28/h36. Outcome-aware refitting improves h28 one-step error to .474 (.469 with weighting), yet no refit passes composition. Learned finite worlds likewise preserve relative algebraic signals or shared charts without held-source affine closure. Within the tested carriers, state availability, causal use, local geometry, and reusable closure are separable. The result is limited to one pretrained model, sampled final-token layers, two finite worlds, and the tested affine or diagnostic function classes.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when hidden state representations in language models support reusable action maps and finds that decodability and causal usability do not guarantee algebraic closure or compositionality.
AI.motivation: To clarify whether internal hidden states in language models that can be decoded or causally manipulated also support robust, reusable algebraic structures ("action maps") that generalize across entities, inputs, and compositions, rather than just working in narrow, test-specific settings.
AI.method: Fit affine action maps on hidden states of Qwen/Qwen3-4B at different layers and test them on a suite of algebraic and causal criteria organized as an evidence lattice: one-step transitions, composition, inverses, decoding, commutativity, and closure under held-out sources or entities. Use held-source and held-entity evaluation, randomized entity splits, structured geometric perturbations (curvature, conjugacy), and matched intervention datasets from a frozen checkpoint to probe causal effects and map geometry in multiple finite-world tasks. Compare final-token layers (h28/h36) to earlier layers (h4/h16) and explore outcome-aware refitting and weighted losses.
AI.result: Affine maps at final-token layers (especially h28) can decode and causally influence states and pass several algebraic tests (one-step, composition, inverse, decoding, commutativity) on known carriers when sources are not held out. However, when testing closure on held-out sources/entities, many cells fail: only 23/30 strongest cells flip a closure gate, suggesting bounded calibration instead of universal algebraic closure. Held-entity errors are higher than cross-fit within-domain errors (.519 vs .398), and seven randomized entity splits plus geometric analysis rule out a purely entity-specific explanation. Earlier layers better fit one-step transitions but show weak decoding and unresolved lexical confounds. Causal interventions show reliable effects only at higher layers (h28/h36). Refitting (including outcome-aware and weighted) improves one-step errors somewhat but still fails composition tests. Similar patterns hold across two finite-world settings.
AI.conclusion: Hidden state decodability and causal manipulability in Qwen/Qwen3-4B do not imply that the model implements clean, reusable algebraic action maps with strong closure and compositionality across entities and domains. Instead, state availability, causal use, local geometric structure, and algebraic closure come apart: models can show strong local or task-specific structure without supporting globally reusable action maps. These findings, though limited to one model, a few layers, two finite worlds, and affine/diagnostic maps, caution against over-interpreting decoded or causally probed representations as evidence of fully formed symbolic or group-like structures.

title: Leading-Silence Augmentation and Multi-Stage Synthetic Supervision for the Second MLC-SLM Challenge
summary: The second Multilingual Conversational Speech Language Model (MLC-SLM) Challenge evaluates two tasks over complete, unsegmented multilingual conversations: speaker diarization and recognition (Task 1) and conversational speech understanding (Task 2). Neither task provides oracle utterance boundaries or speaker labels at evaluation, and Task 2 provides no question-answer training set. For Task 1, we fine-tune VibeVoice-ASR-7B with random leading-silence cropping, consistent timestamp correction, and an exponential moving average (EMA) training strategy. For Task 2, we construct synthetic question-answer pairs through multimodal candidate generation, silent-audio filtering, and distribution-matched augmentation, and fine-tune Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct for tagged direct answering. On the Task 1 evaluation set, cropping reduces tcpMER from 18.30% to 17.27%, and EMA further reduces it to 16.73%. On the Task 2 evaluation set, jointly applying distribution-matched augmentation and tagged direct answering raises accuracy from 83.0% to 86.0%.

AI.tldr: They present systems for the MLC-SLM Challenge, improving multilingual conversational speaker diarization/recognition (Task 1) and question answering without oracle labels or QA training data (Task 2), achieving notable error reduction and accuracy gains through tailored fine-tuning and data augmentation.
AI.motivation: The challenge evaluates realistic multilingual conversational scenarios where utterances are not pre-segmented and speaker labels or QA training sets are unavailable. This setting makes standard supervised approaches less effective and motivates methods that can cope with unsegmented audio, missing oracle metadata, and limited task-specific supervision for conversational understanding.
AI.method: For Task 1 (speaker diarization and recognition), they fine-tune the VibeVoice-ASR-7B model and introduce: (1) random leading-silence cropping to improve robustness to silences; (2) consistent timestamp correction to better align recognized content with time; and (3) an exponential moving average (EMA) of model parameters during training to stabilize and improve performance. For Task 2 (conversational speech understanding without QA training data), they synthesize question-answer pairs by multimodal candidate generation, filter out silent audio, perform distribution-matched augmentation to align synthetic data with the target distribution, and then fine-tune Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct to produce tagged direct answers.
AI.result: In Task 1, on the evaluation set, adding random cropping reduces tcpMER from 18.30% to 17.27%, and adding EMA further reduces it to 16.73%, indicating cumulative gains from both techniques. In Task 2, on the evaluation set, combining distribution-matched augmentation with tagged direct answering increases accuracy from 83.0% to 86.0%, showing that the synthetic QA construction and tailored answering format significantly improve conversational understanding performance.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed fine-tuning strategies and data augmentation can substantially improve multilingual conversational diarization/recognition and understanding in low-supervision, unsegmented conditions. Techniques like silence cropping, timestamp correction, EMA training, and synthetic QA construction with distribution matching and tagged answers yield measurable performance gains in the MLC-SLM Challenge setting.

title: Exploring ESC Winners with Nested Diagrams
comment: Accepted for CONCEPTS 2026 Data Analysis Showcase (CDAS)
summary:
We present ConceptFlow, a scikit-learn-compatible Python library for Formal Concept Analysis that constructs and renders nested line diagrams from many-valued formal contexts. Given a many-valued context and a partition of its attributes into conceptual scales, ConceptFlow performs conceptual scaling, computes the factor lattices, identifies filled nodes of the corresponding subdirect product, and produces an interactive visualization.
  We apply ConceptFlow to the winners of the Eurovision Song Contest from 1975 to 2025, exploring relationships between voting patterns and musical characteristics. Voting support is captured by an outer scale spanning regional, cultural, historical, and political dimensions, while an inner scale captures musical characteristics via tempo and key. The resulting nested line diagram reveals implications across both scales, exposing dependencies between how winning entries were voted for and the musical properties they share.

AI.tldr: ConceptFlow is a Python FCA library that builds and visualizes nested concept lattices from many-valued data, illustrated with Eurovision winner analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing FCA tools and libraries either do not integrate smoothly with common Python/ML workflows or lack automated support for nested line diagrams and conceptual scaling on many-valued contexts. The authors aim to provide a practical, scikit-learn-compatible tool that makes it easy to construct, analyze, and interactively visualize complex conceptual structures from rich, many-valued data.
AI.method: They implement ConceptFlow, a Python library compatible with scikit-learn pipelines. Given a many-valued context and a partition of attributes into conceptual scales, the library automatically performs conceptual scaling, computes factor lattices, detects filled nodes in the corresponding subdirect product, and renders interactive nested line diagrams. They demonstrate the method on a dataset of Eurovision Song Contest winners from 1975–2025, building an outer conceptual scale for voting support (regional, cultural, historical, political dimensions) and an inner scale for musical properties (tempo and key).
AI.result: ConceptFlow successfully generates nested line diagrams from the Eurovision dataset, showing structured relationships between voting patterns and musical features of winning songs. The diagrams reveal implications across the outer and inner scales, making visible dependencies that connect types of voting support with shared musical characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a practical FCA library that integrates with Python/ML ecosystems and enables the construction and interactive visualization of nested concept lattices from many-valued data. The Eurovision case study suggests that ConceptFlow can uncover interpretable dependencies between different types of attributes (here, voting patterns and musical features), illustrating its usefulness for exploratory data analysis in complex, multi-scale domains.

title: How Much Do Legal RAG Systems Still Hallucinate?
summary: Hallucination is a major challenge for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in the legal domain, where ungrounded answers can lead to serious consequences. To better understand this problem, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of hallucination behavior in eight legal RAG systems across two legal corpora, the GDPR (in English) and a national civil law (in French). Using claim-level and answer-level evaluation, we report on hallucination density and severity, analyze performance across question categories and user personas, and validate our findings on an independent set of 142 legal-expert-authored questions. Our results show that hallucinations remain pervasive, ranging from less than 10% of responses for the best-performing systems to nearly half in the worst case. We further find that false-premise questions, containing incorrect assumptions that must be rejected, produce high hallucination rates on the manually-drafted questions.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes hallucination behavior in legal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, showing that hallucinations are frequent and especially triggered by false-premise questions.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations in legal RAG systems can have serious real-world consequences due to incorrect or fabricated legal information. There is a need for a detailed, empirical understanding of how often hallucinations occur, under what conditions, and how severe they are in order to improve the safety and reliability of these systems.
AI.method: The authors evaluate eight different legal RAG systems on two legal corpora: the English GDPR and a French national civil law. They perform both claim-level and answer-level hallucination evaluations, measure hallucination density and severity, compare performance across different question categories and user personas, and confirm patterns with an independent benchmark of 142 questions written by legal experts.
AI.result: Hallucinations are common across systems, with rates ranging from under 10% of answers for the best system to nearly 50% for the worst. False-premise questions—those that embed incorrect assumptions that the system should reject—are found to cause particularly high hallucination rates on the expert-authored question set.
AI.conclusion: Even in specialized legal RAG setups, hallucinations remain pervasive and are strongly influenced by question type, especially false-premise questions. This indicates that current legal RAG systems are not yet reliably safe for unsupervised legal use, and that future work must directly target hallucination reduction, particularly in the face of misleading or incorrect user assumptions.

title: Ontology-Grounded Project Memory for Coding Agents
comment: 5 pages. Accepted at NeSy 2026 (Industry Track); to appear in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research vol. 284. Benchmark artifact: https://github.com/Trivyn/moosedev
summary: Coding agents have become the primary means of generating new code in many software projects, and the resulting velocity of changes makes keeping track of the reasons behind those changes challenging. This paper introduces MOOSEDev, a system designed to give coding agents structured, ontology-grounded project memory. The system captures architectural decisions, lessons, constraints, and rationales in a knowledge graph exposed to agents via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Records carry lifecycle status, provenance, and supersession links, queryable via MOOSE, a proprietary neurosymbolic engine that treats the symbolic layer as the primary reasoning substrate. We compared MOOSEDev against a production vector-memory tool on a neutral public corpus of 835 typed records. MOOSEDev returned the expected answer set essentially in full (0.98-1.00) on supersession, set-completeness, and negation questions, whereas the baseline's top-k retrieval surfaced between 6% and 27%. Conversely, relevance recall and token cost were largely equivalent between the two systems. We also describe a temporal commit-history bootstrap of our own codebase, a pre-registered live trial, and lessons learned.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MOOSEDev, a system that gives coding agents structured, ontology-grounded project memory via a neurosymbolic knowledge graph, and shows it outperforms a vector-memory baseline on complex reasoning queries while maintaining similar relevance and cost.
AI.motivation: Rapid, agent-driven code changes make it hard to retain and surface the rationale, constraints, and architectural decisions behind modifications in a codebase. Existing vector-based memory solutions retrieve related text but struggle with structured reasoning tasks like tracking superseded decisions, completeness of result sets, and negation (e.g., confirming something does not exist). The authors aim to create a more reliable, structured memory layer for coding agents that better reflects software-engineering knowledge and lifecycle semantics.
AI.method: They design MOOSEDev, which structures project knowledge (architectural decisions, lessons learned, constraints, rationales) into an ontology-based knowledge graph. Each record includes lifecycle status, provenance, and supersession relationships. The graph is exposed to coding agents via MCP, and queries are handled by MOOSE, a neurosymbolic engine that uses the symbolic layer as the primary reasoning substrate. They evaluate MOOSEDev against a production vector-memory baseline using a neutral public corpus of 835 typed records. The comparison focuses on supersession tracking, set-completeness, and negation queries, measuring how fully the systems return the expected answer sets, as well as recall and token cost. They also describe a temporal commit-history bootstrap of their own codebase and conduct a pre-registered live trial to test the system in realistic development workflows.
AI.result: On the neutral corpus, MOOSEDev achieved near-perfect performance (0.98–1.00 of the expected answer set) for supersession, set-completeness, and negation questions. The vector-memory baseline, using top-k retrieval, only surfaced 6–27% of the expected answers on these tasks. However, for simpler relevance recall and token cost, the two systems were roughly equivalent. The authors also report qualitative findings from bootstrapping the knowledge graph from commit history and from the live trial, yielding practical insights into how MOOSEDev behaves in real-world development.
AI.conclusion: Structured, ontology-grounded knowledge graphs backed by a neurosymbolic engine can provide coding agents with significantly more reliable project memory for complex reasoning tasks than standard vector-memory approaches, without sacrificing relevance or efficiency. MOOSEDev demonstrates that treating symbolic representations as the primary reasoning substrate enables better handling of lifecycle semantics like supersession and negative evidence, and the authors’ trials suggest this approach is viable for real-world software development workflows.

title: The More Popular, The Harder to Forget: Adaptive Popularity for LLM Unlearning
summary: Popular facts are memorised more deeply during pretraining and resist removal longer than rare ones, yet existing LLM unlearning methods apply uniform gradient pressure regardless of training-data frequency. We propose the AdaPop (Adaptive Popularity) method, which combines local token confidence with a per-fact popularity-dependent exponent derived from an external proxy (e.g., Wikidata sitelinks, LLM-as-Judge), and automates the forget-retain balance via a dual-ascent controller that adjusts the retain penalty each epoch. Across three model families and two benchmarks, AdaPop leaks ~5x less forgotten content than competing methods under paraphrased queries and ~1.6x less under adversarial reformulations. We support our analysis with internal metrics: under our method, forget-set hidden states move further from the pre-unlearning model's states than under other methods, while retain-set representations remain close.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AdaPop, a method that adaptively unlearns facts from LLMs by weighting unlearning strength according to fact popularity and dynamically tuning the retain penalty, achieving better forgetting with less leakage than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM unlearning methods treat all facts equally in terms of unlearning pressure, ignoring that popular, frequently seen facts are more deeply memorized and therefore harder to remove. This leads to incomplete forgetting, especially under paraphrased or adversarial prompts, and risks privacy or safety leaks. The paper aims to create an unlearning approach that is more effective for deeply memorized (popular) facts while still preserving knowledge about retained content.
AI.method: AdaPop scales unlearning gradients using an "adaptive popularity" mechanism: it combines local token confidence (model's own certainty) with a popularity-dependent exponent derived from an external proxy such as Wikidata sitelinks or LLM-as-Judge popularity estimates for each fact. More popular facts receive stronger effective gradient pressure. Additionally, a dual-ascent controller automatically adjusts a retain penalty hyperparameter across epochs to balance forgetting and retention without manual tuning. The method is evaluated across three model families and two unlearning benchmarks.
AI.result: On benchmarks measuring leakage via paraphrased and adversarial queries, AdaPop reduces forgotten content leakage by about 5× compared to baselines for paraphrased prompts and about 1.6× for adversarially reformulated prompts. Internal analyses show that, under AdaPop, hidden states for facts to be forgotten diverge more from the original model’s states (indicating stronger forgetting), while representations of facts to be retained remain closer to the pre-unlearning model (indicating better preservation of non-target knowledge) relative to other methods.
AI.conclusion: Fact popularity significantly affects how strongly an LLM memorizes information, and unlearning methods should account for this. By weighting unlearning based on popularity and dynamically tuning the retain penalty, AdaPop achieves a better trade-off between forgetting and retaining knowledge than existing uniform-gradient approaches, with substantially less leakage of supposedly forgotten content, especially under paraphrase and adversarial tests.

title: Second Thought: Reasoning in Parallel as LLM Agents Act and Observe
summary: LLM agents in the ReAct paradigm alternate between reasoning, acting, and observing, but deliberate reasoning is confined to the Thought phase: while the agent serializes an action and waits for the environment, its reasoning is frozen. We identify this recurring interval for Action and Observation as a reasoning idle window and ask whether it can host additional reasoning in parallel that serves future turns. Therefore, we propose Second Thought, a training-free inference framework that forks four auxiliary branches the instant each Thought phase concludes, decodes them concurrently with the main loop, and merges the generated thoughts back when the environment observation arrives. In this way, Second Thought relocates the added reasoning off the main thread's sequential decoding path. Across three agentic benchmarks and three reasoning LLMs, Second Thought lowers the average turn count in all nine (model,benchmark) pairs and reduces main thread decoding in six of them by up to 43% (roughly 20% on average among those settings), while leaving it essentially unchanged in a seventh; Pass@1 shows no significant change in seven of nine pairs and the two significant differences are +12.4 and +10.2 points. Against a compute-matched control that forces an equivalent budget onto the main thread's own reasoning, it attains strictly higher Pass@1 with 1.3 to 3.2 less sequential decoding in all four settings where the control applies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Second Thought, a training-free framework that performs extra reasoning in parallel during the idle time when an LLM agent waits for environment feedback, reducing total reasoning steps without hurting accuracy.
AI.motivation: In ReAct-style LLM agents, reasoning happens only during the Thought phase. When the agent issues an Action and waits for an Observation, its reasoning is idle, wasting potential compute time. The authors observe these "reasoning idle windows" and ask whether that otherwise unused time can be exploited to improve efficiency or capability by running additional reasoning that will be useful for future turns.
AI.method: The authors introduce Second Thought, an inference-time framework that does not require retraining the model. After each Thought phase, the system forks four auxiliary reasoning branches that continue to decode in parallel with the main agent loop while the agent is waiting for the external environment. These branches explore additional lines of reasoning or future steps. When the Observation from the environment arrives, their outputs are merged back into the main context so the agent can benefit from them. This design moves added reasoning off the main sequential decoding path by exploiting parallelism in otherwise idle windows.
AI.result: Across three agent benchmarks and three different reasoning-focused LLMs (nine combinations in total), Second Thought reduces the average number of turns needed in all nine cases. It also reduces the amount of decoding done on the main thread in six of the nine cases by as much as 43%, with an average reduction of about 20% among those six, and leaves it effectively unchanged in a seventh case. In terms of task performance (Pass@1), seven of nine combinations show no significant change, while two combinations show substantial gains of +12.4 and +10.2 percentage points. When compared to a compute-matched baseline that instead spends the same extra compute budget on the main thread’s own reasoning, Second Thought consistently achieves higher Pass@1 while requiring 1.3 to 3.2 fewer sequential decoding steps in all four applicable settings.
AI.conclusion: Second Thought demonstrates that exploiting the idle windows between Action and Observation in ReAct-style LLM agents allows parallel auxiliary reasoning to improve efficiency and, in some cases, accuracy, without retraining. By offloading additional reasoning onto parallel branches, the approach can cut down main-thread sequential decoding and the total number of interaction turns while maintaining or improving Pass@1 compared with both the standard ReAct process and a compute-matched sequential baseline.

title: SimpleOPD: Simple Tokenizer-Agnostic On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a promising way to transfer reasoning capabilities from stronger teacher models, but applying it to long-context reasoning teachers and short-context students introduces practical challenges, including tokenizer mismatch, teacher-student distribution mismatch, response length explosion, and training instability. In this work, we study this setting by transferring proof-reasoning capabilities from the long-context reasoning model SU-01 to short-context student models. To handle tokenizer differences, we perform OPD in a shared text space and align only tokens that occupy identical text spans under the student and teacher tokenizers. To mitigate the problem of excessive generation length and frequent truncation, we introduce a student reference KL loss and mask the advantages of special termination tokens such as </think> and <|im_end|>. This strategy constrains the student from drifting excessively from its initial policy, thereby mitigating the teacher-student distribution mismatch problem and fostering steady length growth. Experiments on both same-family and different-family student models, including Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Intern-S2, GLM-4.7, Gemma-4, show consistent gains in mathematical reasoning, especially natural-language math proving. Notably, Intern-S2-Preview improves by 21.2 points on ProofBench, reaching 55.2 and surpassing Gemini-2.5-Pro. It also improves on science benchmarks such as HLE and HiPhO, suggesting that OPD transfers reasoning capabilities that generalize beyond the mathematical training domain.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to distill long-context proof reasoning abilities from a strong teacher model into short-context student models using on-policy distillation, addressing tokenizer and distribution mismatches, and shows large gains on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation is promising for transferring reasoning skills from strong LLM teachers, but existing methods struggle when the teacher uses long contexts and different tokenizers from smaller, short-context students. This setting causes practical problems such as tokenizer mismatch, unstable training, overly long or truncated generations, and mismatch between teacher and student behavior. The authors want a robust way to transfer long-context proof reasoning abilities into more efficient, widely usable short-context models.
AI.method: They perform on-policy distillation from the long-context proof-reasoning model SU-01 into various short-context students. To address tokenizer mismatch, they define a shared text space and only align tokens where teacher and student tokenizations cover exactly the same character spans. To control response length and stabilize training, they introduce a student-reference KL loss that penalizes the student from deviating too far from its initial policy, and they mask the advantages of special termination tokens like </think> and <|im_end|> so the student is not incentivized to produce extremely long or truncated outputs. This combination reduces teacher–student distribution mismatch and promotes controlled growth in reasoning length during training.
AI.result: Across multiple student model families (Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Intern-S2, GLM-4.7, Gemma-4), the distilled models show consistent improvements in mathematical reasoning, particularly natural-language proof-style math problems. The Intern-S2-Preview student improves by 21.2 points on ProofBench, achieving a score of 55.2 and outperforming Gemini-2.5-Pro. The distilled students also improve on science reasoning benchmarks such as HLE and HiPhO, indicating that the transferred capabilities are not limited to the math domain.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed on-policy distillation from a long-context reasoning teacher to short-context students—handling tokenizer alignment and controlling teacher–student distribution mismatch—can effectively transfer sophisticated proof reasoning capabilities. The approach yields substantial gains across diverse student architectures and generalizes beyond the math domain to broader scientific reasoning tasks.

title: Learning to Assemble Novel Structures with Unfamiliar Parts under Semantic Constraints
comment: Accepted to, and to appear in the 20th Conference on Neurosymbolic Learning and Reasoning (NeSy 2026)
summary: This paper describes a neurosymbolic architecture for learning to assemble novel structures using evidence from embodied conversations and task demonstrations. We focus on scenarios where an agent encounters, after deployment, semantic constraints on structures--in other words, constraints as to which part types and features make valid structures--that were not available during training, and where it is initially unaware of the relevant structure and component part concepts. The agent must acquire and exploit such knowledge through user interactions while attempting assembly. We study this setting in a simulated toy truck assembly domain, learning from symbolic evidence encoded in natural language and from dense visual observations. Our experiments show that communicating semantic constraints through natural language (e.g., "dump trucks have a dumper") yields more data-efficient online adaptation than relying only on task demonstrations and/or only naming the parts through natural language.

AI.tldr: Neurosymbolic system that learns to assemble new structures by combining language and visual evidence, focusing on post-deployment acquisition of semantic constraints.
AI.motivation: Robots often face new assembly tasks after deployment where rules about valid structures and part relationships were never seen during training. There is a need for systems that can quickly adapt by learning these semantic constraints from human interaction, rather than relying on extensive pre-training data.
AI.method: Propose a neurosymbolic architecture that integrates symbolic information from natural language (about parts and constraints) with dense visual observations from task demonstrations. In a simulated toy truck assembly environment, the agent interacts with a user, receives linguistic descriptions of semantic constraints and part names while attempting to assemble trucks, and updates its internal model online.
AI.result: In experiments on toy truck assembly, providing semantic constraints through natural language (e.g., "dump trucks have a dumper") significantly improves data efficiency for online adaptation compared to using only demonstrations or only language-based part naming without explicit constraints.
AI.conclusion: Encoding semantic constraints via natural language in a neurosymbolic framework enables more efficient and effective post-deployment learning of novel structures than relying solely on demonstrations or simple part naming. This suggests that structured linguistic guidance is a powerful signal for rapid robot adaptation in assembly tasks.

title: Envs-FORGE: Frontier-Optimized Reward-Grounded Environment Synthesis for Agent RL
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for terminal agents needs executable training environments with reliable rewards and useful difficulty. Fixed recipes such as few-shot, Self-Instruct, and Evol-Instruct apply the same prompting policy to every seed, even when the current policy would benefit from a harder, easier, or simply different task. We present Envs-FORGE, a prompting policy that converts verifier rewards into per-seed environment-synthesis actions. Envs-FORGE estimates seed pass rates, scores six projection--direction actions around a target learning frontier, and solves a per-seed mixed-integer linear program (MILP) to choose the action that conditions generation. The selected action drives synchronized rewriting of the instruction, fixtures, oracle solution, tests, and Docker environment; only gold-verified bundles enter RL training. The indexed MILP form also supports optional soft skill coverage for portfolio planning. On Qwen 3.5 35B, Envs-FORGE improves Pass@1 over Base by 9.2 percentage points on tb-core (40.0% to 49.2%) and 6.4 points on tb-2.0 (23.0% to 29.4%), exceeding the strongest fixed-recipe baseline by 2.4 and 2.1 points. It reaches 77.1% on SWE-bench Verified versus 73.4% for Base, and improves tb-core by 6.8--9.2 points across the evaluated 4B--35B models. All synthesis methods export 100 verified environments and use 2.27M--2.88M synthesis tokens, placing the comparison at the same downstream training-set size and the same operational scale. The source code is available at https://github.com/DataArcTech/DataArc-SynData-Toolkit/.

AI.tldr: Envs-FORGE is a prompting-based environment synthesis policy that adaptively generates RL training environments for code agents, using verifier rewards and MILP planning to improve downstream task performance over fixed-recipe data generation methods.
AI.motivation: Existing RL training for terminal/code agents relies on executable environments whose tasks, rewards, and difficulty are statically determined by fixed prompting recipes (e.g., few-shot, Self-Instruct, Evol-Instruct). These approaches do not adapt to the agent’s evolving capabilities: they cannot make tasks harder when the model is ready, easier when it struggles, or simply different when more diversity is needed. This mismatch leads to inefficient learning and suboptimal performance. The paper aims to design an environment-synthesis mechanism that can react to feedback (verifier rewards) and tailor new tasks per seed so that RL training data stays aligned with a desired learning frontier, while also accommodating coverage goals over different skills.
AI.method: The authors propose Envs-FORGE, a prompting policy that transforms verifier feedback into environment-synthesis actions at the per-seed level. For each seed task, Envs-FORGE estimates its current pass rate and then evaluates six candidate projection directions around a target learning frontier, effectively proposing how to adjust difficulty or nature of the task. It formulates a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) per seed to select the best environment-synthesis action under these constraints. The chosen action conditions a coordinated rewriting of all environment components: instruction, fixtures, oracle solution, tests, and Docker runtime. Only environments that pass a gold verifier are kept for RL training. The MILP is indexed so that it can optionally enforce soft constraints on skill coverage, enabling portfolio-style planning over task types. The method is implemented as a prompting pipeline and compared against standard fixed-recipe synthesis baselines with controlled token budgets and environment counts.
AI.result: On Qwen 3.5 35B, Envs-FORGE improves Pass@1 on the tb-core benchmark from 40.0% (Base) to 49.2%, a gain of 9.2 percentage points, and on tb-2.0 from 23.0% to 29.4%, a gain of 6.4 points. Relative to the strongest fixed-recipe baseline, Envs-FORGE still yields additional gains of 2.4 and 2.1 points respectively. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises performance from 73.4% (Base) to 77.1%. Across Qwen models from 4B to 35B parameters, Envs-FORGE boosts tb-core performance by 6.8–9.2 points. All synthesis methods are run under matched conditions: each produces 100 verified environments and consumes roughly 2.27M–2.88M synthesis tokens, ensuring that improvements come from the adaptive policy rather than more data or higher compute.
AI.conclusion: Envs-FORGE demonstrates that turning verifier rewards into per-seed environment-synthesis decisions via MILP-guided prompting leads to more effective RL training for terminal/code agents than fixed instruction-synthesis recipes. By adaptively controlling task difficulty and diversity around a target learning frontier, and by synchronously rewriting all environment artifacts while enforcing verification, the method delivers consistent performance gains at constant data and token budgets. The indexed MILP formulation also enables flexible skill-coverage planning, suggesting a general framework for principled, feedback-driven synthetic environment generation in code-based RL systems.

title: Coverage Aware Active Evaluation for Failure Discovery with Paired Systems
comment: 9 main pages followed by Appendix, total 21 pages, 12 figures
summary: Autonomous systems can fail in rare and heterogeneous ways, making real-world failure discovery difficult under limited testing budgets. Although cheaper proxies such as simulators, lower-fidelity systems, or related policies can be sampled extensively to find failures, proxy failures often do not transfer to the real world due to sim-to-real and system-to-system gaps. The key challenge is therefore to effectively leverage proxy system information for accurate prediction of severe target system failures. We propose an adaptive failure discovery method that combines proxy evaluations with limited target system results to guide scenario selection for target system testing. Our method learns a local predictor of target risk by correcting proxy failure signals using control-variate-inspired residual modeling. To find failures that are both likely and diverse, we combine this predictor with a support-aware mutual-information objective that favors realistic, well-supported regions while expanding coverage across failure modes. Across autonomous driving, manipulation, and quadruped velocity-tracking tasks, our method discovers up to 2$\times$ as many failures as random sampling and active-learning baselines, including severe and diverse failures missed by competing methods.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an adaptive method to discover rare, severe failures in autonomous systems by intelligently combining cheap proxy simulations with limited real-system tests.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems can fail in rare, diverse ways, but testing them extensively in the real world is expensive and constrained by limited budgets. While cheap proxies like simulators or related policies can be used to search for failures, the failures observed in these proxies often do not transfer reliably to the real system because of gaps between simulation and reality or between different systems. There is thus a need for methods that can effectively exploit abundant proxy data together with scarce real-system data to accurately predict and uncover serious failures in the target system.
AI.method: The authors propose an adaptive failure discovery framework that uses evaluations from proxy systems together with a small number of target system test results to guide which scenarios to test on the target system. They build a local predictor of target failure risk by starting from proxy failure signals and then learning a residual correction term, inspired by control variates, to adjust for systematic mismatch between proxy and target. To steer testing toward both likely and diverse failures, they integrate this risk predictor with a support-aware mutual-information objective that prefers realistic, data-supported regions of the scenario space while still encouraging exploration of different failure modes.
AI.result: In experiments on multiple domains—autonomous driving, robotic manipulation, and quadruped velocity-tracking—the proposed method finds up to twice as many failures as random sampling and active-learning-based baselines under the same testing budget. It is able to surface severe and diverse failure cases that competing approaches fail to detect, showing improved efficiency and coverage of the failure space.
AI.conclusion: By leveraging proxy evaluations through residual modeling and an information-theoretic, support-aware objective, the method significantly improves the efficiency and breadth of failure discovery in autonomous systems under limited real-world testing budgets. This demonstrates that carefully calibrated use of proxy data can overcome sim-to-real and system-to-system gaps and reveal more severe, varied failures than existing sampling or active-learning strategies.

title: Local and Global Regimes of Geometric Complexity in Language Model Representations
summary: Intrinsic dimensionality (ID) is widely used to probe the representational complexity of language models, but it remains unclear whether ID differences reflect properties of language itself or artefacts of how the underlying dataset was constructed. In this paper, we focus specifically on how lexical diversity, the number of unique last-token items present in a dataset, affects ID estimates of that dataset. We find a scale-dependent transition between two regimes: at low lexical diversity, conditions with fewer unique final words produce higher ID, while at high lexical diversity, this ordering reverses, and conditions with more unique words produce higher ID. We derive an exact, parameter-free formula for the point at which this reversal occurs, which matches the observed transition point at every scale tested. On the one hand, our results highlight how care must be taken when interpreting the intrinsic dimensionality of a set of representations as a straightforward cue of their complexity. On the other hand, our discovery of the two ID regimes reveals a general principle of organisation of linguistic data in LLMs that sheds new light on their inner manifold structures.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how lexical diversity (number of unique last tokens) in a dataset affects intrinsic dimensionality (ID) estimates of language model representations, finding two opposite regimes separated by an analytically derived transition point.
AI.motivation: Intrinsic dimensionality is widely used to quantify the complexity of language model representations, but it is unclear whether observed ID differences stem from true linguistic complexity or from artefacts of dataset construction. In particular, lexical diversity can vary substantially across datasets, and the authors want to understand systematically how this factor alone shapes ID estimates, to avoid misinterpretation of model complexity and to uncover possible organizing principles of LLM representation manifolds.
AI.method: The authors manipulate lexical diversity by controlling the number of unique last-token items in datasets fed to a language model and then estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of the resulting representations. They analyze the relationship between lexical diversity and ID across scales and identify systematic patterns. They then derive an exact, parameter-free analytical formula for the transition point at which the relationship between lexical diversity and ID qualitatively changes, and compare the theoretical prediction with empirical measurements across different scales.
AI.result: They discover a scale-dependent transition between two regimes: when lexical diversity is low, datasets with fewer unique final tokens exhibit higher intrinsic dimensionality; when lexical diversity is high, the pattern reverses and datasets with more unique final tokens yield higher intrinsic dimensionality. They further show that their analytically derived formula for the reversal point precisely matches the empirically observed transition across all tested scales.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic dimensionality estimates of language model representations are strongly and non-monotonically influenced by lexical diversity, implying that ID cannot be straightforwardly interpreted as a direct measure of representational or linguistic complexity without considering dataset construction. At the same time, the existence of two distinct ID regimes and a precisely predictable transition point reveals a general organizing principle in how linguistic data is embedded in LLM representation manifolds, offering new insight into the internal geometric structure of these models.

title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Pre-registered analysis plan; code and results available
summary:
The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical documentation describing how the system reaches its decisions. Mechanistic interpretability is the obvious source of such evidence, and circuit discovery is its most developed instrument. We ask whether that evidence survives the condition under which it would be relied upon: two competent analysts, the same system, the same tool, different defensible settings.
  We pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, every level taken from a published implementation, and mapped each discovered circuit through a deterministic claim map to a structured Annex IV statement. Across 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small and the indirect object identification task, of which 7,561 produced a claim, the derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738) and the modal claim commands 41.1% of the space. The evidence fails a filability criterion at every tolerance a conformity assessment body would plausibly accept.
  Standardising the single most influential choice, the evaluation metric, leaves the flip rate at 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim entirely and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255 to 0.286), still above the pre-registered threshold. The circuits underlying these claims are structurally near-disjoint, median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%, and functionally uncorrelated at Cohen's kappa 0.015, so the instability is not one mechanism described in different words.
  We give the filability criterion as a standalone protocol, and we report that one of the seven documented discovery objectives does not execute at all on the library's own canonical task. The study covers one model and one task, and whether the conclusion holds at scale is untested.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether mechanistic interpretability-based technical documentation for high-risk AI systems is stable across reasonable analysis choices, finding it is not.
AI.motivation: Under the EU AI Act, providers of high-risk AI must submit technical documentation explaining system behavior. Mechanistic interpretability, and specifically circuit discovery, is a leading candidate for generating such evidence. The authors want to know if this evidence is robust when different competent analysts use defensible but different analysis settings.
AI.method: They pre-register a grid of seven analytic axes (settings), each drawn from prior published implementations, creating 15,840 specifications for circuit discovery on GPT-2 small for the indirect object identification task. Each discovered circuit is mapped via a deterministic claim map to a structured Annex IV-style compliance statement. They then measure how often these derived statements disagree (flip) across different specifications, and analyze structural and functional overlap of the underlying circuits. They also run ablations, standardizing the evaluation metric and removing circuit size from the claim.
AI.result: Out of 15,840 specifications, 7,561 yield a claim. Across pairs of specifications, the compliance statement flips in 73.2% of cases (95% CI 0.725–0.738). The most common claim occurs in only 41.1% of the space. With the evaluation metric standardized, the flip rate is still 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding it fixed still leaves a 27.1% flip rate (95% CI 0.255–0.286), exceeding their pre-registered robustness threshold. The circuits that support these claims are structurally almost disjoint (median Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s κ = 0.015). One of the seven documented discovery objectives fails to run on the canonical library task.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability evidence, in the form of circuit discovery, is highly unstable under reasonable, pre-registered changes in analysis settings, at least for GPT-2 small on an indirect object identification task. This instability persists even after controlling for key choices like evaluation metric or circuit size, and the underlying circuits differ both structurally and functionally. As a result, such evidence fails a proposed “filability” criterion for EU AI Act technical documentation, casting doubt on the reliability of current mechanistic interpretability methods for regulatory compliance. The authors provide the filability protocol as a standalone tool and note that results are limited to one model and task, leaving open whether similar instability occurs at larger scales.

title: A Survey of Large Models in Sports
comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to Findings of ACL 2026
summary: Sports have witnessed growing global enthusiasm in recent years, serving as a vital force for physical health, cultural exchange, social connection, and economic growth. The rapid advancement of large models, particularly (multimodal) large language models (M)LLMs, has demonstrated transformative potential to reshape sports understanding, analysis, and interaction across diverse domains. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of large models in sports, including (i) an overview of tasks and applications across different participant groups; (ii) a detailed analysis of sports-related datasets and benchmarks; and (iii) a critical discussion of current challenges and future directions. Our goal is to establish a foundation for advancing research and practical development of large-model-driven sports intelligence. An open-source GitHub repository is maintained at: https://github.com/Road2Redemption/Awesome_Large_Models_In_Sports1.

AI.tldr: Survey of how large (including multimodal) language models are being used in sports, covering tasks, datasets/benchmarks, and open challenges/future directions.
AI.motivation: Sports play a major role in health, culture, social life, and the economy, and recent advances in (multimodal) large language models show strong potential to transform how sports are analyzed and experienced. However, the field is fragmented: tasks, applications, datasets, and benchmarks in sports+LLMs are not systematically organized, making it hard for researchers and practitioners to navigate or build upon existing work.
AI.method: Conduct a comprehensive literature survey on the use of large models in sports. Categorize work by participant groups and task types, catalog and analyze available sports-related datasets and benchmarks, and synthesize limitations, challenges, and promising research directions. Provide an accompanying open-source GitHub repository to organize and continually update relevant resources.
AI.result: A structured taxonomy of sports-related tasks and applications where large models are used; an organized inventory and analysis of sports datasets and benchmarks relevant to large models; and an articulated set of current challenges and gaps in the field, along with candidate future research directions. All materials are consolidated and shared via an open-source GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: Large (multimodal) language models hold significant promise for advancing sports intelligence, but systematic understanding of tasks, resources, and open problems has been lacking. This survey fills that gap by organizing existing efforts, clarifying challenges, and outlining future directions, thereby providing a foundation and reference point for further research and practical development in large-model-driven sports applications.

title: Simulation-Aware In-Context Policy Improvement for LLM-Aided Analog Layout Refinement
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on LLM-Aided Design (ICLAD 2026)
summary: Analog IC layout design remains a labor-intensive iterative process dominated by simulation-driven refinement. Although end-to-end layout generators accelerate initial placement and routing, they still require experts to manually tune layout optimization parameters with repeated post-layout simulations for stringent design specifications. While Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely adopted for parameter tuning in analog IC design, at the layout level it typically requires hundreds to thousands of evaluations, each involving costly parasitic extraction and post-layout simulation, which makes it impractical. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in improving the sample efficiency of such simulation-driven tuning. However, their restricted access to geometric layout context and design-specific heuristics limits their ability to manipulate the layout optimization process. In this paper, we propose a simulation-aware LLM multi-agent framework that performs in-context policy improvement (ICPI) by iteratively updating layout optimization parameters exposed by an analog layout generator through an act-observe-reflect loop on compact structured layout representations. Experiments on real-world analog circuits show that, with only tens of post-layout simulations, our approach improves post-layout performance over the generator's built-in heuristics and BO-based tuning method.

AI.tldr: They propose an LLM-based multi-agent framework that tunes analog IC layout generator parameters using few post-layout simulations, outperforming built-in heuristics and Bayesian optimization.
AI.motivation: Analog IC layout design is slow and labor-intensive, with end-to-end generators still requiring manual expert tuning and many costly post-layout simulations. Existing Bayesian Optimization methods need hundreds to thousands of evaluations at the layout level, which is too expensive. LLMs could help improve sample efficiency but currently lack access to geometric layout context and design-specific heuristics, limiting their usefulness for layout optimization.
AI.method: They design a simulation-aware multi-agent framework powered by an LLM that performs in-context policy improvement (ICPI). The framework interacts with an analog layout generator via an act-observe-reflect loop, where the LLM updates exposed layout optimization parameters based on compact, structured representations of the layout and observed post-layout performance after simulation.
AI.result: On real-world analog circuit benchmarks, the framework achieves better post-layout performance than both the layout generator’s built-in heuristic tuning and a Bayesian Optimization-based tuning approach, while requiring only tens of post-layout simulations instead of hundreds or thousands.
AI.conclusion: By giving an LLM structured access to layout information and embedding it in an ICPI multi-agent loop, the approach makes analog layout parameter tuning far more sample-efficient and effective, demonstrating that LLM-guided layout optimization can practically surpass standard heuristic and BO-based methods under tight simulation budgets.

title: Information Satisfaction: A Reader-Centered Axis for Summarization Evaluation
summary: The majority of work on summarization evaluation focuses on general summary quality (e.g., ROUGE, BERTScore) or specific desired properties (e.g., readability, factuality). However, these metrics fail to measure the utility of a summary to an individual user. For example, a biomedical researcher learning about the latest vaccine research will have different informational needs from a family doctor. Query-focused summarization captures part of this need, but in practice, users rarely state everything relevant in a query: a single short query is likely inadequate to distinguish the needs of a researcher from those of a physician. By contrast, a reader's background or persona (their role and expertise) is comparatively stable across queries and recovers much of this missing context, which makes it a practical signal for assessing whether a summary satisfies that reader's needs. In this work, we assess how sensitive popular summarization metrics are to both informational and persona differences, and find that many popular metrics, including strong LLM-as-judge metrics, fail basic perturbation tests of informational content. We additionally conduct an expert human evaluation, measuring summary preferences based on information satisfaction given a specific person's background and use case. We find that both traditional and LLM-based metrics are insufficient measures of information satisfaction and agree poorly with human judgment.

AI.tldr: This paper studies whether current summarization evaluation metrics reflect how well summaries satisfy the information needs of different users, and finds that they generally do not.
AI.motivation: Existing summarization metrics like ROUGE, BERTScore, or LLM-as-judge mainly assess overall quality or narrow properties such as readability and factuality. They do not capture whether a summary is actually useful for a specific user with a particular background, role, or expertise. Users with different personas (e.g., biomedical researcher vs. family doctor) have distinct, stable information needs that are not fully expressed in short queries, so persona information is a promising, underexplored signal for evaluation. The authors want to understand if current metrics are sensitive to these informational and persona differences and whether they correlate with real users’ information satisfaction.
AI.method: The authors analyze popular summarization metrics—including traditional overlap-based ones and modern LLM-as-judge scores—under controlled perturbation tests where the informational content of summaries is systematically varied. They test whether metric scores change appropriately when key information relevant to different user personas (roles and expertise levels) is added, removed, or altered. They then run an expert human evaluation: domain experts with specific backgrounds and use cases judge summaries based on how well the information satisfies their own needs. The agreement between human preferences and automatic metric scores is quantified to assess metric adequacy for information satisfaction.
AI.result: Many widely used summarization metrics, including strong LLM-as-judge approaches, fail basic sensitivity checks: they often do not respond reliably to changes in the informational content of summaries that should matter for different users. In the expert user study, both traditional and LLM-based metrics show low agreement with human judgments of which summaries better satisfy a given persona’s information needs, indicating that these metrics do not capture information satisfaction well.
AI.conclusion: Current summarization evaluation metrics are poorly aligned with user-specific information needs and are not sufficiently sensitive to informational or persona-driven differences between summaries. Even advanced LLM-based evaluators fail to track information satisfaction from the perspective of real users with distinct backgrounds and use cases. The authors conclude that evaluating summaries requires new, persona-aware or information-satisfaction-oriented metrics rather than relying solely on general-quality or property-specific measures like ROUGE, BERTScore, or generic LLM-as-judge scores.

title: FLARE MCMC: Fidelity-based Layer-Adaptive REcursive proposals for MCMC
comment: This is the author's accepted manuscript of an article published in SIAM Journal on Uncertainty Quantification. The final version is available at \url{https://doi.org/10.1137/25M1795194
summary: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) requires only the ability to evaluate the likelihood, making it a common technique for inference in complex models. However, it can have a slow mixing rate, requiring the generation of many samples to obtain good estimates and an overall high computational cost. FLARE MCMC is a multi-fidelity layered MCMC method that exploits lower-fidelity approximations of the true likelihood calculation to improve mixing and leads to overall faster performance. Such lower-fidelity likelihoods are commonly available in scientific and engineering applications where the model involves a simulation whose resolution or accuracy can be tuned. Our technique uses recursive, layered chains with simple layer tuning; it does not require the likelihood to take any form or have any particular internal mathematical structure. We demonstrate experimentally that FLARE MCMC achieves larger effective sample sizes for the same computational time across different scientific domains including hydrology and cosmology.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FLARE MCMC, a multi-fidelity, layered MCMC method that uses cheaper approximate likelihoods to speed up sampling while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard MCMC often mixes slowly and is computationally expensive when each likelihood evaluation is costly, as in complex simulations. Many scientific and engineering applications have tunable-resolution simulators that naturally provide cheaper, lower-fidelity approximations, but standard MCMC does not systematically exploit them.
AI.method: Introduce FLARE MCMC, which runs recursive, layered Markov chains where lower layers use cheaper, lower-fidelity likelihoods and higher layers use more accurate, expensive likelihoods. The chains are coupled so that information from cheap layers accelerates exploration of the state space, with simple tuning procedures and no assumptions on the functional form or structure of the likelihood.
AI.result: Experiments in multiple domains, including hydrology and cosmology, show that for the same wall-clock computation time, FLARE MCMC produces larger effective sample sizes than conventional MCMC, indicating faster mixing and more efficient exploration.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging multi-fidelity approximations of the likelihood via a layered MCMC framework significantly improves sampling efficiency in complex scientific models without requiring special structure in the likelihood, making FLARE MCMC a practical, broadly applicable enhancement over standard methods.

title: You Only Pass Once: Answering and Abstaining Together in a Single Forward Pass of a Frozen Language Model
comment: 24 pages. Ziyang Luo and Zhongyao Chu contributed equally
summary: A frozen language model on reasoning tasks has two coupled weaknesses: it under-uses evidence its own residual stream already encodes, and it fails to detect when the input is insufficient to answer, so it confabulates. This paper consolidates two research lines that address these on the same residual stream: a conditional steering probe writes the stream at mid-stack layers and recovers reasoning accuracy from a frozen backbone, and a zero-shot sufficiency direction reads the stream and abstains when information is insufficient. Deployed in one forward pass they interfere: the steering write shifts the state the direction reads, costing up to 8 AUROC points of cross-domain transfer on small models; a separate clean pass doubles inference cost. We keep the direction fixed and train a small network to reconstruct the pre-steering residual from the steered one -- mean-squared error on (steered, clean) pairs, no sufficiency labels -- and read the direction on the reconstruction. The resulting system, YOPO (You Only Pass Once), answers, steers, and abstains in one forward pass of a frozen Qwen2.5 backbone (1.5B/3B/7B). End to end, three-way accuracy more than doubles the frozen baseline (0.375->0.798 on 1.5B alphaNLI) and one pass beats the two-pass reference at every scale (0.798/0.830/0.893 vs 0.753/0.790/0.863) and on ten backbones across six model families. We chart the capacity-transfer frontier quantifying the principle that abstention should not be trained in; a source-side audit catches our own alphaNLI construction leaking a surface artifact, so architectural claims are anchored on native-label replications (SQuAD2, RepLiQA, MuSiQue); and on the standard four-domain suite we contribute, to our knowledge, the first answer-or-abstain benchmark, where our gate tops every in-domain dataset and the label-free direction is the only gate family to survive domain transfer.

AI.tldr: They propose YOPO, a method that lets a frozen language model both perform steered reasoning and abstain when information is insufficient, using only a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: Frozen language models have two coupled problems on reasoning tasks: (1) they fail to fully exploit evidence already present in their residual stream, hurting reasoning accuracy, and (2) they cannot reliably detect when the input is insufficient to answer, leading to confabulation instead of abstaining. Existing methods that steer reasoning and detect insufficiency both operate on the residual stream but interfere with each other when run in a single pass, forcing either degraded performance or costly two-pass inference. There is a need for a method that enables both accurate steering and reliable abstention in one pass, without retraining the large backbone or requiring abstention labels.
AI.method: They study a setting where a frozen Qwen2.5 backbone is augmented with two components acting on the residual stream: (1) a conditional steering probe that writes into mid-layer residuals to improve reasoning accuracy, and (2) a zero-shot sufficiency direction that reads from the residual stream to decide whether to abstain. Directly combining them in a single pass fails because the steering write perturbs the residual state that the sufficiency direction expects. To resolve this, they keep the sufficiency direction fixed and train a small reconstruction network that approximates the pre-steering residual from the post-steering residual. This network is trained via mean-squared error on pairs of (steered, clean) residuals, using no sufficiency labels. At inference, YOPO uses one forward pass of the frozen backbone with steering enabled; the reconstruction network recovers an approximation of the clean residual, on which the fixed sufficiency direction is applied to decide answer vs. abstain, while the steered residual is used to produce the answer when not abstaining. They evaluate across multiple scales (1.5B/3B/7B) and backbones, study cross-domain transfer, and analyze the capacity-transfer trade-off between steering and abstention.
AI.result: YOPO enables answer, steering, and abstention in a single forward pass of a frozen backbone, avoiding two-pass inference and the interference between steering and sufficiency readouts. On alphaNLI with a 1.5B Qwen2.5, three-way accuracy (answer correctly, answer incorrectly, abstain) improves from 0.375 for the frozen baseline to 0.798 with YOPO, more than doubling performance and surpassing a two-pass reference system at every scale: single-pass YOPO achieves 0.798/0.830/0.893 vs. 0.753/0.790/0.863 for the two-pass approach on 1.5B/3B/7B models. Across ten backbones from six model families, the one-pass YOPO consistently outperforms two-pass references. Their analyses show that training abstention directly into the model is suboptimal, supporting a capacity-transfer frontier where steering capacity should not be spent on abstention. A source-side audit reveals surface artifacts in their alphaNLI construction, so they ground architectural claims in additional native-label datasets (SQuAD2, RepLiQA, MuSiQue). On a new four-domain answer-or-abstain benchmark, their gate achieves top performance on all in-domain datasets, and the label-free sufficiency direction is the only gating approach that remains robust under domain transfer.
AI.conclusion: YOPO provides an effective way to combine steering and abstention in frozen language models using only a single forward pass, by reconstructing an approximation of the pre-steering residual for sufficiency detection. This design removes the interference between steering writes and sufficiency reads while avoiding the computational cost of two-pass inference. Empirically, YOPO substantially boosts three-way accuracy on reasoning tasks, outperforms two-pass baselines across multiple model sizes and families, and yields a sufficiency gate that is both strong in-domain and robust under cross-domain transfer. The work also emphasizes that abstention mechanisms should be kept separate from the main model’s capacity and demonstrates the value of careful dataset auditing and answer-or-abstain benchmarks for evaluating reliability in reasoning systems.

title: From Passive Delegates to Strategic Negotiators: Reinforcing Social Reasoning in Small Language Models with SocialRL
summary: AI agents increasingly act on their users' behalf, handling tasks such as scheduling meetings, comparing offers, and haggling over prices. These principal-driven tasks routinely place the agent across from a counterpart (another user's agent, a seller, a recruiter) whose goals may conflict with its principal's. Yet the dispositions that make an assistant pleasant can make it a poor delegate: a friendly, helpful frontier model may disclose its principal's private information unprompted and concede at the first sign of resistance. We present SocialRL, a general recipe that trains social reasoning directly, and apply it to a 4B model across six domains: Deal-or-No-Deal, CaSiNo, Craigslist, Job Interview, Calendar, and Marketplace. Every domain is trained in-domain under the same recipe, and every policy is evaluated on all six. We find that (1) in-domain training reaches the frontier: on held-out scenarios the 4B matches or exceeds the GPT-5 family per domain, closing 73-122% of the baseline-to-frontier gap on the negotiation games, with 78% of buyer openings anchoring below target versus 3% untrained; (2) cross-domain transfer follows game structure: structurally paired games lift each other, a broad multi-issue donor lifts nearly all domains, and structurally isolated games transfer nothing; (3) guided by this transfer structure, two strategies, cascade RL and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD), consolidate the per-domain specialists into a single unified 4B that reaches 0.627 average utility across all six environments, matching or exceeding GPT-4.1 (0.625), GPT-5.1 (0.619), and GPT-5.2 (0.613); (4) an explicit theory-of-mind scaffold helps only through training: distilling the ToM trace, rather than actions alone, lifts utility on every environment and generalizes better across them, and of the two ToM skills, only next-action prediction predicts negotiation outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SocialRL, a reinforcement learning framework that trains small AI agents to negotiate and socially reason as effective delegates for users, achieving performance comparable to much larger frontier models across six diverse social/negotiation tasks.
AI.motivation: AI assistants are increasingly acting as delegates in social, strategic settings (e.g., negotiating prices, scheduling, recruiting) where counterpart goals may conflict with the user’s interests. Current "friendly" frontier models tend to over-disclose private information and concede too easily, making them poor representatives. There is a need for methods that directly train social reasoning and negotiation behavior—rather than just politeness or helpfulness—so smaller models can reliably protect user interests and perform well across varied interaction domains.
AI.method: The authors propose SocialRL, a unified reinforcement learning recipe for training social reasoning policies. They apply it to a 4B-parameter model across six domains: Deal-or-No-Deal, CaSiNo, Craigslist, Job Interview, Calendar, and Marketplace. Each domain is trained in-domain using the same RL recipe. Policies are evaluated across all six domains to study both in-domain performance and cross-domain transfer. They further analyze structural transfer patterns between games and use this insight to build unified agents with two strategies: cascade RL and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD), which consolidate specialized per-domain policies into a single model. They also incorporate an explicit theory-of-mind (ToM) scaffold during training, distilling not just actions but also intermediate ToM traces, and examine which ToM subskills predict negotiation outcomes.
AI.result: (1) In-domain SocialRL training allows the 4B model to match or exceed GPT-5-family performance per domain on held-out test scenarios, closing 73–122% of the performance gap between an untrained baseline and frontier models on negotiation games. For instance, 78% of buyer openings anchor below the target price after training versus only 3% for the untrained model. (2) Cross-domain transfer depends on game structure: structurally similar games mutually improve each other’s performance, a complex multi-issue donor domain improves nearly all others, but structurally isolated games do not transfer. (3) Using these transfer patterns, cascade RL and multi-teacher OPD successfully merge per-domain specialists into a single 4B model achieving 0.627 average utility across all six domains, matching or exceeding GPT-4.1 (0.625), GPT-5.1 (0.619), and GPT-5.2 (0.613). (4) Adding an explicit ToM scaffold during training helps: distilling the ToM reasoning traces improves utility on all environments and yields better cross-domain generalization, and among ToM components, only next-action prediction is predictive of negotiation success.
AI.conclusion: Directly training social reasoning with SocialRL enables a relatively small 4B model to act as an effective negotiating delegate across diverse social tasks, rivaling much larger frontier models. Social and negotiation skills transfer according to underlying game structure, which can be exploited to build strong unified agents from domain specialists via cascade RL and multi-teacher OPD. Incorporating explicit theory-of-mind reasoning during training—by distilling intermediate ToM traces rather than actions alone—further improves performance and generalization, with next-action prediction emerging as the key ToM component linked to negotiation outcomes.

title: SDO: Subspace Deconflicting Operator for Multi-Adapter Composition
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Accepted by ACM MM 2026 Main Track
