summary: Composing independently trained adapters within a shared diffusion backbone provides a modular approach to multi-character generation, but naive joint deployment often causes identity mixing, cross-character attribute leakage, and unstable scene composition. We study this interference from a parameter-space perspective and hypothesize that it arises partly from conflicts between overlapping dominant subspaces in shared layers. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SDO}, a \textbf{S}ubspace \textbf{D}econflicting \textbf{O}perator for multi-adapter composition. SDO reconstructs layer-wise low-rank updates from the selected adapters, extracts compact subspace signatures, measures pairwise conflict through output-subspace overlap, and applies a permutation-equivariant transformation that suppresses harmful shared directions while retaining identity-specific characteristics. The resulting representations are mapped back to standard adapter updates and can be directly incorporated into existing diffusion inference pipelines. Experiments demonstrate that SDO consistently improves identity fidelity and compositional stability, with particularly clear gains as the number of jointly composed adapters increases.

AI.tldr: They propose SDO, a subspace deconflicting operator, to better compose multiple independently trained adapters in a shared diffusion model backbone, reducing interference and improving multi-character generation.
AI.motivation: Naively combining multiple character adapters in a shared diffusion backbone leads to undesirable interactions like identity mixing, attribute leakage between characters, and unstable scene composition. The authors seek a principled way to understand and mitigate these interferences from a parameter-space perspective.
AI.method: The paper introduces SDO, a Subspace Deconflicting Operator. For selected adapters, SDO reconstructs layer-wise low-rank parameter updates, extracts compact subspace signatures from these updates, measures pairwise conflicts by quantifying overlap between their output subspaces, and then applies a permutation-equivariant transformation to attenuate directions that are shared and conflict-prone while preserving identity-specific components. These transformed representations are then mapped back into standard adapter update form and plugged into the diffusion inference pipeline.
AI.result: Experiments show that SDO yields more faithful character identities and more stable compositions in multi-character generation tasks. The benefits become more significant as more adapters are composed together, indicating that SDO effectively scales to complex multi-adapter scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Managing interference between adapters at the subspace level is effective for modular multi-character diffusion models. SDO provides a plug-and-play operator that can be integrated into existing diffusion backbones to systematically deconflict adapters, leading to better identity preservation and compositional robustness, especially when many adapters are used simultaneously.

title: Joint Optimization of Memory and Computing Frequency for Energy-Efficient DNN Inference
summary: Deep neural network (DNN) inference on mobile devices often incurs high latency and energy consumption due to limited computing and memory resources. To enable energy-efficient DNN inference, most existing studies focus on dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) for adjusting the computing frequency, while the impact of memory frequency on the inference performance has been greatly overlooked. In this paper, we consider the impact of memory frequency and computing frequency on DNN inference time, and jointly optimize these two frequencies together with communication resources for energy-efficient DNN inference. Based on a realistic inference time model, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the energy consumption of all mobile devices under the deadline constraint. For local inference, we derive a near-optimal closed-form solution via convex optimization, while an optimal closed-form solution for transmission power is obtained for edge inference with the given bandwidth. Furthermore, we propose a low-complexity heuristic algorithm to effectively solve the overall problem with polynomial time complexity. Simulation results based on measured data show that the proposed near-optimal solution for local inference can achieve optimal performance under strict deadline constraints, with a performance gap of up to 2.5% compared with the optimal solution. Meanwhile, our proposed algorithm significantly reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 10.4% compared to other methods.

AI.tldr: The paper jointly optimizes CPU frequency, memory frequency, and communication resources to reduce energy consumption for mobile DNN inference under latency (deadline) constraints, achieving up to 10.4% energy savings versus prior methods with near-optimal performance guarantees.
AI.motivation: Mobile devices running deep neural network inference suffer from high latency and energy usage because of constrained compute and memory. Existing work mainly tunes CPU/GPU frequencies via DVFS and usually ignores memory frequency, which can also strongly affect inference time and energy. There is a need for a principled framework that captures both compute and memory effects, and also incorporates communication (for edge offloading), to minimize total energy while meeting real-time deadlines.
AI.method: The authors build a realistic inference time model that explicitly accounts for both computing frequency and memory frequency. They then formulate a constrained optimization problem that minimizes total energy consumption of all mobile devices under a deadline constraint, considering both local inference and edge inference (with communication). For local inference, they use convex optimization techniques to derive a near-optimal closed-form solution for the optimal compute and memory frequencies. For edge inference, given a fixed bandwidth, they derive an optimal closed-form solution for the transmission power. Finally, they design a low-complexity heuristic algorithm with polynomial time complexity to solve the joint optimization problem that couples all variables and devices.
AI.result: Simulations based on measured (realistic) data show that the near-optimal closed-form solution for local inference is essentially optimal under tight deadline constraints, with at most 2.5% performance loss compared to the true optimum. Across scenarios, the proposed overall heuristic algorithm reduces the energy consumption of mobile devices by up to 10.4% compared with representative existing methods that do not jointly optimize compute frequency, memory frequency, and communication resources.
AI.conclusion: Taking memory frequency into account, in addition to computing frequency and communication parameters, is crucial for achieving energy-efficient DNN inference on mobile devices under latency constraints. The proposed optimization framework, closed-form solutions, and heuristic algorithm together offer a practical, low-complexity way to approach optimal energy savings, as validated by simulations, and can significantly improve the energy efficiency of mobile DNN inference compared to existing DVFS-centric approaches.

title: MemoryLake on MemoryArena: A Matched Study of Agent Memory Backends
summary: Most agent-memory benchmarks test post-hoc recall, whereas MemoryArena evaluates whether memory supports interdependent, multi-session task completion. We compare MemoryLake, a structured multi-track memory backend, with Mem0, text-embedding-3-small vector RAG, and a long-context control across all five MemoryArena domains. The systems share the same agent framework, requested gpt-5-mini model alias, task samples, and scoring code; the memory integration is the intentionally changed component. Because each backend bundles write, retrieval, consolidation, budgeting, and prompt-assembly choices, the study is a matched system-level comparison, not a representation-only ablation or a cost-matched experiment. On the shared evaluation sets, MemoryLake has the highest observed success rate (SR) in mathematics (9/40), physics (12/20), and progressive retrieval (4/20). Every system has zero SR in travel planning, and web shopping yields a single bundle-level success (long context, 1/150); MemoryLake ranks third on both the travel soft process score and shopping step match. Following MemoryArena's suite-level convention, a post-hoc equal-weight average over the five SRs is 20.5% for MemoryLake versus 13.6% for the best comparator. These are point estimates: sample sizes are modest, confidence intervals overlap, and we do not report paired significance tests. A separate MemoryLake-only run over all 221 progressive queries yields a failure-counted SR of 26.7% (59/221) and is not a baseline comparison. The results support a workload-dependent view of memory backends and an observed lead among the four evaluated systems on the shared sets; they do not establish benchmark-wide state of the art or a causal advantage of representation structure.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates different AI memory backends on a multi-session, interdependent task benchmark (MemoryArena), finding that the structured MemoryLake system generally performs best but without claiming state-of-the-art or causal superiority.
AI.motivation: Most existing agent-memory benchmarks only test simple post-hoc recall, which doesn’t reflect the complex, multi-step, multi-session tasks real agents face. The authors want to understand how different memory system designs affect an agent’s ability to complete such tasks and whether more structured memory offers practical advantages over standard vector-based RAG or long-context approaches.
AI.method: They use the MemoryArena benchmark, which has five domains (mathematics, physics, progressive retrieval, travel planning, and web shopping) that require interdependent, multi-session task completion. They plug three different memory backends—MemoryLake (a structured multi-track memory), Mem0 (vector RAG using text-embedding-3-small), and a long-context setup—into the same agent framework, using the same model (gpt-5-mini alias), tasks, and scoring code. Each backend is evaluated end-to-end, including its own choices for writing, retrieving, consolidating, budgeting, and prompt assembly. They then compare success rates across domains and compute an equal-weighted average SR per MemoryArena convention. They also run an expanded, MemoryLake-only evaluation on 221 progressive retrieval queries.
AI.result: On the shared evaluation sets, MemoryLake achieves the highest observed success rates in mathematics (9/40), physics (12/20), and progressive retrieval (4/20). All systems fail on travel planning (0 SR), and only the long-context system succeeds on a single web shopping bundle (1/150). MemoryLake ranks third on the softer travel and shopping process metrics. Averaging success rates equally across the five domains yields 20.5% for MemoryLake versus 13.6% for the best alternative. In an additional, non-comparative run, MemoryLake achieves a 26.7% success rate (59/221) on progressive queries. However, sample sizes are modest, confidence intervals overlap, and no significance tests are reported.
AI.conclusion: The study suggests that memory backend performance is strongly workload-dependent and that, within the tested setup and tasks, the structured MemoryLake backend tends to outperform the other three systems on the shared evaluation sets. However, due to limited data and lack of formal significance testing, the authors do not claim benchmark-wide state-of-the-art performance or a definitive causal benefit of MemoryLake’s structured representation design.

title: When Personal Memory Has No Single Answer: Evaluating LLM Agents under Irreducible Conflict
summary: LLM agents increasingly maintain personal memory across sessions, but it can conflict. Preferences depend on context, behavior evolves, and sources can conflict. When a query lacks context, time, or source authority to interpret conflict, treating one memory as definitive converts unresolved conflict into an unjustified, overconfident action. Existing benchmarks recover one answer from conflicting evidence, overlooking whether agents recognize underdetermination, preserve alternatives, seek missing information, and choose appropriate actions. We introduce \underline{T}esting \underline{A}gents' \underline{N}avigation of \underline{G}enuine, \underline{L}atent, and \underline{E}ntangled Memory Conflicts (\textsc{TANGLE}), a benchmark for genuinely unresolvable memory conflicts. It comprises 541 instances across 40 personas and three types: Context-Partitioned Conflict (CPC), Behavior-Oscillation Conflict (BOC), and Source-Contradiction Conflict (SCC). We evaluate two tracks---an oracle track with curated memory and a pipeline track that extracts memory from multi-session dialogues---on five dimensions: conflict perception, causal reasoning, confidence calibration, clarification seeking, and memory faithfulness. Experiments reveal pipeline challenges. With curated memory, models recognize conflicts more reliably than they calibrate actions or seek targeted clarification. With end-to-end pipeline memory, extraction fails to preserve conflict-bearing relations needed for downstream reasoning. Policy comparisons show fixed rules are insufficient when actions must reflect conflict. These findings motivate Conflict-Aware Action Policy (CAAP), which adapts actions to each conflict using available evidence. \textsc{TANGLE} frames conflict handling as recognizing underdetermination, retaining conflicting evidence, and acting without forcing a definitive answer.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TANGLE, a benchmark for evaluating how LLM agents detect and handle genuinely unresolvable conflicts in their long-term memories, and proposes a conflict-aware action policy to guide appropriate behavior under such uncertainty.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly use persistent personal memories across sessions, but those memories can conflict due to contextual preference shifts, behavioral changes over time, or contradictory sources. Existing benchmarks typically assume there is a single correct answer and thus reward agents for picking one resolution, ignoring the crucial abilities to recognize underdetermined situations, maintain alternative possibilities, seek clarification, and act cautiously rather than overconfidently when conflict cannot be resolved. The authors aim to fill this evaluation gap and improve how agents behave in the presence of genuine memory conflicts.
AI.method: The authors construct TANGLE, a benchmark consisting of 541 conflict instances across 40 personas and three conflict types: Context-Partitioned Conflict (CPC), where different contexts license different preferences; Behavior-Oscillation Conflict (BOC), where behavior changes over time; and Source-Contradiction Conflict (SCC), where information from different sources directly disagrees. TANGLE supports two evaluation tracks: (1) an oracle track where the agent is given curated, structured memory; and (2) a pipeline track where memory is automatically extracted from multi-session dialogues. Agents are evaluated along five dimensions: conflict perception (recognizing that a conflict exists), causal reasoning (understanding why it exists), confidence calibration (avoiding unwarranted certainty), clarification seeking (asking good follow-up questions), and memory faithfulness (using the stored evidence accurately). The authors run experiments across models and policy strategies to assess performance, including a comparison of simple fixed rules versus a more adaptive policy.
AI.result: Experiments show that LLMs perform better at detecting conflicts when provided with curated memory than when relying on end-to-end pipelines that must first extract memory from dialogues. In the pipeline setting, memory extraction often loses or distorts the relational structure needed to represent conflicts, which undermines downstream reasoning about them. Even in the oracle setting, models tend to recognize that conflicts exist but struggle with appropriately calibrating their actions, such as choosing cautious or information-seeking behaviors instead of arbitrarily picking a side. Simple fixed decision rules do not handle the diversity of conflict situations well. Overall, the benchmark exposes significant weaknesses in current memory systems and policies for acting under unresolved conflict.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that handling memory conflict in LLM agents requires more than just selecting a single answer from inconsistent evidence. Agents must detect underdetermination, preserve and reason over conflicting memories, and choose actions—such as seeking clarification or hedging recommendations—that respect the unresolved status of the information. TANGLE provides a systematic way to evaluate these skills and demonstrates that current models and fixed policies are inadequate, especially in realistic pipeline settings where memory is automatically extracted. To address this, the authors propose Conflict-Aware Action Policy (CAAP), which conditions agent behavior on the particular structure and evidence of each conflict instance, and argue that future work on long-term LLM agents should explicitly incorporate conflict-aware reasoning and action policies.

title: Never the Number: Structural Abstention for AI Systems Whose Answers Are Consumed as Fact
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Technical report. Describes architecture and design principles only; contains no code, schemas, datasets, or performance metrics
summary:
Large language models have made natural language interfaces to databases (NLIDB) newly credible, but LLM text-to-SQL systems fail in a way that matters for deployment: a hallucinated column or a mis-aggregated total yields a fluent wrong answer, indistinguishable at the point of use from a right one. Where the consumer cannot inspect the generated query, as in enterprise AI deployments and operational dashboards, and increasingly where the consumer is a tool-using agent rather than a person, accuracy alone is insufficient: nothing marks which answers to distrust. This is a reliability problem before it is an accuracy problem.
  We propose an architectural pattern for such systems, a trusted kernel with a generative shell, resting on one invariant: a component that can fabricate may influence which question the system answers, never which value it returns. A generative shell interprets underspecified input and phrases replies; a deterministic kernel matches fully specified questions against a bounded set of answerable question shapes and compiles them to queries by deterministic execution. The two meet at a confirmation the user reads before any value is computed, and requests the kernel cannot express are declined rather than approximated. We call this structural abstention, and distinguish it from the statistical abstention of selective prediction and calibrated confidence: refusal here needs no confidence estimate, because unanswerable requests are unrepresentable.
  We specify the pattern implementation-independently, give a five-decision recipe and work it across three domains, extend the invariant from returned values to the actions of agentic systems, and report a two-year production case study alongside two generative alternatives, a fine-tuned parser and a tool-retrieval agent. We close against enterprise and reliability benchmarks published since.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reliability‑first architecture for LLM-based text-to-SQL and agent systems, separating a generative "shell" from a deterministic "trusted kernel" that alone determines returned values or actions.
AI.motivation: LLM-based natural language interfaces to databases can generate syntactically valid but semantically wrong queries (e.g., hallucinated columns, wrong aggregations). In many enterprise or agentic settings, users cannot inspect queries, so fluent but incorrect answers are indistinguishable from correct ones. This poses a reliability problem: users lack signals about which answers to distrust, and traditional accuracy metrics or confidence-based abstention are inadequate.
AI.method: The authors define an architecture with a strict invariant: any component that can fabricate (the generative model) may influence what question is asked but never what value is returned. They introduce a "trusted kernel" that handles fully specified, structurally validated queries via deterministic execution, and a "generative shell" that interprets underspecified input and phrases responses. The system enforces a confirmation step humans see before computation; queries outside a bounded set of representable question shapes are rejected (structural abstention) instead of approximated. They provide an implementation-independent specification, a five-decision design recipe, examples in three domains, an extension of the invariant to agent actions, and a production case study comparing against two alternative generative approaches.
AI.result: The architectural pattern is shown to be implementable in multiple domains and to support reliable text-to-SQL and agent behaviors where unanswerable or unsafe requests are structurally unrepresentable and therefore declined rather than approximated. In a two-year production deployment, the trusted-kernel pattern compares favorably to a fine-tuned parser and a tool-retrieval agent, and aligns well with recently proposed enterprise and reliability benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reliability in LLM-based NLIDB and agent systems should be treated as a structural design problem rather than only an accuracy or calibration problem. By enforcing the invariant that generative components cannot directly influence returned values or actions, and by using structural abstention via a deterministic trusted kernel, systems can provide safer, more dependable behavior in enterprise and operational settings where users cannot inspect intermediate queries or tools.

title: AI Research Preference Models
summary: AI research agents (AIRA) can now propose, implement, and evaluate their own machine learning experiments, but progress on frontier tasks is throttled by cost: a candidate solution can be written in minutes, whereas evaluating it can take hours to days of GPU time. An agent can therefore propose far more candidates than it can afford to run, and its progress depends on its research preference: how it allocates a fixed execution budget across many candidates. We introduce AI Research Preference Models (RPMs) that predict which of multiple candidate solutions are most worth executing, without paying the cost of executing them all. We build RPMs from frozen pretrained language models (with no task-specific training), in two forms: an inference-only model that reasons over candidate plans, code, and prior executed solutions, and an agentic model that additionally runs small-scale pilot experiments before deciding. We integrate both into the AIRA-dojo search agent and evaluate on AIRS-Bench, a recent benchmark of machine learning research tasks for AI research agents. The two variants raise the average normalized score from 0.684 to 0.711 and 0.729 respectively, and reach the unguided agent's 24-hour performance in roughly 15 hours, using less than two-thirds of its execution budget. Our best RPMs also yield new state-of-the-art results on two AIRS-Bench tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AI Research Preference Models (RPMs) to help AI research agents choose which candidate ML experiments to run under limited compute, improving efficiency and performance on a benchmark of research tasks.
AI.motivation: AI research agents can quickly generate many candidate ML experiments but evaluating each one is extremely expensive in GPU time. Since only a small subset can actually be run, overall progress is constrained by how well the agent chooses which candidates to execute. Existing systems lack effective, general-purpose mechanisms for prioritizing experiments without fully running them, creating a bottleneck for scalable autonomous ML research.
AI.method: The authors propose AI Research Preference Models (RPMs) that score and prioritize candidate solutions before full execution. They instantiate RPMs using frozen pretrained language models, avoiding task-specific finetuning, in two variants: (1) an inference-only model that reasons over candidate research plans, code, and historical executed solutions to predict which are promising; and (2) an agentic model that, in addition, conducts small, cheap pilot experiments and uses their results to refine its preferences. These RPMs are integrated into the AIRA-dojo search agent and evaluated on the AIRS-Bench benchmark of ML research tasks.
AI.result: Both RPM variants significantly improve the efficiency and performance of the AIRA-dojo agent on AIRS-Bench. The baseline average normalized score of 0.684 increases to 0.711 with the inference-only RPM and to 0.729 with the agentic RPM. With guidance from RPMs, the agent matches the unguided baseline’s 24-hour performance in about 15 hours while using under two-thirds of the computation budget, and the best RPM configurations set new state-of-the-art results on two AIRS-Bench tasks.
AI.conclusion: Preference modeling over research candidates, using frozen LMs and optionally small pilot runs, is an effective way to reduce compute waste and accelerate progress for AI research agents. RPMs allow agents to allocate limited execution budgets more intelligently, improving both sample efficiency and absolute performance on challenging ML research benchmarks, and establishing a new state of the art on parts of AIRS-Bench.

title: HELIX: Model-Harness Co-evolution for Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Scaling agent capability has largely focused on improving the model, yet an interactive agent acts through a runtime harness that mediates context, tools, control flow, and stopping. The harness shapes both what a model can accomplish and the trajectories from which it learns. This coupling motivates model-harness co-evolution for recursive self-improvement: build harnesses for a fixed model, update the model from verified sibling trajectories, and rebuild the harnesses as model capabilities change. Realizing this loop requires a controlled way to evolve harnesses while preserving intervention identity and effect. We present HELIX, a source-traceable substrate for harness evolution. HELIX decomposes agent systems into typed ports, reusable atoms, recipes, product shells, and runtime policies. It makes interventions explicit and auditable while retaining trajectories, test outcomes, and provenance. Harness evolution thus serves two linked roles: improving fixed-model execution and producing matched successes, regressions, near misses, and alternative solutions as data for subsequent model improvement. We evaluate HELIX in one evolution round on code repair. A 65-candidate portfolio discovers a fixed harness that improves task coverage by 4.0% over Pi, while the full portfolio exposes up to 58.0% more verified coverage through complementary sibling behavior. Selected candidates are assessed with repeated runs and the SWE-bench evaluator. A 200-slot sibling slice yields 438 verified SFT, critic, filter, and preference records. These results show how harness, model, and data form a feedback system: harness evolution expands current capability and creates learning signal for the next model; model updates motivate the next round of harness evolution. HELIX provides an auditable interface for studying this recursive process. Code is available at https://github.com/HKUDS/HELIX.

AI.tldr: HELIX is a framework for systematically evolving and auditing the runtime harnesses around LLM agents, enabling recursive co-improvement of harness, model, and training data.
AI.motivation: Most work on scaling agent capabilities focuses on making the underlying model better, but real agents act through a complex runtime harness (tools, control flow, context management, stopping criteria). This harness heavily constrains what the model can do and what trajectories are available as learning signals. There is a need for a principled way to co-evolve this harness with the model, keeping changes traceable and ensuring that interventions remain interpretable and auditable so they can be used for further model training.
AI.method: The paper introduces HELIX, a source-traceable substrate for defining and evolving agent harnesses. HELIX decomposes agent systems into typed ports, reusable atoms (building blocks), recipes (compositions), product shells, and runtime policies. It records interventions, trajectories, test outcomes, and provenance, enabling explicit, auditable manipulation of harness structure and behavior. The authors run one round of harness evolution on a code-repair task, generating a portfolio of 65 harness candidates (and larger sibling slices) and evaluating them with repeated runs and SWE-bench-style evaluation to identify improved and complementary harness behaviors.
AI.result: In a code-repair setting, a 65-candidate HELIX portfolio discovers a single fixed harness that improves task coverage by 4.0% over a Pi baseline. Considering the entire portfolio of sibling harnesses, they can expose up to 58.0% more verified task coverage due to complementary behaviors across harness variants. A 200-slot sibling slice produces 438 verified supervision signals (SFT data, critic outputs, filters, and preference records), demonstrating that harness evolution not only improves immediate performance but also yields diverse, labeled trajectories for training future models.
AI.conclusion: Harness design is a first-class lever for scaling agent capability and generating high-quality training signals, not just a peripheral implementation detail. HELIX provides an auditable, modular representation of agent harnesses that supports controlled evolution while preserving intervention identity and effect. The experiments on code repair show that evolving the harness around a fixed model can both increase current task coverage and generate rich data for subsequent model training. This establishes a feedback loop in which harness evolution improves performance and creates learning signal, updated models then justify new rounds of harness evolution, and HELIX serves as the structured interface for studying and managing this recursive process.

title: Implementing Computational Law in Wolfram Language for the Governance of Artificial Intelligence
comment: 25 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables, 12 code listings. Wolfram Language implementation and verification script (31 assertions) available at https://github.com/Zaffer/research-computational-law
summary: How do we govern AI systems whose reasoning we cannot fully inspect? Governance does not require understanding a system's reasoning. It requires stating what the system is obliged, permitted, and forbidden to do, and checking whether it complied. I present an implementation of Reified Input/Output Logic, the formalism behind the DAPRECO knowledge base, in Wolfram Language: the core I/O axioms, obligations, permissions, constitutive norms, reified eventualities, and temporal operators. I then test whether GPT-4 can translate English legal statements into the formalism, and report the failures: hallucinated functions, omitted temporal scope, deviation from the formalism, and (in the worst cases) code that runs, reads plausibly, but silently encodes the wrong norm. A case study, an AI guard dog operating under a computational contract, shows how formalized rules can extend from a contract directly into the operational code of an embodied agent, producing symbolic, auditable justifications for its behaviour. I argue that computational law can be used as a governance tool and that a desirable goal would be to formalize the law that can and ought to be programmatically executable.

AI.tldr: The paper implements a formal logic framework in Wolfram Language to encode legal norms and explores using it to govern AI systems by executable, auditable rules rather than by understanding their internal reasoning.
AI.motivation: As advanced AI systems become less interpretable, traditional governance approaches that rely on understanding internal reasoning are insufficient. The author wants a way to govern such systems by specifying clear obligations, permissions, and prohibitions in a machine-readable, legally grounded form that can be checked against system behavior. This aims to bridge AI governance and computational law, making legal constraints directly executable by AI agents.
AI.method: The author implements Reified Input/Output Logic—the formal basis of the DAPRECO legal knowledge base—in Wolfram Language. This includes encoding core I/O axioms, obligations, permissions, constitutive norms, reified eventualities, and temporal operators. Then, GPT-4 is tasked with translating English legal statements into this formalism, and its performance is analyzed, focusing on specific error types. Finally, a case study of an AI guard dog governed by a computational contract demonstrates how the formal norms can be integrated into operational code to generate symbolic, auditable justifications.
AI.result: The implementation shows that Reified Input/Output Logic can be operationalized in Wolfram Language to represent complex legal norms, including temporal and constitutive aspects. The experiments with GPT-4 reveal several systematic failure modes in translating natural language law into the formalism: hallucinated functions, missing temporal scopes, deviations from the specified syntax and semantics, and instances where syntactically valid code encodes incorrect norms. The case study indicates that a contract’s formalized rules can be wired directly into an embodied agent’s control logic, enabling rule-based justifications of behavior.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that understanding an AI system’s internal reasoning is not strictly necessary for governance if its behavior is constrained and auditable via executable legal norms. Computational law—specifically reified I/O logic implemented in a programming environment—can function as a practical governance tool. The author advocates for formalizing those parts of the law that can and should be made programmatically executable, so that legal constraints can directly shape and audit AI behavior in deployed systems.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B on Apple Silicon: Fixing Deployment Bugs and Decreasing Looped Transformer Memory Overhead
summary: Nanbeige4.2-3B is a 3B-parameter agentic model built around a Looped Transformer (LT) that reuses one stack of layers for a second forward pass, adding effective depth without additional parameters. Evaluated on Apple Silicon (MPS), we identify five independent bugs which prevent the released checkpoint from running via Hugging Face transformers out of the box (including a silently-zeroed RoPE buffer and calls to removed transformers cache APIs). Furthermore, we show that fixing these bugs is still not sufficient for agentic tasks, due to the LT's layer-reuse strategy (which effectively doubles peak attention memory) used to achieve parameter efficiency. We thus introduce a chunked-prefill strategy which alleviates the incurred memory-capacity penalty, extending allowable context width by $2.7 \times$ on 32~GiB shared memory. However, even with the reduced memory overhead, we show that patches are required to render Nanbeige4.2-3B usable; resolving both system prompt and MPS-native memory bugs finally allows reliable evaluation on standard MCP and tool-calling benchmarks. On a subset of MCPMark, the debugged model completes up to 30\% of real agentic tasks (up from the original's 0\%), while, on BFCL, it is near-perfect at single tool calls (yet fails the majority of multi-tool tests). We release the patched checkpoint, system prompt optimizer, and evaluation harnesses at https://github.com/johnhalloran321/Nanbeige4.2-3B-mps-fix.

AI.tldr: Paper analyzes and fixes Nanbeige4.2-3B, a 3B-parameter Looped Transformer model, identifying bugs and memory issues on Apple Silicon and proposing a chunked-prefill strategy plus patches to make it usable for agentic tasks.
AI.motivation: Nanbeige4.2-3B is promising as a small, agentic model but is unusable out-of-the-box on Apple Silicon (MPS) and performs poorly on real agentic benchmarks. There is a need to (1) debug the released checkpoint and software integration, (2) address memory overhead caused by the Looped Transformer architecture, and (3) establish realistic performance of the model on tool-using benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors empirically evaluate the released Nanbeige4.2-3B checkpoint with Hugging Face transformers on MPS, systematically uncovering five independent implementation bugs, including RoPE buffer zeroing and outdated cache API calls. They repair these issues and analyze memory usage stemming from the Looped Transformer’s layer-reuse strategy, which doubles peak attention memory. To counteract this, they design a chunked-prefill decoding strategy that segments context processing to reduce memory peaks. They additionally identify and patch system prompt and MPS-native memory bugs, then benchmark the resulting system on MCPMark (agentic tasks) and BFCL (tool-calling), using a custom evaluation harness and a system prompt optimizer.
AI.result: Fixing the initial five bugs enables the model to run but still leaves it constrained by memory and ineffective for agentic tasks. The chunked-prefill strategy extends usable context length by about 2.7× on 32 GiB shared memory, alleviating the Looped Transformer’s memory penalty. Further patches to system prompts and MPS-native memory handling allow reliable evaluation. On a subset of MCPMark, the debugged model completes up to 30% of real agentic tasks (versus 0% originally). On BFCL, it achieves near-perfect performance on single tool calls but fails most multi-tool scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Nanbeige4.2-3B’s initial release is both buggy and architecturally challenging for agentic use on Apple Silicon. Through systematic debugging, memory-aware decoding (chunked prefill), and prompt and runtime patches, the model becomes practically usable and shows nontrivial but limited agentic capability. The authors provide an open-source patched checkpoint, system prompt optimizer, and evaluation harnesses to support reproducible research and further improvements on small agentic models and Looped Transformer architectures.

title: Regime-Conditional Verification: Correctness Estimation for Adapting and Monitoring Safety Classifiers
summary: Safety classifiers deployed with large language models often fail for two reasons: their decisions reflect the policy learned during training rather than the deployer's desired policy, and their performance degrades as deployment traffic evolves. We present Regime-Conditional Verification (RCV), a lightweight wrapper that adapts an off-the-shelf safety classifier without retraining it. RCV estimates, from the classifier's internal representations, the probability that each prediction disagrees with the deployer's policy, and selectively corrects predictions likely to be wrong. The same correctness estimates also provide a label-free signal for detecting distribution shift, enabling a maintenance loop that updates the correctness estimation layer and resorts to classifier fine-tuning only when necessary. Across three off-the-shelf safety classifiers and two benchmark datasets, RCV improves adherence to the deployer's policy in every classifier-dataset combination, catching up to 0.81 of previously missed unsafe content without modifying the underlying classifier. In a deployment study with ten attack campaigns, each a harm category held out of RCV's training, RCV detects every campaign in a dedicated injection panel; in the maintenance census most drift episodes are repaired without updating the classifier, and the fine-tune is reserved for the residual episodes that repair does not restore.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Regime-Conditional Verification (RCV), a lightweight wrapper that improves safety classifier alignment with a deployer’s policy and maintains performance under distribution shift without retraining the base classifier.
AI.motivation: Safety classifiers for large language models often misalign with the deployer’s intended policy and degrade as traffic distribution shifts over time. Retraining or fine-tuning these classifiers can be costly, slow, and brittle, motivating a method that can adapt existing off-the-shelf classifiers to new policies and evolving data with minimal overhead.
AI.method: RCV wraps an existing safety classifier and uses its internal representations to estimate the probability that each prediction disagrees with the deployer’s desired policy. Based on this estimated disagreement, RCV selectively overrides predictions that are likely incorrect. These correctness estimates also act as an unsupervised signal to detect distribution shift. When drift is detected, RCV updates only the correctness estimation layer in a maintenance loop, and triggers fine-tuning of the underlying classifier only when such lightweight repair fails to restore performance.
AI.result: On three off-the-shelf safety classifiers and two benchmark datasets, RCV improves adherence to the deployer’s policy in every evaluated setting, recovering up to 81% of unsafe content that the original classifiers missed, without changing the base classifier. In deployment with ten adversarial attack campaigns corresponding to harm categories unseen during RCV training, RCV successfully detects all campaigns via a dedicated injection panel. During maintenance, most distribution-drift episodes are fixed by updating the correctness estimation layer alone, with full fine-tuning needed only for the remaining difficult cases.
AI.conclusion: RCV offers an effective, low-overhead way to adapt pre-existing safety classifiers to a specific deployer policy and to maintain robustness under distribution shift. By leveraging internal representations for disagreement estimation and drift detection, it improves safety coverage and reduces the need for frequent, costly retraining of the underlying classifier, while remaining effective even on previously unseen harm types.

title: Content Depth Matters in Short-Video Recommendation: Rethinking the Attention Economy
summary: Driven by the attention economy, short-video Recommender Systems (RSs) are primarily optimized to maximize user engagement by promoting videos that capture attention within seconds. These systems inherently favor shallow-content videos that are effective at attracting immediate attention. However, growing evidence suggests that prolonged exposure to such content may negatively affect users' cognitive engagement and mental well-being, raising concerns about the long-term societal impact of the short-video platform. To tackle this challenge, this paper introduces a new metric, the \textbf{Content Depth Score (CDS)}, to quantify the content depth of short videos. CDS measures the extent to which a video is expected to stimulate higher-order cognitive processes, using a seven-level scale grounded in established theories of cognitive psychology and learning. As an initial step toward this vision, we present \textbf{SCOPE-Bench}, the first benchmark for content-depth evaluation in short-video recommendation. Built upon a large-scale open-source short-video dataset, SCOPE-Bench provides CDS annotations for 150K videos, enabling systematic evaluation of RSs from a cognitive-content perspective. Leveraging SCOPE-Bench, we evaluate 13 representative RSs and reveal a consistent preference for shallow-content videos. Moreover, we find that these algorithms recommending cognitively deep content are only marginally better than random selection, highlighting a previously overlooked limitation of existing recommendation objectives. Our code and datasets are available at https://liweidengdavid.github.io/SCOPE-Bench/.

AI.tldr: Defines a metric and benchmark to evaluate and improve the cognitive depth of content in short-video recommender systems, revealing current systems’ strong bias toward shallow content.
AI.motivation: Short-video platforms, driven by engagement optimization, prioritize content that grabs attention quickly, which often leads to shallow content. Evidence links prolonged exposure to such content with reduced cognitive engagement and potential harm to mental well-being, raising concerns about long-term societal impact. There is currently no standardized way to quantify or benchmark the cognitive depth of short-video content, making it hard to assess or improve recommender systems from this perspective.
AI.method: The authors propose Content Depth Score (CDS), a seven-level scale grounded in cognitive psychology and learning theory, to quantify how much a video is expected to stimulate higher-order cognitive processes. They construct SCOPE-Bench, a benchmark dataset based on a large-scale open-source short-video collection, and annotate 150K videos with CDS. Using this benchmark, they systematically evaluate 13 representative recommendation algorithms to measure their tendencies to recommend shallow vs. deep content.
AI.result: SCOPE-Bench provides CDS labels for 150K short videos, enabling content-depth evaluation of recommender systems. Experiments on 13 representative RS models show a consistent and strong bias toward recommending shallow-content videos. Algorithms that do surface deeper, cognitively engaging content perform only slightly better than random selection in this dimension, indicating that existing objectives do not meaningfully favor deep content.
AI.conclusion: Current short-video recommender systems, optimized mainly for engagement, systematically under-recommend cognitively deep content and perform near-random when tasked with surfacing such content. The proposed CDS metric and SCOPE-Bench benchmark offer a foundation for measuring and ultimately redesigning RS objectives to account for cognitive depth and potential long-term user well-being, rather than only short-term engagement.

title: MathForm: Scaling Mathematical Autoformalization with Knowledge Retrieval and Verification-Guided Refinement
summary: Autoformalization is commonly framed as translating natural-language mathematical statements into machine-verifiable formal languages such as Lean 4. However, faithful formalization requires more than translation. Models must map mathematical concepts to the complex hierarchy of types and definitions in formal libraries such as Mathlib, while ensuring that generated statements preserve the meaning of the source propositions. Existing approaches struggle because they rely heavily on the model's parametric memory for library-specific knowledge, while common data construction pipelines often resort to filtering single-pass outputs and lack mechanisms for feedback-driven revision. To address these challenges, we introduce MathForm, an autoformalization framework for constructing verified training data through Mathlib knowledge retrieval and verification-guided iterative refinement. Before generation, a retrieval planner gathers relevant definitions and existing formalizations from Mathlib to guide the formalization generator. Generated statements are then revised using compiler diagnostics and semantic-consistency feedback. Using this framework, we construct FormalVerse, a Lean 4 dataset containing approximately 367K verified examples across diverse mathematical domains and sources. We then train MathForm-8B through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Across six benchmarks, MathForm-8B achieves average Pass@8 rates of 88.06% under Syntax Check (SC) and 72.37% under Consistency Check (CC), outperforming multiple specialized 32B autoformalizers. On the challenging FATE-H and FATE-X subsets, it attains CC pass rates of 63% and 37%, exceeding the strongest specialized baselines in both cases.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MathForm, a retrieval- and verification-guided autoformalization framework that builds a large, verified Lean 4 dataset (FormalVerse) and trains an 8B-parameter model that outperforms larger specialized systems on multiple math formalization benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Autoformalizing mathematical text into formal proof assistants like Lean 4 is difficult because it requires aligning informal concepts with rich, evolving libraries (e.g., Mathlib) and preserving semantic meaning, not just translating syntax. Existing methods over-rely on the model’s internal memory of the library, use single-pass generation, and lack mechanisms for feedback and iterative correction, leading to low-quality or inconsistent formalizations. The authors aim to build a more reliable pipeline that can generate high-quality, verified training data and a stronger, smaller autoformalization model.
AI.method: They introduce MathForm, a multi-stage autoformalization framework with (1) a retrieval planner that queries Mathlib to collect relevant definitions, theorems, and prior formalizations before generation; (2) a guided formalization generator conditioned on the retrieved artifacts; and (3) a verification-guided iterative refinement loop that uses Lean compiler diagnostics and semantic-consistency feedback to revise and correct generated statements. Using this pipeline, they build FormalVerse, a Lean 4 dataset of about 367K automatically generated yet verified examples across many mathematical topics and source styles. They then train MathForm-8B via supervised fine-tuning on FormalVerse, followed by reinforcement learning to further improve formalization quality and consistency.
AI.result: The resulting dataset, FormalVerse, contains roughly 367,000 Lean 4 examples that all pass verification, spanning diverse mathematical domains. The trained MathForm-8B model achieves strong performance across six standard autoformalization benchmarks, with an average Pass@8 of 88.06% when only syntax validity is checked (Syntax Check) and 72.37% when both syntax and semantic consistency are enforced (Consistency Check). These results surpass those of several specialized autoformalization models with 32B parameters. On the particularly difficult FATE-H and FATE-X benchmark subsets, MathForm-8B attains Consistency Check pass rates of 63% and 37%, respectively, outperforming the strongest specialized baselines.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that combining retrieval from formal libraries with verification-guided iterative refinement is an effective strategy for autoformalization. This framework enables the automatic construction of a large, high-quality, verified Lean 4 dataset and supports training a relatively small (8B) model that outperforms larger, specialized autoformalizers on multiple benchmarks. The results suggest that future autoformalization systems should emphasize tight integration with proof assistant libraries and feedback from compilers and semantic checks, rather than relying primarily on a model’s parametric memory or single-pass generation.

title: Simulation-Driven Vehicular Traffic Data Augmentation: Extending Sensor Coverage Through Virtual Sensing
summary: Urban traffic management relies on sensor networks whose spatial coverage is limited by deployment costs and privacy regulations. Machine learning models trained on such sparse data cannot generalize to unmonitored locations and must be retrained whenever the sensor infrastructure changes. We propose a simulation-based methodology that addresses this problem by generating augmented traffic count datasets in which each physical sensor is replaced by a virtual sensor placed at a surrogate location in the road network. Virtual sensors are selected by a graph-search heuristic that jointly maximises vehicle-flow continuity and traffic-metric similarity between the original and surrogate locations, while enforcing a minimum spatial displacement to ensure diversity of observed traffic conditions. We validate the method on two Belgian cities: Brussels, using a calibrated model, and Namur, using synthetic models. The augmented datasets preserve the bimodal daily demand profile and the dynamics of traffic at the observed locations.

AI.tldr: They introduce a simulation-based method that replaces each real traffic sensor with one or more carefully chosen virtual sensors in a traffic model, generating augmented datasets that preserve key traffic patterns while enabling better generalization and robustness to sensor changes.
AI.motivation: Urban traffic models depend on data from physical sensors that are expensive, sparsely deployed, constrained by privacy, and often reconfigured over time. Models trained on such limited data perform poorly at unmonitored locations and must be retrained when the sensor layout changes. There is a need for a way to expand training data and make models robust to changes in sensor infrastructure without violating privacy or incurring large deployment costs.
AI.method: They build a simulation-based data augmentation pipeline. In a traffic simulation of the road network, each physical sensor is replaced by a virtual sensor chosen via a graph-search heuristic. This heuristic jointly maximizes (1) vehicle-flow continuity along the network and (2) similarity of relevant traffic metrics between the original and surrogate locations, while (3) enforcing a minimum spatial displacement to ensure that virtual sensors cover different traffic conditions. The result is an augmented traffic count dataset where observed time series from physical sensors are complemented with time series from best-matching surrogate positions.
AI.result: Applying the method to two Belgian cities (Brussels with a calibrated model and Namur with synthetic models), they show that the augmented datasets retain important temporal and spatial properties of real traffic: the bimodal daily demand curve (e.g., morning and evening peaks) and the local traffic dynamics at monitored locations. This suggests that the chosen virtual sensors are realistic surrogates for the originals and that the augmentation does not distort key patterns.
AI.conclusion: Simulation-guided virtual sensor placement can successfully augment sparse urban traffic count datasets while preserving essential traffic patterns. This approach can help train machine learning models that generalize better across the network and remain usable even when physical sensor configurations change, potentially reducing the need for costly sensor deployments and retraining.

title: Grounding Without Corrective Control: Truth-Tracking Profiles for Large Language Models
comment: 24 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. A six-page methodological supplement, reproducible R script, and constructed data are included as ancillary files
summary:
Recent work suggests that some large language model representations have content or reference. Grounding can secure either without supplying live routes for correction. This paper asks what follows from that gap. An output is answerable when discrepancies can affect what a target- and task-specific arrangement produces, accepts, or withdraws. The arrangement has corrective control only when live, sufficiently independent routes can detect and repair fresh discrepancies. A route profile records which routes constrain the arrangement and how they are related. Those profiles support analysis of truth-tracking: patterned support for representational success.
  Language models are the pressure case; text-only arrangements provide a task-relative limiting case. Text-trained models inherit patterns of testimony, coherence, and prior correction. Where target-sensitive correction survives training, these can supply derivative answerability (inherited constraint); live answerability is the relation supplied by a current route for fresh discrepancies. Fluent failures should follow when a task requires independently informative access to the facts. Self-consistency, retrieval, tools, code execution, multimodal input, and feedback should help selectively. Route-by-task interactions test the distinctions. The decomposition's empirical burden is to predict held-out route--task combinations or improve intervention choice without conceptual refitting. Surface improvement and truth-tracking improvement can come apart.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when outputs from large language models (LLMs) are genuinely answerable and truth-tracking, by decomposing the notion of “routes” of correction and grounding, and distinguishing different kinds of constraint and error-correction that underwrite reliable representation.
AI.motivation: There is growing evidence that LLMs’ internal states can be interpreted as representing or referring to things in the world. But having representations is not the same as being reliably correct or correctable. Existing discussions of grounding often show how models latch onto content but do not explain how mistakes can be systematically detected and corrected in real time. The paper aims to clarify what is missing between mere representational content and robust answerability/truth-tracking, especially for systems—like text-only LLMs—that are trained only on text and operate without direct access to the world.
AI.method: Conceptual and structural analysis: the author introduces a framework centered on “answerability,” “corrective control,” and “route profiles.” A route is any channel or process through which discrepancies between outputs and facts can be detected and corrected (e.g., perception, tools, retrieval, feedback). The paper distinguishes: (a) inherited or derivative answerability from training data and prior corrections; and (b) live answerability from current, independent routes that can catch fresh errors. It then classifies route-by-task interactions and uses this decomposition to predict when augmentations (retrieval, tools, code, multimodal input, feedback, etc.) should or should not improve truth-tracking for different tasks.
AI.result: The paper argues that text-only LLMs, by default, mostly exhibit derivative answerability: they inherit patterns of correction, coherence, and testimony baked into their training data, but often lack live, independent routes for detecting new errors. As a consequence, they can produce “fluent failures”—highly plausible but wrong answers—especially on tasks that require direct or independently informative access to the facts. The framework predicts that adding specific routes (retrieval, tools, code execution, multimodal sensors, user or environment feedback) will improve performance only on tasks for which those routes provide genuinely independent corrective information. Route profiles can in principle be used to predict behavior on unseen route–task combinations and to guide which interventions or augmentations to deploy for better truth-tracking.
AI.conclusion: Having representational content in LLMs does not suffice for robust answerability or truth-tracking. What matters is the availability and structure of corrective routes: how a system’s outputs are constrained and can be corrected in light of discrepancies with target facts. Text-trained language models primarily rely on inherited constraints from their data rather than live corrective routes, which explains their susceptibility to fluent errors. By decomposing systems into route profiles and examining route-by-task interactions, we can better understand, evaluate, and engineer AI systems with stronger truth-tracking properties and more reliable, task-appropriate forms of answerability.

title: Buy the Rumor, Sell the News: When Is News Priced In?
summary: Two old market sayings hold that news is already priced in by the time it is published, and that the rumor is bought while the news is sold. Both place the price move associated with a piece of news before and at publication rather than after it. Whether the claims hold, for which kinds of news, and by how much are basic questions about how fast markets absorb public information. We test them on 4.57 million financial news articles covering roughly 3,000 US stocks (2023-2026). A large language model teacher, distilled into a compact classifier through active learning, assigns each article one of 17 event tags and five attributes; articles are clustered into stories to separate first reports from follow-up coverage; and beta-adjusted abnormal returns are measured around the resulting 1.68 million stock-day events, with 364,405 neutral-sentiment events as a placebo group. Three results follow. First, the price move associated with news concentrates before and at publication: pooled across all signed events, the cumulative move in the news direction by the close of publication day is 2.8 times its value 20 days later, and for rumor-flagged events the rumor day captures the entire move while the subsequent confirmation contributes nothing. Second, measured against the placebo of comparable stocks, markets underreact to numbers and overreact to stories: quantified fundamental news (earnings, dividends, guidance, analyst actions) keeps drifting in the direction of the news for weeks, while soft story-driven news (launches, macro commentary, leadership) gives back its move. Third, news carries width as well as direction: publicity raises volatility before the publication day, and volatility declines once the news is out, because publication resolves uncertainty. The study also produces a table of measured drift for each event tag, usable as a prior in news-conditioned forecasting models.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically tests old market adages about how quickly and in what pattern stock prices react to news, using millions of news articles and a news-classification system built from a large language model.
AI.motivation: There are longstanding claims that markets price in news before it is officially published and that investors buy on rumors and sell on the actual news, but these have not been systematically tested at scale across many event types. Understanding the timing and pattern of price adjustment to different kinds of news is central for market efficiency, trading strategies, and forecasting models.
AI.method: The authors collect 4.57 million financial news articles for about 3,000 US stocks over 2023–2026. They use a large language model, distilled via active learning into a compact classifier, to tag each article with one of 17 event types and five attributes. Articles are clustered into stories to distinguish initial reports from follow-ups. They then compute beta-adjusted abnormal returns around 1.68 million stock-day ‘event’ observations, with a large set of neutral-sentiment events serving as a placebo benchmark. They analyze return patterns before, on, and after publication, and compare across event tags.
AI.result: (1) Most of the price impact associated with news occurs before and on the publication day; by the close of the news day, the cumulative move in the direction of the news is 2.8 times its value 20 days later. For rumor-flagged events, the entire move happens on the rumor day, and subsequent confirmation adds no further price change. (2) Relative to placebo stocks, markets underreact to hard numerical fundamentals (earnings, dividends, guidance, analyst actions), which continue to drift in the news direction for weeks, but overreact to softer, story-based news (product launches, macro commentary, leadership), which partially reverses. (3) News affects volatility as well as direction: volatility rises before publication and falls thereafter, consistent with uncertainty being resolved by publication. The authors also provide a table of post-news drift by event tag.
AI.conclusion: The study validates and quantifies the idea that stock prices largely move before and at the time of news publication, especially for rumor-related news, while revealing systematic underreaction to quantitative fundamentals and overreaction to narrative-style stories. News also affects the width of the return distribution by elevating volatility before and calming it after publication. These quantified patterns can be used as priors in models that forecast returns conditional on specific types of news events.

title: AnchorBench: A Multi-Pathway Benchmark for the Anchoring Effect in LLMs
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026
summary: The anchoring effect is a cognitive bias in which an initial reference value shifts a later judgment toward itself. This effect is well established in human judgment and decision-making, and recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) exhibit similar behavior. However, existing work on anchoring in LLMs typically evaluates only a narrow set of anchor pathways and rarely distinguishes irrelevant from plausible anchors. We introduce AnchorBench, a benchmark for the anchoring effect in LLMs that evaluates multiple anchor pathways under an explicit anchor relevance axis. Across fourteen models, including ten open-weight models and four frontier API models, and a large set of controlled prompts, we find that (1) anchoring is strongly pathway-dependent, (2) plausible anchors usually induce larger shifts than irrelevant ones when introduced through stronger pathways, (3) anchor influence generally weakens as the anchor moves farther from the evidence-supported answer, most clearly on External and RAG, and (4) high task accuracy on the anchor-free control condition (Acc$_{10}$: answers within 10 points of gold) does not guarantee robustness: even frontier API models above 95% control accuracy remain susceptible to plausible anchors.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AnchorBench, a benchmark to systematically evaluate anchoring effects in large language models across different prompting pathways and anchor relevances, finding that anchoring is pathway-dependent, stronger for plausible anchors, decreases as anchors deviate from evidence, and persists even in highly accurate models.
AI.motivation: While anchoring is well known in humans and has been observed in LLMs, prior work has examined only limited ways anchors can influence models and has not clearly separated irrelevant from plausible anchors. This leaves an incomplete understanding of when and how LLMs are vulnerable to anchoring, particularly given their widespread use in high-stakes decision support. A systematic, controlled evaluation framework is needed to characterize anchoring behavior across models, prompt types, and anchor properties.
AI.method: The authors construct AnchorBench, a benchmark that embeds numerical anchors into question-answering tasks via multiple prompting pathways (e.g., in the query, as external context, via RAG, etc.) and labels anchors along an explicit relevance axis (irrelevant vs. plausible). They evaluate fourteen LLMs—ten open-weight and four frontier API models—on a large set of controlled prompts with and without anchors, measuring how model answers shift toward anchors, how this varies by pathway and relevance, how sensitivity changes as the anchor diverges from the evidence-supported answer, and how this relates to baseline accuracy on anchor-free controls (Acc_10).
AI.result: Experiments show that (1) the magnitude of anchoring depends strongly on the pathway through which the anchor is introduced; (2) when delivered via strong pathways, plausible anchors typically cause larger shifts in model outputs than irrelevant anchors; (3) across models, the influence of an anchor generally diminishes as its value gets farther from the evidence-based correct answer, particularly when anchors are provided via external context or RAG; and (4) even models with very high control accuracy (Acc_10 > 95%) remain vulnerable to plausible anchors, indicating that strong baseline performance does not imply robustness to anchoring bias.
AI.conclusion: AnchorBench reveals that anchoring in LLMs is nuanced, pathway-specific, and sensitive to anchor plausibility and distance from the correct answer. High raw accuracy without anchors is not sufficient to ensure robustness to cognitive-style biases like anchoring. The benchmark provides a systematic way to probe and compare models’ susceptibility to anchoring, highlighting the need for more bias-aware model design, evaluation, and deployment practices.

title: Residual Dominance as a Structural Account of Last-Item Reliance in Causal Self-Attention Recommenders
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys'26)
summary: Transformer-based sequential recommenders with causal self-attention often rely heavily on the most recent interaction at inference time, but how this behavior is structurally expressed in the representation used for prediction remains unclear. We combine prediction-time diagnostics with norm-based analysis of the full attention block. First, we show that SASRec-style models exhibit highly localized last-item reliance. We then find that, although self-attention aggregates contextual information, residual addition sharply shifts the full-block representation toward same-position contributions, which we term residual dominance. To probe this interpretation, we use inference-time residual scaling as a controlled diagnostic intervention. Changing the residual strength induces a monotonic trade-off between structural mixing and last-item reliance, while reducing residual strength recovers a subset of final-position misses for which representations at non-final positions already rank the ground-truth item correctly. Our results provide a structural account linking extreme last-item reliance to residual dominance at inference time. The code is publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why Transformer-based sequential recommenders (like SASRec) rely so strongly on the last interacted item, and links this behavior to the dominance of residual connections over self-attention mixing at inference time.
AI.motivation: Transformer recommenders with causal self-attention tend to over-rely on the most recent item in a user’s history, but it is unclear how this emerges from the model’s internal representations. Understanding the structural cause of this last-item reliance can help diagnose, interpret, and potentially fix failure modes such as missing relevant items that appeared earlier in the sequence.
AI.method: The authors study SASRec-style Transformer recommenders using (1) prediction-time diagnostics that inspect which positions contribute most to the final prediction, and (2) norm-based analysis of the full attention block to measure how much different components (self-attention vs. residual connections) contribute to the representation. They identify a phenomenon they call “residual dominance,” where residual connections push representations toward same-position information. To test this, they perform an intervention at inference time by scaling the residual connections up or down and observing the effect on last-item reliance and prediction behavior.
AI.result: They find that SASRec-style models indeed display highly localized reliance on the last item. Norm analysis shows that, despite self-attention mixing contextual information, residual addition strongly biases the final block representation toward same-position content (residual dominance). By scaling the residual connection at inference time, they observe a monotonic trade-off: stronger residuals increase last-item reliance and reduce structural mixing, while weaker residuals reduce last-item dominance and can fix some errors where non-final positions already encode the correct recommendation.
AI.conclusion: Extreme last-item reliance in Transformer-based sequential recommenders is structurally linked to residual dominance in the attention blocks. Residual connections overpower the contextual mixing of self-attention, causing the model’s prediction representation to be dominated by the final position. Adjusting residual strength at inference time alters this balance, demonstrating a causal connection between residual dominance and last-item reliance and opening up avenues for more controlled and interpretable recommendation behavior.

title: Wrong but Useful: Trajectory Value Beyond Answer Correctness in Multi-Agent Messages
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Includes an appendix and an ancillary reproducibility artifact
summary: Multi-agent reasoning systems often use agreement, confidence, or automated scores to decide which messages should shape a final answer. Such filtering assumes that a message likely to be correct is also worth keeping. Yet a wrong answer can contain a useful decomposition, constraint, or scientific principle. We test this distinction with Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation (DHD), a controlled measurement protocol that caches five independently generated messages and replays the same downstream solver, called the integrator, with each message available or hidden. The replay comparison measures a message's trajectory value: whether making the message available helps or harms subsequent reasoning. Across five mathematics and science benchmarks and two openly available model families, gpt-oss-120b and gemma-4-31B-it, wrong-helpful messages appear in every benchmark-model combination. Among wrong-answer messages that change final correctness, more than four in ten changes are helpful in each model. Controlled repeats show that the number of repeatable message effects is unlikely to arise from replay variation alone (p=0.0002). A focused intervention on repeatable wrong-helpful messages finds that the complete message works best, while retaining its reasoning preserves more success than retaining only its answer; the source of the complete-message advantage remains open. Within the same problem, repeated trajectory-value evidence also identifies a better keep-or-remove choice than answer correctness alone. Answer correctness is therefore informative but does not determine trajectory value. DHD measures this missing property and produces reusable labels for learning when agents should listen.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation (DHD), a protocol to measure how individual messages in a multi‑agent system affect downstream reasoning, showing that even incorrect answers can significantly help final performance.
AI.motivation: Current multi‑agent reasoning systems typically decide which intermediate messages to keep or discard based on agreement, confidence, or automated correctness‑oriented scores. This implicitly assumes that messages that are likely correct are the only ones worth preserving. However, in complex reasoning tasks, an incorrect final answer can still carry highly useful structure, such as good decompositions, constraints, or valid principles. There is no standard way to measure how much an individual message helps or harms subsequent reasoning—its "trajectory value." The authors aim to separate answer correctness from this trajectory value and to build a controlled protocol to quantify it.
AI.method: They propose Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation (DHD), a measurement protocol where five independent messages (hypotheses) are generated and then, for each message, a fixed downstream solver (the integrator) is re-run with that message either available or hidden. By comparing outcomes across these replays, they estimate each message's trajectory value—whether its presence improves or degrades final correctness. They apply DHD across five math and science benchmarks using two open model families (gpt-oss-120b and gemma-4-31B-it). They analyze how often wrong answers are still helpful, perform controlled repeats to separate real effects from run-to-run stochastic variation, and run a focused intervention in which they selectively keep full messages, just reasoning, or just final answers to see which components drive the helpfulness.
AI.result: Across all benchmark–model pairs, they find that messages that are wrong but helpful exist consistently. Among wrong-answer messages that actually change the integrator's final correctness, more than 40% of those changes are helpful for each model. Statistical tests (p=0.0002) show that the observed number of repeatable message effects is highly unlikely to be due to replay randomness alone. In targeted interventions, preserving the entire wrong-helpful message outperforms keeping only its reasoning or only its answer, though the exact reason for this advantage remains unresolved. They also show that, within the same problem, aggregating repeated trajectory-value evidence leads to better decisions about whether to keep or remove a message than using answer correctness alone.
AI.conclusion: Answer correctness is an informative but incomplete signal for deciding which agent messages to keep in multi-agent reasoning systems. A significant fraction of incorrect answers can still be trajectory-helpful, improving downstream reasoning and final correctness when made available to an integrator. The proposed DHD protocol directly measures this trajectory value and yields reusable labels that can be used to train systems to decide when to listen to particular agents or hypotheses. Thus, correctness and trajectory value are distinct properties, and multi-agent systems should be designed to exploit helpful structure even in wrong answers.

title: Agent-Orchestration in Autonomous Chip Design
summary:
Recent developments in large language models (LLMs) and tool-using agents encourage people to explore the potential of using agents in chip design. The core question is what kind of AI we really need in such a sophisticated industry.
  To this end, we bring the idea of modeling a chip-design superintelligence as an enormous \textit{AI-organization}.

AI.tldr: The paper explores how to conceptualize and build an "AI-organization"—a coordinated system of many AI agents—for complex chip design tasks, rather than relying on a single monolithic model.
AI.motivation: LLMs and tool-using agents have recently shown strong capabilities in complex reasoning and automation, prompting interest in applying them to chip design. However, chip design is an extremely sophisticated, multi-stage, collaborative process, and it is unclear what form of AI system is most suitable: a single powerful model, many specialized models, or something else. The authors aim to rethink AI for chip design by viewing a chip-design superintelligence as an organized collection of interacting agents, akin to a large organization.
AI.method: Conceptual and architectural: the paper proposes modeling a chip-design superintelligence as an enormous AI-organization. This likely involves decomposing chip design workflows into roles, hierarchies, and communication protocols among multiple AI agents and tools, instead of focusing on a monolithic LLM. The method is to import ideas from organizational theory and multi-agent systems into the design of AI for EDA workflows.
AI.result: From the abstract segment provided, concrete empirical results are not yet stated. The main result is a conceptual framework: defining and motivating the notion of an AI-organization for chip design, positioning it as a better fit for the industry's complexity than a single-agent view.
