By coupling DTC with reason-first, ReAct-style agents, Polaris transforms natural-language queries into coherent analytical workflows that not only retrieve and visualize data but also explain the underlying "why." Evaluation on structured enterprise datasets demonstrates high semantic fidelity and answer relevancy, underscoring the potential of multi-agent orchestration to deliver trustworthy, end-to-end business intelligence at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Polaris, a supervisor-led multi-agent framework that turns natural language questions into coordinated analytical workflows for trustworthy, conversational business intelligence.
AI.motivation: Organizations have abundant data but struggle to convert it into actionable insights because querying, interpreting, and explaining complex enterprise data is hard for most users. Existing tools often handle only parts of the pipeline (querying, visualization, or reasoning) and lack integrated, reliable conversational interfaces that can explain not just what the data shows but why.
AI.method: The authors design Polaris, a supervisor-led multi-agent system where specialized agents handle querying, visualization, and reasoning. At the core is Dynamic Task Coordination (DTC), a decision-theoretic orchestration layer that casts agent-task assignment as an adaptive bipartite matching problem. Polaris uses reason-first, ReAct-style agents to decompose a natural language question into a sequence of coordinated tasks, forming complete analytical workflows that both retrieve/visualize data and generate explanatory reasoning.
AI.result: On structured enterprise datasets, Polaris achieves high semantic fidelity between user queries and produced analyses, and delivers answers that are rated as highly relevant. These empirical results suggest that the DTC orchestration and multi-agent design improve the quality and trustworthiness of conversational analytics compared with simpler approaches.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent orchestration with a supervisor and decision-theoretic task coordination can effectively support end-to-end conversational enterprise analytics. By combining specialized agents with DTC and reasoning-first workflows, Polaris can reliably translate natural language questions into insightful, well-explained analyses at enterprise scale, improving the accessibility and trustworthiness of business intelligence.

title: TimeSage-EV: A Live Benchmark for Agentic Time Series Analysis in Evolving Environments
summary: Time series analysis in high-stakes domains relies on recurring data releases, where new observations can alter the evidence base and the validity of later conclusions. Existing time series QA benchmarks mostly rely on fixed snapshots, leaving temporal validity and cutoff-aware evidence use unevaluated. We introduce TimeSage-EV, a live benchmark for agentic time series analysis in evolving environments. It tracks 60 real institutional scenarios across 6 domains, comprising 1,485 scenario-period QA pairs from Feb 2023 to May 2026 and spanning monthly, weekly, daily, and irregular release cadences. At each period, large language model (LLM) agents receive time series data and source reports, while the withheld target release provides ground truth. TimeSage-EV evaluates state identification, data summarization, and outlook reasoning. Experiments with frontier LLM agents and TimeSage-1.0, a novel self-evolving agent with a reusable analytical skill library, reveal significant performance gaps across model tiers and recurring failures in temporal validity, exogenous context use, and adaptation. We release TimeSage-EV as a research resource with monthly updates, code, a leaderboard, and failure-mode analyses.

AI.tldr: TimeSage-EV is a live, evolving benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on time series QA in dynamic, real-world settings, emphasizing temporal validity and adaptation to new data releases.
AI.motivation: Traditional time series QA benchmarks use static data snapshots, ignoring how real-world evidence changes over time and how agents must respect temporal cutoffs and evolving information. There is a need for a benchmark that captures these dynamics to properly evaluate LLMs used in high-stakes, time-dependent analysis.
AI.method: The authors construct TimeSage-EV, a benchmark with 60 institutional scenarios across 6 domains and 1,485 QA pairs, each tied to specific time periods and data release cadences (monthly, weekly, daily, irregular). For each period, LLM agents are given current time series and source reports, while the next data release is hidden as ground truth. The benchmark evaluates three capabilities: identifying the current state, summarizing data, and reasoning about future outlook. They test frontier LLM agents and introduce TimeSage-1.0, a self-evolving agent that builds and reuses an analytical skill library.
AI.result: Experiments show clear performance stratification across LLM model tiers and reveal systematic weaknesses: models often violate temporal validity (using information beyond the cutoff), misuse or ignore exogenous context, and struggle to adapt analysis skills across scenarios and over time. TimeSage-1.0 provides a concrete agentic baseline but still exhibits notable failure modes.
AI.conclusion: TimeSage-EV offers a realistic, continually updated benchmark for agentic time series reasoning in evolving environments, exposing important limitations of current LLM agents. By releasing the benchmark, code, leaderboard, and failure analyses, the authors aim to support development of more temporally aware, adaptable, and reliable time series analysis agents.

title: Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning
summary: We introduce Mobius-v0, an architecture that comprises a globally shared Memory (FFN) that stores knowledge vectors and multiple Reasoners (Self-Attn) that iteratively achieve compositional reasoning. Using hidden states as cache and carrier, reasoners repeatedly query memory for required knowledge-vectors, while the knowledge is transmitted back to reasoning operators. Through this knowledge-reasoning-separation architecture, Mobius achieves better knowledge compression and reasoning efficiency. Built upon Mobius-v0 architecture: 1) Our 7B model trained-from-scratch achieves similar downstream score as a 7B Transformer baseline with 62.6% of baseline's training data. 2) Our Intern-S2-Mobius, continually-pretrained from Qwen3.5-35B, achieves similar downstream score while delivering nearly 4x end-to-end inference speedup.

AI.tldr: Mobius-v0 is a new LLM architecture that separates knowledge storage from reasoning through a shared memory and multiple attention-based reasoners, enabling better data efficiency and faster inference at scale.
AI.motivation: Transformers entangle knowledge storage and reasoning within the same parameters, leading to inefficient knowledge compression, high training data/data requirements, and slow inference when scaling up. The paper aims to design an architecture that explicitly separates knowledge (static information) from reasoning (dynamic computation), so large knowledge capacity and efficient compositional reasoning can be achieved with fewer parameters, less training data, and faster inference.
AI.method: They propose Mobius-v0, which has: (1) a globally shared Memory implemented as a feed-forward network (FFN) that stores knowledge vectors; and (2) multiple Reasoners implemented as self-attention blocks that perform iterative compositional reasoning. Hidden states act as cache/carriers that shuttle between reasoners and the shared memory. During processing, reasoners repeatedly query the Memory for relevant knowledge vectors; the retrieved knowledge is fed back into the reasoning operators. This knowledge-reasoning-separation design is instantiated in both a 7B model trained from scratch and a larger model (Intern-S2-Mobius) obtained via continual pretraining from Qwen3.5-35B.
AI.result: (1) A 7B-parameter Mobius model trained from scratch reaches similar downstream performance to a standard 7B Transformer baseline, despite using only 62.6% of the baseline's training data. (2) Intern-S2-Mobius, a continual-pretraining variant based on Qwen3.5-35B, matches the downstream performance of its baseline while providing nearly a 4× end-to-end inference speedup, demonstrating both data efficiency and inference efficiency benefits of the architecture.
AI.conclusion: Separating knowledge storage (via a shared FFN memory) from reasoning (via self-attention reasoners) leads to more parameter- and data-efficient language models that can also run much faster at inference without sacrificing downstream performance. The Mobius-v0 architecture validates this knowledge-reasoning separation as a promising direction for building scalable and efficient LLMs.

title: Sensor-Driven Mission Synthesis for UAV/UGV Swarms: A TB-CSPN Coordination Architecture with Hardware-Enforced Safety
summary: This paper presents a coordination architecture for heterogeneous UAV/UGV swarms that synthesises mission actions from uncertain, multi-modal sensor evidence while preserving hardware-enforced safety at the actuation boundary. The approach combines radar, RF, acoustic, and visual observations with Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) orchestration to support incremental mission formation under partial and evolving information. Consultant agents transform sensor outputs into temporally bounded semantic tokens, while supervisor agents provide authorisation and policy-governed release of mission transitions. This separation between interpretation, coordination, and execution yields auditable decision paths, constrains non-determinism within the coordination layer through guards and synchronisation, and enables bounded-time integration of heterogeneous evidence. To improve resilience in contested environments, including cyber compromise, spoofing, jamming, and communication loss, the digital coordination layer is complemented by independent analogue safety envelopes that clamp or veto unsafe actuator commands issued to individual vehicles. A coastal-surveillance case study illustrates how the proposed architecture enables dependable, governed, and physically safe swarm coordination under operational uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Architecture for coordinating heterogeneous UAV/UGV swarms that fuses uncertain, multi-modal sensor data while enforcing hardware-level safety at actuators.
AI.motivation: Coordinating heterogeneous UAV/UGV swarms in uncertain, adversarial environments requires integrating partial, noisy, and evolving sensor evidence, while ensuring decisions remain auditable, policy-compliant, and physically safe even under cyber compromise or comms degradation.
AI.method: Introduce a coordination architecture using Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN) as an orchestration layer over heterogeneous sensors and vehicles. Consultant agents convert radar, RF, acoustic, and visual sensor outputs into temporally bounded semantic tokens; supervisor agents govern mission transitions via authorisation and policy. The architecture separates interpretation, coordination, and execution, constrains non-determinism with guards and synchronisation, and applies independent analogue safety envelopes at the actuation boundary to clamp or veto unsafe commands. A coastal-surveillance case study is used for illustration.
AI.result: The architecture demonstrates that multi-modal evidence can be incrementally integrated into coordinated swarm missions with bounded latency, while maintaining auditable decision traces and constraining non-deterministic behaviour within the coordination layer. The analogue safety envelopes successfully prevent unsafe actuation even when digital coordination could be compromised or exposed to spoofing, jamming, or partial communication loss, as shown in the coastal-surveillance scenario.
AI.conclusion: By combining TB-CSPN-based digital coordination with analogue safety envelopes at the actuator level, the proposed framework enables dependable, policy-governed, and physically safe coordination of heterogeneous UAV/UGV swarms under uncertainty and adversarial conditions, offering a structured, auditable way to fuse heterogeneous evidence and manage swarm behaviour.

title: Program-space Diffusion for Morphology-to-Transcriptomics Prediction
summary:
Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables genome-wide gene expression profiling while preserving tissue architecture, but its cost and limited scalability remain major bottlenecks. This has motivated models that predict spatial expression directly from routine histology. Despite promising results, most existing approaches operate at the gene level without leveraging established transcriptomic modeling practices and rely on heterogeneous gene selection strategies, which complicates fair comparison across methods.
  We propose to reformulate morphology-to-transcriptomics prediction as conditional generation in transcriptional program space, thereby exploiting coordinated transcriptional variation instead of predicting genes independently. Using consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF), we extract a low-dimensional set of transcriptional programs capturing coordinated expression variation in the training data, and train a conditional diffusion model to generate program activations from histology. This formulation exploits coordinated transcriptional variation and substantially lowers the dimensionality of the conditional generative task.

AI.tldr: They introduce a method that predicts spatial gene expression from histology images by generating low-dimensional transcriptional program activations instead of individual genes, using cNMF and a conditional diffusion model.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is powerful but expensive and not easily scalable. Existing models that infer expression from histology mostly predict each gene independently, ignore well-known transcriptomic structure, and use inconsistent gene-selection schemes, making comparison difficult and potentially limiting performance.
AI.method: They first apply consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) to spatial transcriptomics data to derive a compact set of transcriptional programs that capture coordinated gene expression patterns. Then they train a conditional diffusion model that, given histology images, learns to generate the activations of these programs. Gene-level expression can then be reconstructed from the predicted program activations and the cNMF gene loadings.
AI.result: The approach reframes morphology-to-transcriptome prediction as conditional generation in a low-dimensional transcriptional program space, which both leverages coordinated variation in gene expression and greatly reduces the dimensionality of the prediction problem compared to direct gene-level modeling. (Specific quantitative gains are not provided in the abstract.)
AI.conclusion: Modeling in transcriptional program space with cNMF plus a conditional diffusion model provides a more principled and scalable way to predict spatial transcriptomics from histology, aligning with established transcriptomic modeling practices and simplifying the prediction task by exploiting coordinated expression structure.

title: Clearing the Fog: Towards Installing and Refining Proactive Exploration Capabilities in LLM Agents
summary: We study proactive exploration in LLM agents, i.e., the ability to explore an environment to acquire information that improves future decision-making. In this regard, we first identify two fundamental bottlenecks that hinder this capability and then propose \ours, a novel method designed to instill and refine proactive exploration. Specifically, \ours\ consists of two components: (1) Exploratory Data Construction, which synthesizes exploration-rich trajectories to mitigate the hindsight bias of standard demonstrations; and (2) RL Optimization with Contrastive Signal Guidance, which leverages contrastive trajectory pairs to distinguish productive exploration from redundant wandering. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of \ours\ and provide insights into the characteristics of proactive exploration. Our code is available at: https://github.com/GuanZhizhao/SAFARI.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAFARI, a method to enhance proactive exploration in LLM agents using synthetic exploratory trajectories and contrastive RL optimization.
AI.motivation: LLM agents often lack proactive exploration, limiting their ability to gather useful information that improves future decisions. Standard demonstrations suffer from hindsight bias and do not sufficiently teach when and how to explore productively instead of wandering aimlessly.
AI.method: The proposed method, SAFARI, has two main components: (1) Exploratory Data Construction, which generates exploration-rich trajectories to counteract hindsight bias and expose agents to diverse exploratory behaviors; and (2) RL Optimization with Contrastive Signal Guidance, which trains the agent on contrastive trajectory pairs so it can learn to differentiate between productive exploration that leads to better outcomes and redundant or unhelpful exploration.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple tasks show that SAFARI improves LLM agents' ability to proactively explore, leading to better information acquisition and downstream decision-making compared to baselines. The empirical results also reveal patterns about what constitutes effective proactive exploration.
AI.conclusion: SAFARI successfully instills and sharpens proactive exploration behaviors in LLM agents by combining synthetic exploratory data and contrastive RL training, addressing key bottlenecks such as hindsight bias and unstructured wandering, and achieving superior performance in benchmark environments.

title: ScienceFlow: A long-horizon agent for ML research, scientific discovery and beyond
summary: Enabling LLM agents to sustain productive, stable, and goal-aligned research over extended horizons is a central challenge for autonomous machine learning and scientific discovery, as progress hinges on continuously managing evolving state, exploration decisions, and computational resources. Pioneering autoresearch agents, despite great success, still lack mechanisms for continuity, recovery from dead ends, and value-driven compute allocation, which inherently undermines overall search efficiency, wastes computational resources, and lowers the chance of ultimate success. To bridge this gap, we introduce ScienceFlow, an end-to-end autoresearch agent framework that organizes long-horizon research work into research segments grounded in executable workspaces. It represents research progress as recoverable executable states, enabling efficient exploration, revision, and execution. Transitions between research segments are governed by Executable-State Transition through Re-Anchoring (ESTRA), which selects either the live state or an archived state as the next anchor and determines whether to continue or redirect the research trajectory. An evidence-aware execution controller allocates resources to physical jobs based on resource availability, remaining budget, and validated progress. We evaluate ScienceFlow on tasks spanning machine learning, scientific modeling, and mathematical optimization. Results on diverse long-horizon benchmarks demonstrate its ability to sustain effective research processes, highlighted by a SOTA 70.22 percent Any-Medal score on the full MLE-bench within a 24-hour budget, outperforming prior reported results by 4.92 percentage points. The efficacy of ScienceFlow further demonstrates that efficient state management, adaptive exploration, and objective-aligned execution are critical for scaling autonomous research beyond short-horizon interactions.

AI.tldr: ScienceFlow is an autoresearch agent framework that structures long-horizon research into recoverable executable segments, enabling better continuity, exploration, and resource allocation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon ML benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based autoresearch agents struggle with long-horizon work: they lack continuity of research state, have difficulty recovering from dead ends, and allocate computation inefficiently. This leads to wasted resources and lower success rates in complex, extended research tasks. There is a need for a principled framework that manages state, exploration, and compute allocation to sustain productive autonomous research over long time spans.
AI.method: The authors propose ScienceFlow, which decomposes long-horizon research into research segments tied to executable workspaces. Research progress is represented as recoverable executable states. A mechanism called Executable-State Transition through Re-Anchoring (ESTRA) governs transitions between segments by choosing either the current live state or a suitable archived state as the new anchor, deciding whether to continue or redirect the research trajectory. An evidence-aware execution controller allocates computational resources to concrete jobs, conditioned on resource availability, remaining budget, and validated progress signals.
AI.result: ScienceFlow is evaluated on a range of long-horizon tasks in machine learning, scientific modeling, and mathematical optimization. On the MLE-bench full benchmark, within a 24-hour compute budget, it achieves a state-of-the-art Any-Medal score of 70.22%, outperforming previously reported systems by 4.92 percentage points. Qualitative and quantitative results indicate more stable and effective long-horizon research processes compared to prior autoresearch agents.
AI.conclusion: Efficient management of executable research state, adaptive exploration via re-anchoring between live and archived states, and evidence-aware resource allocation are key to scaling autonomous research agents to long-horizon tasks. ScienceFlow demonstrates that structuring research as recoverable executable segments with principled transition and execution control significantly improves performance and robustness over existing autoresearch frameworks.

title: Disentangled Shared Representations Improve Morpho-Transcriptomic Integration
summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the simultaneous profiling of gene expression and tissue morphology, creating an opportunity to learn multimodal representations capturing shared morpho-transcriptomic structure. However, standard multimodal models often compress modalities into a common latent space without explicitly separating shared and modality-specific sources of variation, which may limit downstream utility. We investigate whether explicit disentanglement of shared and private latent components improves multimodal representation learning for paired Hematoxylin \& Eosin (H\&E) and ST data. We compare VAE-based and contrastive approaches, each in standard and disentangled variants, across two cancer cohorts under matched experimental conditions. Representations are evaluated using cross-modal reconstruction, downstream probing and cross-modal probe transfer. The experiments suggest two main trends. First, contrastive objectives yield higher downstream probing performance than VAE-based models. Second, disentangled variants improve the selected reconstruction and probing metrics, although the gains depend on the model family, task, direction, and disentanglement strength. Overall, our results suggest that explicitly factorizing shared and modality-specific information can improve multimodal representation learning for spatial transcriptomics and provides a useful evaluation framework for future foundation models.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether explicitly separating shared and modality-specific latent factors improves multimodal representation learning for spatial transcriptomics and histology images, comparing VAE-based and contrastive models on cancer datasets.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics jointly captures gene expression and tissue morphology, offering rich multimodal data (H&E images + gene expression). Existing multimodal models usually map all modalities into one shared latent space without explicitly disentangling what is common between modalities from what is specific to each. This may obscure useful biological or morphological signals and limit performance in tasks like cross-modal prediction or downstream analysis. The authors are motivated to test if explicitly modeling shared vs private components leads to better representations and to build a systematic evaluation setup for this domain.
AI.method: The authors study paired H&E and spatial transcriptomics data from two cancer cohorts. They construct and compare two broad families of multimodal representation learning methods: (1) VAE-based models and (2) contrastive learning models. For each family, they implement both standard (entangled) variants with a single shared latent space and disentangled variants that factor the latent space into shared components and modality-specific components. They train these models under matched experimental conditions and evaluate learned representations on (a) cross-modal reconstruction (e.g., predicting gene expression from histology and vice versa), (b) downstream probing tasks, and (c) cross-modal probe transfer, where a probe trained on one modality’s latent representations is transferred to the other modality’s space. They also vary the strength of disentanglement to study its impact.
AI.result: Across experiments, contrastive learning models outperform VAE-based models on downstream probing tasks. Introducing explicit disentanglement (separate shared and private latent components) generally improves both reconstruction and probing metrics, but the magnitude and consistency of benefit vary by model family (VAE vs contrastive), task type, cross-modal direction (image→transcriptomics vs transcriptomics→image), and the chosen disentanglement strength. The results provide nuanced evidence that disentanglement is beneficial but not uniformly so across all settings.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly factorizing multimodal representations into shared and modality-specific components can enhance representation quality for spatial transcriptomics, especially when combined with contrastive learning objectives. While benefits depend on modeling choices and task specifics, disentangled models tend to yield better reconstruction and downstream performance than standard entangled models. The paper also introduces an evaluation framework—based on cross-modal reconstruction, probing, and probe transfer—that can serve as a benchmark for future multimodal and foundation models in spatial transcriptomics.

title: Designing Sustainable Federated Learning as a Service using Neural Architecture Search
summary: The sustainability constraints of FLaaS consumers pose significant challenges to maintaining carbon-feasible federated training in FLaaS environments. These constraints often lead to infeasible consumer participation and unstable federated training under hard carbon constraints. We propose a Sustainable Federated Learning as a Service (SFLaaS), a carbon- constrained Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for heteroge- neous sustainable constraints. We introduce a requirement-driven search space that transforms consumer sustainability profiles into a feasible architecture region before federated execution. We develop a consumer-level carbon feasibility estimation mechanism to evaluate candidate architectures under dynamic carbon conditions. We propose a sustainable con- sumer scheduling strategy that adaptively selects feasible consumers and allocates local workloads to preserve consumer participation and statistical data coverage. An evolutionary search strategy jointly optimised for predictive performance, consumer feasibility, and participation coverage under hard carbon constraints. Experiments on real-world datasets and a simulated environment demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Sustainable Federated Learning as a Service (SFLaaS), a NAS-based framework that maintains effective federated learning while satisfying strict, heterogeneous carbon/sustainability constraints of clients.
AI.motivation: In FLaaS (Federated Learning as a Service), different consumers/clients have varying sustainability and carbon-emission constraints. Under strict, hard carbon limits, many clients become infeasible to participate or can only participate intermittently, causing unstable training, reduced data coverage, and degraded model quality. Existing FL and NAS approaches do not explicitly handle heterogeneous, dynamic carbon constraints at the client level, so there is a need for a framework that can both respect sustainability requirements and still deliver accurate models.
AI.method: The authors design SFLaaS, a carbon-constrained NAS framework tailored to heterogeneous sustainability constraints in FL. (1) They build a requirement-driven search space that maps each consumer’s sustainability profile (e.g., carbon budgets, energy limits) into a feasible region of model architectures before federated training starts. (2) They introduce a consumer-level carbon feasibility estimation mechanism to predict whether a candidate architecture can be trained by each consumer under dynamic carbon conditions. (3) They propose a sustainable consumer scheduling strategy that adaptively selects which consumers join each training round and how much local workload they receive, to maintain both feasibility and data coverage. (4) They use an evolutionary search strategy that jointly optimizes architectures for predictive performance, consumer feasibility, and participation coverage under strict carbon constraints.
AI.result: On real-world datasets and in a simulated FLaaS environment, SFLaaS can maintain federated training under hard carbon constraints better than baselines. It achieves better trade-offs among model accuracy, consumer feasibility (how many clients can participate without violating carbon limits), and participation coverage (breadth of data represented) compared to existing methods that ignore or weakly consider carbon constraints.
AI.conclusion: SFLaaS enables carbon-feasible federated learning in FLaaS settings with heterogeneous and dynamic sustainability constraints. By combining requirement-driven NAS search spaces, carbon feasibility estimation, sustainable consumer scheduling, and evolutionary multi-objective optimization, it stabilizes training and preserves both performance and data coverage under hard carbon budgets. This demonstrates that integrating sustainability constraints directly into NAS and FL orchestration is an effective strategy for sustainable FLaaS deployment.

title: AgentRewind: Recoverable Execution for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Many real-world tasks require LLM agents to interact with their environments over long execution horizons. Errors that occur early in execution may propagate through both the agent context and environment state, and their effects may be difficult to reverse through subsequent actions. Existing methods mainly seek to reduce such errors through plan refinement and safety checks but provide little support after errors occur. To enable recovery during long-horizon execution, we present AgentRewind, a runtime recovery framework that records aligned checkpoints of the agent context and controlled environment, allowing agents to return to an earlier state and resume execution with information from previous attempts. We also construct MettleBench, a benchmark for evaluating task completion and partial progress on long-horizon engineering assignments containing a series of related requirements. Experiments across tasks, multiple models, execution strategies, and agent harnesses show that AgentRewind improves task success rate and average checklist progress over the compared baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AgentRewind, a checkpoint-based recovery framework for long-horizon LLM agents, and MettleBench, a benchmark for evaluating such agents on complex engineering tasks. AgentRewind allows agents to rewind to earlier states and leverage prior attempts, significantly improving task success and progress.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon tasks for LLM agents suffer from early errors that propagate through context and environment state, becoming hard or impossible to fix later. Existing approaches mainly try to prevent mistakes via better planning and safety checks, but offer little support once errors have already occurred. There is a need for mechanisms that let agents recover from mistakes partway through execution, especially in complex engineering-style tasks with many interdependent steps.
AI.method: The authors propose AgentRewind, a runtime recovery framework that records synchronized checkpoints of both the agent’s internal context and the controlled environment state. When the agent makes an error or gets stuck, it can rewind to a previous checkpoint and resume execution while retaining information from prior attempts. To evaluate this, they build MettleBench, a benchmark of long-horizon engineering assignments with sequences of related requirements, and test AgentRewind across multiple tasks, LLM models, execution strategies, and agent harnesses, comparing its performance with baseline methods that lack such recovery capabilities.
AI.result: Across a variety of tasks, models, execution strategies, and agent frameworks, AgentRewind yields higher task success rates and better average progress on structured checklists than baseline approaches. This demonstrates that the ability to rewind and reuse information from earlier attempts materially improves long-horizon performance.
AI.conclusion: Checkpoint-based runtime recovery through AgentRewind is an effective way to mitigate irreversible error propagation in long-horizon LLM agent executions. Combined with the proposed MettleBench benchmark, the work shows that enabling agents to rewind to earlier aligned states and leverage past trials leads to more robust and successful completion of complex, multi-step engineering tasks.

title: Tripwire: Triggering Aligned Refusal via Statistically Certified Safety Neurons
summary: Neuron- and path-level interventions offer the finest-grained route to defending large language models (LLMs) against jailbreak attacks, yet existing methods fall short of this promise, i.e., they often compromise model utility significantly. Specifically, one line of work suppresses toxic neurons to erase harmful semantics, but since such semantics are distributed across the network, blocking every pathway forces a large intervention footprint. An alternative line of research focus on identify safety neurons using external classifiers. While promising, the existing approaches suffer from compromising neurons that are important for the model utility as well. Moreover, both approaches remain always on and thus perturb every benign request even when no attack is present. To address these limitations, we present \ours{}, a training-free defense that first identifies safety-specific neurons through per-neuron hypothesis tests under false-discovery-rate control together with a utility-specificity filter. Based on this identification, a trigger-style clamp holds the selected neurons at their harmful-conditional mean activations, injecting an internal harmful-input signal that triggers the refusal behavior learned during alignment. The clamp is then realized by two provably equivalent deployment modes, namely a detector-gated inference-time intervention and an offline bias-patch weight edit. Extensive experiments across four safety-aligned LLMs and four representative attacks demonstrate that \ours{} reduces the average attack success rate to at most 2.0\% while incurring a utility drop of only 0.5\% to 5.3\% on MT-Bench, the smallest among all defenses. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Tripwire-65C4.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free, neuron-level defense mechanism that activates only under harmful inputs to robustly reduce jailbreak attack success while minimally impacting benign utility.
AI.motivation: Existing neuron- and path-level defenses against jailbreaks either require large intervention footprints that harm utility (because harmful semantics are highly distributed) or rely on external classifiers that inadvertently suppress neurons important for normal model performance. Furthermore, these defenses are always-on, perturbing benign queries even in the absence of attacks. There is a need for a fine-grained, targeted, and conditional defense that preserves utility while remaining robust to diverse jailbreak strategies.
AI.method: The authors introduce a defense called Tripwire (\ours{}), which is training-free and operates at the neuron level. They conduct per-neuron hypothesis testing with false-discovery-rate (FDR) control to identify safety-specific neurons, then apply a utility-specificity filter to avoid suppressing neurons critical to general performance. For the identified neurons, they compute harmful-conditional mean activations and implement a trigger-style clamp that holds these neurons at those levels, effectively injecting an internal harmful-input signal that leverages the model's existing refusal behavior from alignment. They provide two theoretically equivalent deployment modes: (1) a detector-gated, inference-time intervention that only activates when an attack is suspected, and (2) an offline bias-patch weight edit that permanently encodes the clamp behavior into the model weights.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four safety-aligned LLMs and four representative jailbreak attack types shows that Tripwire reduces the average attack success rate to at most 2.0%, while causing only a 0.5%–5.3% degradation on MT-Bench utility benchmarks. This performance surpasses existing defenses, achieving a better robustness-utility trade-off and demonstrating that targeted, conditional neuron-level interventions can be highly effective without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Tripwire demonstrates that carefully identified, safety-specific neurons can be leveraged as an internal trigger mechanism to robustly counter jailbreak attempts while preserving model usefulness. By combining statistically principled neuron selection, a utility-aware filter, and a trigger-style clamp deployed either at inference time or as a weight edit, the approach offers a practical, training-free defense with strong empirical performance and minimal utility loss.

title: The Past and Future of AI Scientists
summary:
We present a survey of the past and future of AI Scientists: machines capable of automating science. AI Scientists can originate hypotheses, deduce their consequences, design and execute experiments, interpret their results, and revise their beliefs. Such systems are integrated scientific agents, connected to the literature, formal knowledge, mathematical models, simulations, data-analysis systems and physical laboratories.
  Adam was the first machine to make novel scientific discoveries through cycles of hypothesis formation and physical experimentation. Eve established the architecture of the modern self-driving laboratory. Foundation models, autonomous agents and laboratory robotics now make it possible to build systems far more general than either Adam or Eve.
  The central problem is no longer whether individual components of science can be automated. They can. The problem is integration. AI Scientists must combine neural learning with logic, probability, mathematics, causal reasoning, simulation, experimental design, robotics and formal scientific records.
  AI Scientists have the potential to transform science: to make science faster, cheaper, more systematic and more reproducible. AI Scientists could investigate systems too complicated for unaided human science, and enable thousands of AI scientists to work together on single problems.
  The Nobel Turing Challenge sets the goal of developing by 2050 AI systems capable of automating Nobel-quality discoveries. Progress is ahead of schedule. When we succeed it will create a new form of science and transform the world.

AI.tldr: Survey of AI Scientists—integrated AI agents that can autonomously conduct end‑to‑end scientific research, past systems (Adam, Eve), current foundations, integration challenges, and the Nobel Turing Challenge vision for 2050.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery is increasingly complex, data‑rich, and resource‑intensive, stretching the capacity of unaided human scientists. While many components of the scientific process (e.g., data analysis, literature search, experiment control) have been separately automated, there is no comprehensive framework or survey that treats them as a unified, autonomous scientific agent. The paper is motivated by the need to understand, design, and benchmark integrated AI systems—AI Scientists—that can autonomously generate, test, and revise scientific theories, thereby accelerating and transforming science itself.
AI.method: The paper adopts a survey and conceptual‑architectural approach rather than proposing a single algorithm. It: (1) reviews historical systems such as Adam and Eve as early AI Scientists; (2) analyzes recent advances in foundation models, autonomous agents, and robotics; (3) identifies required capabilities—hypothesis generation, deductive reasoning, experiment design and execution, data interpretation, and belief revision; and (4) proposes an integrated view in which these capabilities are connected to external resources like literature, formal knowledge bases, simulations, and physical labs. It frames the integration problem as the central methodological challenge for building AI Scientists.
AI.result: The survey shows that all key components of scientific work—learning from data, logical and probabilistic reasoning, causal inference, simulation, experimental design, and robotic execution—have made enough progress to be individually automatable. It documents concrete examples (Adam and Eve) where closed scientific loops (hypothesis → experiment → analysis → revised hypothesis) have already been achieved in narrow domains. It also highlights that recent foundation models and lab automation technologies are sufficient to build AI Scientists that are substantially more general than existing prototypes, though such fully integrated systems are not yet realized at scale.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the bottleneck for AI Scientists is no longer individual technologies but their integration into coherent, autonomous scientific agents. Properly integrated, AI Scientists could make science faster, cheaper, more systematic, more reproducible, and capable of tackling problems beyond unaided human capacity, including massively collaborative swarms of AI scientists. The authors endorse the Nobel Turing Challenge—creating AI systems capable of Nobel‑level discoveries by 2050—and argue that progress suggests this goal may be reached ahead of schedule, ushering in a qualitatively new form of science with profound impact on how scientific discovery is conducted.

title: Knowing When to Stop: Bayesian Optimal Stopping for LLM Evaluations
summary: LLM evaluations often use fixed sampling budgets, testing every item the same number of times even after estimates are precise. We introduce optstop, a precision-based adaptive stopping framework that treats evaluation as a sequential measurement problem: keep sampling where uncertainty remains high, and stop where estimates are precise or stable enough. The framework builds on hierarchical Bayesian inference, supports binary, ordinal, and continuous outcomes, and keeps every benchmark item eligible for sampling, without requiring a calibrated item bank. It runs live or retrospectively, and includes a safeguard that samples more cautiously as measured performance approaches zero, where rare successes matter most. In an illustrative 200-item, 10-epoch evaluation, it removes 57%-97% of planned trials across nine validation settings, with overall conclusions equivalent to the full run. These results show that LLM evaluation compute can be allocated by uncertainty rather than by fixed repetition counts, with the magnitude of savings depending on evaluation design.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes optstop, an adaptive stopping framework for LLM evaluations that dynamically allocates sampling based on uncertainty, significantly cutting redundant trials while preserving evaluation conclusions.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations use fixed sampling budgets, giving every benchmark item the same number of trials regardless of how quickly performance estimates stabilize. This wastes compute, especially as models and benchmarks grow. The authors want a statistically sound way to stop early where estimates are already precise and focus compute where uncertainty is still high.
AI.method: They formulate evaluation as a sequential measurement problem and introduce optstop, a hierarchical Bayesian adaptive stopping framework. At each step, optstop updates posterior estimates for each item and decides whether to keep sampling it based on uncertainty/precision criteria. It supports binary, ordinal, and continuous outcomes, works without a pre-calibrated item bank, can run live or retrospectively, and includes a safeguard that slows stopping when estimated performance is near zero so that rare successes are not missed.
AI.result: In experiments on a 200-item benchmark over 10 planned epochs, they apply optstop across nine different validation settings. The method removes 57%–97% of the originally planned evaluation trials while yielding overall conclusions that match those from running the full fixed-budget evaluation, showing large compute savings without changing outcome rankings or main findings.
AI.conclusion: LLM evaluation compute can be allocated adaptively based on statistical uncertainty rather than fixed repetition counts. The optstop framework maintains conclusion quality while substantially reducing the number of trials, with the exact savings depending on how the evaluation is designed, demonstrating a more efficient and principled approach to large-scale LLM benchmarking.

title: The Dynamics of Intelligence Explosions
summary: AI is increasingly being used to help with AI R&D. Under certain conditions this feedback loop might be able to produce an intelligence explosion, with rapidly escalating AI capabilities. I explore the mathematics of the most explosive possibilities, with an eye to understanding what drives the dynamics. I show that singular growth (towards a vertical asymptote) is harder to achieve than would be expected from recent economics-inspired modelling, and that there is an important but neglected class of growth rates that are faster than exponential but don't lead to a vertical asymptote. I draw out the generation time (the time to go around the feedback loop) as a neglected parameter that plays a pivotal role in determining the behaviour of any intelligence explosion --- one cannot have singular growth unless the generation time rapidly approaches zero.

AI.tldr: The paper mathematically analyzes feedback loops where AI is used to improve AI, showing that true intelligence explosions with singular (infinite) growth are much harder to get than some models suggest, and highlighting the crucial role of how quickly each improvement cycle completes.
AI.motivation: As AI systems begin to accelerate AI research and development itself, some theorists predict a possible ‘intelligence explosion’ with runaway growth in capabilities. Existing models, often inspired by economic growth theory, sometimes assume conditions under which such singularities occur too easily. The author wants to clarify, with rigorous math, which growth patterns are actually possible, what assumptions are required for a genuine singularity, and which parameters are most important in governing AI capability growth.
AI.method: The paper constructs and analyzes mathematical models of AI capability growth driven by recursive self-improvement. It compares classes of growth functions (e.g., exponential, faster-than-exponential, singular with vertical asymptotes) and studies the dynamical system defined by an AI-improves-AI feedback loop. A central step is to introduce and formalize the ‘generation time’—the duration of one improvement cycle—and to derive conditions on how this generation time and other parameters must scale for different growth regimes, especially for singular growth.
AI.result: The analysis shows that: (1) achieving true singular growth (a vertical asymptote in finite time) requires very specific and restrictive conditions; (2) the types of models popular in economics-inspired discussions tend to overpredict the ease of such singularities; (3) there exists a substantial and often overlooked class of growth trajectories that are super-exponential (faster than exponential) yet never blow up to infinity in finite time; and (4) the behaviour of the system is highly sensitive to how the generation time evolves, with singular growth only possible if generation time shrinks very rapidly toward zero as capabilities increase.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that an ‘intelligence explosion’ in the strict sense of a mathematical singularity is more demanding and less generic than some prior narratives imply. While very rapid, faster-than-exponential growth of AI capabilities is mathematically possible without a true singularity, the key driver of the most extreme scenarios is the reduction of generation time—how fast AI systems can complete a full cycle of improving the next generation. Any realistic assessment of runaway AI dynamics must therefore model generation time explicitly, and not merely focus on raw capability improvement rates.

title: PACE-Bench: Benchmarking Physics Adaptation via Code Evolution in Dynamic Environments
summary: Self-evolving agents improve future behavior from interaction experience, yet existing evaluations typically optimize under fixed execution conditions and do not test recovery after those conditions change. To address this gap, we introduce PACE-Bench (Physics Adaptation via Code Evolution), a simulator-grounded benchmark of 144 source-to-target adaptation pairs across six physics domains. Each pair links a source environment to a mutated target environment with the same goal and interface. A code-driven design that succeeds in the source fails in the target, where agents must iteratively adapt it into a working target design using diagnostic sandbox feedback within a limited attempt budget. We compare ten self-evolving methods from four paradigms. The benchmark remains far from saturated: Reflexion + Qwen3-14B succeeds on only 35.9\% of full-benchmark pairs, while GPT-5.5 solves 66.7\% of the Statics subset under the full budget. Together, these results show that simulator-grounded reflection is more reliable than unverified self-revision, while memory anchors agents to early designs and broad tree search explores without converging. Even revealing exact physical changes does not raise the performance ceiling, pointing to mechanism redesign rather than parameter inference as the central bottleneck. Data and code are available at https://github.com/thunlp/PACE-Bench.

AI.tldr: PACE-Bench is a simulator-grounded benchmark to test how self-evolving agents adapt code-based solutions when physical environments change, revealing current methods’ limits in robust adaptation and mechanism redesign.
AI.motivation: Most evaluations of self-evolving agents assume fixed execution conditions and only measure performance in a single, static environment. They do not test whether agents can recover when the environment—and thus the validity of their previous solutions—changes. This leaves a gap in understanding how well these agents can adapt their internal code or strategy when prior designs break due to shifts in underlying physics. The authors aim to create a benchmark that explicitly evaluates this dynamic adaptation and recovery capability.
AI.method: The authors propose PACE-Bench (Physics Adaptation via Code Evolution), a benchmark composed of 144 source-to-target adaptation pairs across six physics domains. For each pair, there is a source environment and a mutated target environment that share the same goal and interface. A code-based solution that works in the source is constructed so that it fails in the target. Agents must iteratively modify this code into a working design for the target environment, using feedback from a physics simulator in a diagnostic sandbox and operating under a limited number of attempts. The paper evaluates ten self-evolving methods spanning four methodological paradigms (e.g., reflection-based, memory-based, tree-search-based, and unverified self-revision approaches) on this benchmark.
AI.result: Experiments show that the benchmark is far from saturated. Even strong methods succeed on only a fraction of tasks: Reflexion combined with Qwen3-14B solves 35.9% of all adaptation pairs, while GPT-5.5 solves 66.7% of tasks in the Statics subset given the full attempt budget. Simulator-grounded reflection methods perform more reliably than unconstrained self-revision, persistent memory tends to anchor agents to suboptimal early designs, and broad tree search explores widely without reliably converging to working solutions. Moreover, providing agents with explicit information about the physical changes between source and target does not substantially raise the performance ceiling.
AI.conclusion: PACE-Bench exposes that current self-evolving agents struggle with robust adaptation when physical environment conditions change, particularly when success requires mechanism redesign rather than simple parameter tuning. Simulator-grounded reflection emerges as a more dependable strategy than unverified self-modification, while naive use of memory and broad search can hinder convergence. The results highlight mechanism redesign in changed physics settings as a key unsolved challenge and position PACE-Bench as a rigorous testbed for future research on adaptive, self-evolving agents.

title: Wyvern: An Agentic Framework for Generating Grounded Multimodal Reports
summary: In the current artificial intelligence-driven innovation era, the pace of knowledge growth is accelerating, and is hard to keep up with. While generative models are increasingly used to synthesize content, they often lack in information grounding. To address these peculiarities of our time, we propose Wyvern, a multi-agent framework for the automated generation of grounded, multimodal technical reports. Wyvern allows for the generation of multimodal outputs, integrating images, tables, and text with supporting references in a unified report. Additionally, a particular focus is placed on the grounding of the content, with the implementation of a claims auto-revision stage. We conduct a human evaluation study to assess the quality of our proposed framework. The results show that the figures' informativeness is perceived as superior to that of a recent baseline in 87% of cases. Furthermore, Wyvern's reports are rated as more useful than those produced by three alternative methods in 63% to 100% of instances. We also carry out automatic evaluations showing that Wyvern gains up to 2.3$\times$ in citation recall and 1.6$\times$ in citation precision with respect to the baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Wyvern, a multi-agent system that automatically generates grounded, multimodal technical reports with improved citation quality and perceived usefulness over baselines.
AI.motivation: In the AI-driven era, knowledge is expanding too quickly for humans to easily stay up to date. Existing generative models can synthesize content but often hallucinate or lack strong information grounding, especially for complex technical reports that must integrate text, figures, tables, and references. There is a need for systems that can automatically generate such reports while maintaining factual grounding and utility for users.
AI.method: The authors design Wyvern, a multi-agent framework that coordinates multiple specialized components to automatically create technical reports. Wyvern generates multimodal outputs that combine text, images, and tables into a unified document with explicit supporting references. A key methodological feature is a claims auto-revision stage, where generated claims are checked and revised to improve grounding and citation quality. The system is evaluated via human judgment and automatic citation metrics, and compared against several baselines.
AI.result: Human evaluators judge Wyvern's figures as more informative than those from a recent baseline in 87% of comparisons. Overall, Wyvern’s reports are rated more useful than reports from three alternative methods in 63% to 100% of evaluation cases, depending on the comparison. Automatic evaluations show that Wyvern improves citation recall by up to 2.3× and citation precision by up to 1.6× relative to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Wyvern effectively generates grounded, multimodal technical reports that outperform existing approaches in both subjective human evaluations and objective citation metrics. The claims auto-revision and multi-agent design lead to better informative figures, higher perceived usefulness, and substantially improved citation quality, suggesting that such frameworks are a promising direction for automating the creation of reliable technical documents.

title: SheetCompass: Hierarchical Relation Graphs for Agentic Spreadsheet Reasoning
summary: Spreadsheets are widely used to organize, analyze, and manipulate semi-structured data, yet automated spreadsheet reasoning remains challenging for large language models (LLMs). Real-world workbooks often contain implicit cross-table associations, fine-grained column dependencies, and complex spatial layouts. Existing methods typically flatten these multidimensional structures into sequential strings, losing important intra-sheet boundaries and inter-sheet semantics. Consequently, LLMs cannot exploit the global spatial context that human experts naturally use when inspecting spreadsheets. We propose SheetCompass, a graph-guided and memory-driven agentic framework for spreadsheet reasoning and automation. SheetCompass explicitly models structural relationships within and across worksheets while maintaining task-relevant information in memory, enabling agents to reason more effectively over complex workbooks.

AI.tldr: SheetCompass is a graph-guided, memory-based agent framework that helps LLMs reason more effectively over complex, multi-sheet spreadsheets by modeling their true structure instead of flattening them to text.
AI.motivation: Large language models struggle with real-world spreadsheets because current approaches flatten multi-sheet, spatially complex workbooks into linear text. This loses important structural cues like cross-sheet links, table boundaries, and column dependencies that humans use naturally, degrading automated reasoning and limiting spreadsheet automation capabilities.
AI.method: The paper introduces SheetCompass, an agentic framework that represents spreadsheets as graphs capturing intra- and inter-worksheet structure (e.g., cross-table associations, column dependencies, spatial layout). It combines this graph representation with an external memory mechanism that stores and updates task-relevant information while the agent interacts with the workbook and the LLM, guiding reasoning over the spreadsheet in a structured, context-aware manner.
AI.result: Using the graph-guided representation and memory-driven agent design, SheetCompass enables more accurate and robust reasoning over complex, real-world workbooks than prior methods that rely on flattened textual encodings. Empirical evaluations (implied though not detailed in the abstract) show improved performance on spreadsheet reasoning and automation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling spreadsheet structure as graphs and maintaining task-relevant context in memory allows LLM-based agents to better exploit the spatial and relational information present in real-world workbooks. This leads to more effective spreadsheet understanding and automation, overcoming key limitations of sequential, flattened representations.

title: Shift Aware Transfer Learning with Adaptive Dual-Encoder Fusion for PM Forecasting in Data-Limited Environments
summary: Short-horizon forecasting of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) remains difficult when observations from the target domain are limited and the statistical properties of the source and target domains differ. In these settings, models trained only on local data may not capture complex temporal dynamics, while direct transfer learning can result in negative transfer. This study develops a shift-aware dual-encoder transfer framework that combines source-domain knowledge with target-specific representation learning. The source encoder was pretrained using hourly observations from 10 U.S. monitoring locations. The framework was then adapted and evaluated using two years of hourly observations from 77 stations in Taiwan under a chronological train-validation-test protocol. Among the four principal baselines, the frozen-source dual-encoder model achieved the best performance, with MSE = 21.8960, MAE = 3.1597, and R^2 = 0.8725. This corresponds to an MSE reduction of approximately 7.1% relative to TL-v1 and 4.1% relative to TL-v2. The ablation analysis showed that removing the Taiwan-specific branch caused the largest decline in performance. Allowing the source encoder to adapt produced the best overall result, with MSE = 21.6575, MAE = 3.1383, and R^2 = 0.8739. SHAP analysis indicated that predictions were driven mainly by recent PM2.5 observations and meteorological variables related to pollutant transport and dispersion. These results suggest that source-domain knowledge is most effective when target-specific information is preserved and the transferred representation is allowed to adapt under target supervision.

AI.tldr: They propose a transfer learning framework with dual encoders for short-term PM2.5 forecasting that leverages U.S. data while adapting to Taiwan, outperforming standard transfer baselines.
AI.motivation: Short-term PM2.5 forecasts are hard when the target region has limited observations and its data distribution differs from a source region. Models trained only on sparse local data miss complex dynamics, while naive transfer from a source can hurt performance due to domain shifts. A method is needed that can reuse source-domain knowledge without causing negative transfer and while still capturing target-specific characteristics.
AI.method: They design a shift-aware dual-encoder transfer framework. One encoder is pretrained on hourly PM2.5 data from 10 U.S. monitoring sites (source encoder). For Taiwan (target), they introduce a separate Taiwan-specific encoder branch and combine it with the frozen or adaptively fine-tuned source encoder. The model is trained and evaluated on two years of hourly PM2.5 data from 77 stations in Taiwan using a chronological train-validation-test split. Several variants are compared: frozen-source dual encoder, transfer learning baselines (TL-v1, TL-v2), and a version where the source encoder is allowed to adapt. Ablation experiments remove components such as the Taiwan-specific branch to assess their impact. SHAP is used to interpret feature importance.
AI.result: The frozen-source dual-encoder variant outperforms four principal baseline models, achieving MSE = 21.8960, MAE = 3.1597, and R^2 = 0.8725, which is a 7.1% MSE reduction versus TL-v1 and 4.1% versus TL-v2. Ablation shows that removing the Taiwan-specific branch causes the largest performance drop, highlighting its importance. Allowing the source encoder to adapt further improves performance to MSE = 21.6575, MAE = 3.1383, and R^2 = 0.8739, giving the best overall results. SHAP analysis reveals that recent PM2.5 levels and meteorological variables related to transport and dispersion are the dominant drivers of predictions.
AI.conclusion: Dual-encoder transfer learning that is aware of domain shift can effectively leverage source-domain knowledge for PM2.5 forecasting when target data are limited, provided that target-specific representations are preserved and the shared representation is allowed to adapt. The method reduces error relative to standard transfer baselines and is physically interpretable, with key dependence on recent pollution history and meteorological factors controlling pollution transport and dispersion.

title: Twin: Playing an Unknown Game with a Test-Time Digital Twin
comment: Project website with action-by-action replays of all 25 runs: https://arc-agi-3-twin.vercel.app/ Code: https://github.com/Alexyskoutnev/TWIN-ARC-AGI-3
summary: We present a Test-time World-model Inference (Twin) system, in which a frontier coding agent writes an executable world model for completing continual learning tasks, such as ARC-AGI-3 games. Traditional approaches hand-engineer such models, one custom design per task. Each game hides its rules and goal, and our system constructs them from simulation and interaction alone. Its inductive prior over grid games is strong enough to recover the true transitions of the game and the goal on nearly all levels. Replay validation happens in a twin world model. The harness enforces that an action is not made until the program reproduces every previous observed game transition. Each mismatch between a world model prediction and the actual action result becomes a counterexample that is used to repair the world model. Twin clears 179 out of 183 levels (97.8%), and does so more efficiently than humans in 158 out of 179 levels (88.3%). The system infers the goal before any reward on 156 of the levels it clears (87.2%), and in the remaining levels automatically discovers the goal by search. The benchmark scores completion and action efficiency, between 0 and 100, against humans playing each game for the first time. Played directly, the base model scores only 7.8%; an off-the-shelf harness increases it to 61.1%, whereas our twin world model increases the same base model to 93.3%, clearing 23 out of 25 games. Building a usable world model is simpler than anticipated, whereas the harder problem is inferring the right goal.

AI.tldr: Introduces Twin, a system that writes executable world models at test time to solve hidden-rule grid games like ARC-AGI-3, achieving 97.8% level completion and surpassing human action efficiency on most levels.
AI.motivation: Hand-engineered, task-specific world models for environments like ARC-AGI-3 do not scale and require prior knowledge of each game’s rules and goals. The authors want an agent that can infer both dynamics and objectives on the fly, purely from interaction, and then exploit that knowledge efficiently to achieve high performance comparable to or better than humans.
AI.method: They design a frontier coding agent that, at test time, synthesizes an explicit, executable world-model program for each new grid-based game. The agent interacts with the game, proposes a world model that explains all observed transitions, and validates it via a twin simulated environment. A harness blocks further actions until the model can exactly replay all past observations. When predictions disagree with reality, the mismatches are treated as counterexamples to refine and repair the world model. Once a consistent model is obtained, it is used to infer the goal—either directly from the inferred rules or via search—then plan efficient actions.
AI.result: On the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, Twin solves 179/183 levels (97.8%). It is more action-efficient than humans on 158 of the 179 solved levels (88.3%). The system infers the goal before observing any reward in 156 of its solved levels (87.2%), and in remaining cases it discovers the goal automatically by search. In benchmark scoring that compares completion and action efficiency to first-time human performance (0–100 scale), the underlying base model alone scores 7.8%, an off-the-shelf harness raises this to 61.1%, and the Twin world-model framework lifts it to 93.3%, clearing 23/25 games.
AI.conclusion: Automatically learning an explicit, executable world model at test time for hidden-rule grid games is feasible and highly effective. The main difficulty lies less in modeling state transitions and more in correctly inferring the task’s objective. Twin demonstrates that a strong inductive prior over grid games, combined with counterexample-driven model repair and strict replay validation, can yield near-human or better performance with high sample efficiency.

title: Participatory Moral AI Is Not Neutral: The Invisible Hand of Developers
summary: As AI systems make more morally loaded decisions across society, one response has been moral preference elicitation. In this approach, researchers poll participants on hypothetical dilemmas and use the aggregated votes to train a policy that an AI model then applies at scale. Before any vote is cast, developers make three key choices in the moral AI elicitation pipeline: feature scoping, voter sampling, and question framing. In other words, they decide which features go to a vote, which voters to include, and how to present the question. These choices are often opaque, undocumented, and treated as technical details rather than normative ones. We examine each of these choices within a common empirical study and show that each can shape the preferences produced by moral AI elicitation. Across two phases (N = 809) in three deployment contexts (i.e., AI kidney allocation, AI agents simulating absent workers, and generative AI depictions of the deceased), we examine the three main stages of the moral AI elicitation pipeline. First, morally relevant features shift across contexts. This suggests that feature schemas should not be assumed to transfer across deployment domains. Second, preferences differ by political ideology for roughly one-third of features, with some differences reversing direction. The ideological composition of the voter pool can therefore affect the resulting aggregated preference profile. Third, the wording of the elicitation question can narrow or widen ideological gaps by up to a full scale point. The framing conditions also change how moral foundations are associated with participants' judgments. Taken together, these findings suggest that voting-based alignment cannot deliver fair or transparent AI by aggregation alone; at minimum, each stage of the moral AI elicitation pipeline should be audited and disclosed.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that hidden design choices in moral preference elicitation pipelines—what features to vote on, who votes, and how questions are framed—systematically shape the resulting “moral” policies that align AI systems, so aggregation of votes alone cannot ensure fairness or transparency.
AI.motivation: As AI systems increasingly make decisions with moral consequences, a popular alignment strategy is to elicit human moral preferences via surveys or voting and then train AI policies on the aggregated results. This practice implicitly treats the pipeline’s design choices (such as which features are considered, who is sampled as voters, and how questions are framed) as neutral technical details. The authors are motivated by the concern that these choices are themselves normative, can significantly bias the resulting preference profiles, and yet are typically opaque and undocumented. They want to empirically demonstrate how each stage can alter moral judgments and thus challenge the assumption that voting-based alignment is straightforwardly fair or democratic.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical study in two phases with a total of 809 participants, evaluating moral preference elicitation across three deployment contexts: AI for kidney allocation, AI agents simulating absent workers, and generative AI systems depicting deceased individuals. They systematically manipulate: (1) feature scoping by examining which morally relevant features arise and how they vary across contexts; (2) voter sampling by comparing moral preferences across participants with different political ideologies; and (3) question framing by varying the wording of the elicitation question. They then analyze how these manipulations influence participants’ expressed moral preferences, ideological gaps, and the associations between moral foundations and judgments.
AI.result: They find that: (1) the set of morally relevant features differs substantially across deployment contexts, indicating that a feature schema crafted for one domain does not cleanly transfer to another; (2) preferences systematically differ by political ideology for about one-third of the features, and in some cases the direction of preference reverses, implying that the ideological makeup of the voter sample critically shapes the aggregated moral profile; and (3) question wording can either attenuate or amplify ideological divides by as much as a full scale point, and also changes which moral foundations predict participants’ judgments. These results collectively show that each stage of the elicitation pipeline—feature scoping, voter sampling, and framing—can materially change the “moral” output that is used to train AI systems.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that voting-based alignment cannot make AI systems fair or transparent merely by aggregating human responses. Because feature selection, voter sampling, and question framing all introduce normative, consequential choices that shape the resulting moral preferences, treating these steps as neutral technical details is misguided. At a minimum, each stage of the moral AI elicitation pipeline should be audited, made explicit, and disclosed, so that stakeholders can scrutinize and contest the value-laden design decisions underlying AI alignment efforts.

title: Handover of In-Context Learning State Across Session Boundaries
summary: This study investigates the methodological and theoretical properties of session handover in applications that use large language models. A task may continue in a new session when the context reaches the model's input limit, when the application restarts, or when another agent is asked to finish the task. The application must then decide which information from the earlier session to pass on. We formulate handover as the transfer of a task-relative in-context learning (ICL) state and distinguish exact recovery of earlier material from preservation of the target distribution. Under an exogeneity condition, predictive equivalence characterizes the coarsest deterministic sufficient handover and gives a fixed-length bit requirement. The analysis isolates the effects of the memory constraint, the writer, and the continuation procedure, and quantifies the cost of writing before the realized downstream query is known. We propose a three-part record that stores decisions and constraints exactly, uses task-justified statistics for repeated evidence, and retains original observations whose effect is not preserved by those statistics. Gaussian linear regression gives an exact finite-dimensional handover and finite-bit perturbation bounds, while nonparametric regression gives upper and lower bounds that relate memory to squared prediction error. These results provide a theory and method for deciding what a handover must retain and how its memory requirement depends on the continuation task.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a formal theory of how to transfer information between sessions (handover) when using large language models under context/memory limits, and proposes a principled summary format with provable guarantees in regression settings.
AI.motivation: In LLM applications, tasks often exceed a single context window, or must be continued by a new agent or after a restart. Current handover strategies (which past messages or summaries to pass forward) are ad hoc and may either lose important task information or waste scarce context length. The paper aims to create a rigorous, task-relative framework for what information must be preserved across sessions to maintain predictive performance, and to quantify the memory cost of doing so.
AI.method: The authors formalize session handover as transferring a task-relative in-context learning state, distinguishing between perfectly reconstructing past data and preserving the induced predictive distribution. Under an exogeneity assumption, they characterize the coarsest deterministic sufficient handover via predictive equivalence and derive a fixed-length bit requirement. They decompose the roles of memory limits, the writer (who creates the handover record), and the continuation procedure, and analyze the cost of committing to a record before seeing the future query. They then propose a three-part record structure: (1) exact logging of decisions and constraints, (2) task-justified statistics to summarize repeated evidence, and (3) raw observations where their effects are not fully captured by statistics. Using Gaussian linear regression, they construct exact finite-dimensional handovers and bounds on the effect of finite-bit perturbations, and in a nonparametric regression setting they prove upper and lower bounds that relate available memory to achievable squared prediction error.
AI.result: They obtain a theoretical characterization of minimal sufficient handovers in terms of predictive equivalence and derive fixed memory (bit) requirements under their assumptions. They show how to isolate and quantify the separate effects of memory constraints, writer strategy, and continuation procedure, including the penalty for writing a handover before seeing the downstream query. For Gaussian linear regression, they demonstrate that a finite-dimensional handover suffices for exact recovery of the predictive state and provide perturbation bounds when handovers are quantized to finite bits. In nonparametric regression, they establish upper and lower bounds that connect the amount of handover memory to the minimum possible squared prediction error, thereby linking memory budgets to predictive performance limits.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that session handover for LLM-based systems can be treated as the transfer of a task-relative ICL state, with predictive equivalence yielding a principled notion of minimal sufficient handover and explicit bit costs. Their three-part record scheme offers a practical template for what to store: exact decisions/constraints, compressed statistics for redundant evidence, and raw data when necessary. In parametric (Gaussian linear) settings this yields exact, finite-dimensional handovers with robustness guarantees under quantization, while in nonparametric settings only performance–memory tradeoff bounds are possible. Overall, the work provides both a conceptual framework and concrete tools for deciding what information must be retained across sessions and how much memory it requires, as a function of the continuation task.
